articles.title: Ukraine’s scramble to secure critical air defenses stalls
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — Ukraine is racing to protect its skies from Russian missiles, but it’s running out of options — and money — to source new interceptors.
Kyiv has launched a fresh campaign asking Western partners for air defense equipment and cash amid growing fears that Moscow will dramatically ramp up its missile attacks this winter.
But a series of meetings this week — from an informal gathering of EU defense ministers to a special meeting of NATO ambassadors — all came up empty.
Advertisement
Countries with stocks of PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors for U.S.-made Patriots — ranging from Greece and Spain to Japan and South Korea — are hanging on to their own supplies and balking at giving them to Kyiv.
Despite Ukraine's efforts to get more cash for defense purchases, there is a global squeeze on interceptors as the U.S. is scrambling to rebuild its own stocks after firing hundreds of missiles against Iran. The production of missile interceptors for Patriots and rival systems is also backlogged.
Ukraine’s inability to beef up its air defenses comes as Moscow last week said it was preparing “massive strikes” against Kyiv’s energy infrastructure, with Ukrainian cities already struggling to intercept Russia's daily missile barrage.
“I'm really — for the first time in the last five years — afraid of what [Russia] can achieve in these couple months,” said Solomiia Bobrovska, a lawmaker with the opposition Holos party who sits on the Ukrainian parliament’s defense committee.
Kyiv is growing increasingly annoyed at dwindling transfers of critical weapons.
Advertisement
“We are grateful to our partners,” said a senior Ukrainian government official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. But “it’s an endless, frustrating saga when you have to beg for every single unit” that is delivered.
Out of stocks
With Kyiv’s stocks of Patriots effectively at zero, the Ukrainian government official explained, NATO’s PURL scheme — where allied countries buy critical U.S. arms — remains the “only credible source” of Patriots. In July, Kyiv said 95 percent of its stock arrived through that program.
However, that amounts to roughly “10 to 20 missiles per month,” said Dmytro Zhmailo, a military expert and deputy head of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre think tank, far short of what Kyiv needs given Russia fired 195 missiles in July alone.
Adding to Ukraine's air defense problems, Russia is increasingly deploying upgraded jet-powered Shahed drones which fly faster and lower, making them difficult to shoot down, Zhmailo said. Kyiv is testing four prototypes to tackle the new drones, but for now it relies on limited stocks of expensive anti-aircraft missiles and artillery systems, he added.
“Ukraine has manufacturers capable of carrying out this task,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a social media post on Thursday. “Prototypes have been developed, and work is underway to bring this new weapon to the required level of effectiveness.”
Out of options
Kyiv this week shared its three broad priorities with European countries, the Ukrainian official said, including air defense equipment, investments in the country's drone and missile production and long-range artillery.
Advertisement
Zelenskyy has said Kyiv needs 300 Patriot interceptors to get through the winter. But more broadly, it also wants AMRAAM, IRIS-T and AIM-9X air-to-air missiles, as well as HAWK systems that are particularly effective against jet-powered drones, the official said.
Germany, which is hosting a virtual meeting of European countries to drum up support for more aid on Sept. 8, is expected to announce the delivery of new IRIS-T air defense missiles this month. France and Italy have also promised to supply Kyiv with Aster 30 interceptor missiles by October.
Five of the seven EU countries known to deploy Patriot systems — Germany, Poland, Romania, Spain and the Netherlands — have so far all transferred battery components or missiles to Ukraine. Greece and Sweden have not publicly transferred any, even if Stockholm has funded Patriot-related aid for Kyiv.
Athens and Madrid this week came under pressure to send missiles, with several countries informally raising the issue on the sidelines of a meeting of EU defense ministers in Ireland on Tuesday, two EU diplomats said. However, the meeting ended with no new pledges.
Spain has already delivered some Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, a Spanish government official said, noting it was not ruling out giving more in future. The Greek ministry of defense didn't respond to a request for comment by POLITICO, but its long-held refusal to share comes amid rising tensions with Turkey and existing air defense obligations toward Middle Eastern countries.
Advertisement
At NATO too, “there is very intense lobbying,” one alliance diplomat said. During a closed-door meeting of ambassadors Wednesday, NATO chief Mark Rutte encouraged allies to continue supplying military aid to Ukraine, two NATO diplomats said. While several countries said they were considering new aid packages, there were no specific offers.
Tokyo “doesn’t have any plan to send interceptors to Ukraine,” said one Japanese official, pointing to the danger posed by North Korea. Seoul prefers to focus on “measures to help Ukraine recover peace and rebuild,” a South Korean official said.
Out of money
Even if there were interceptors on the market, Ukraine is strapped for cash.
Kyiv faces a €23 billion hole in its defense budget this year, Zelenskyy said last week, arguing the gap came after the defense ministry brought forward spending originally planned for the second half of 2026.
So far this year, Ukraine has been allocated around €22.1 billion of the €28.3 billion it can spend on defense from the EU's €90 billion loan, said Zhmailo, the military expert. On Monday, the EU will discuss allocating several billion more for interceptors after Kyiv requested more money.
Advertisement
Funding for NATO’s PURL scheme is also on shaky ground, with pledges so far this year running far below Rutte's goal of raising $12 billion.
NATO is currently preparing “four-to-five” new aid packages, with some announcements expected “in the coming weeks,” said a person familiar with the matter. But “we’re a little bit behind,” they acknowledged.
That’s prompting renewed pleas for both cash and interceptors from Europe.
“If they want Russia to win, the answer now is clear,” said Bobrovska, the lawmaker. “But if they want to see Ukraine winning, so we need [more] — it’s a matter of surviving.”

articles.title: Why Russia’s Iskander-M Missile Still Relies on Western Chips for Its Most Critical Functions
articles.body:
- Category
- Investigations
Why Russia’s Iskander-M Missile Still Relies on Western Chips for Its Most Critical Functions
About 78% of the identified components in the inertial navigation system of Russia's 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missile are US-made, an independent analysis has found.
The Independent Anti-Corruption Commission (NAKO) reached that figure after examining the missile's inertial navigation system, a core element that fixes the weapon's position and tracks its movement in flight. The share applies to the components identified within that single analyzed system, not to the missile as a whole.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The parts NAKO traced are not peripheral. According to the commission, the chips perform critical functions—signal processing, analog-to-digital conversion, digital isolation, power management, and memory.
Where the components come from
Two US firms account for most of the American share. NAKO traced almost 40% of the identified US components to Analog Devices and roughly 12% to Texas Instruments, with the remaining 48% spread across 11 other manufacturers.
American suppliers were the largest but not the only foreign source. NAKO's breakdown of the identified components by origin ran as follows:
- American manufacturers accounted for 78% of the parts;
- Japanese suppliers made up 9.4%;
- Taiwanese firms, 6.3%;
- Swiss firms, 6.3%.
Russia's "import substitution"
Moscow has pressed import substitution across its defense industry, and NAKO acknowledged that Russia has replaced some foreign parts—mostly simpler, less sophisticated ones. The commission described the Oreshnik as its most localized missile to date.
Where systems demand high-precision signal processing and data conversion, though, the reliance on Western components persists.
That unevenness, NAKO argued, matters for sanctions design. Rather than trying to choke off every electronic part reaching Russia, the commission urged a focus on the components that specific weapons cannot function without.
Not an isolated case
The Iskander missile is not the only weapon of its kind. On August 10, 2026, specialists from Ukraine’s Defense Ministry’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) demonstrated foreign components extracted from Russian missiles, drones, and other weaponry to Ukrainian diplomats.
As of August 2026, the directorate had identified 5,816 foreign components across 202 Russian weapons systems, it reported, alongside numerous Russian and Belarusian parts.
Among the samples were an American Nvidia Jetson Orin microcomputer taken from a Russian S-71M cruise missile and an inertial module carrying parts from Texas Instruments and Japan's TDK.
A presentation at the Office of the President of Ukraine last week underscored the same dependency. Ukraine's presidential commissioner for sanctions policy, Vladyslav Vlasiuk, pointed to the Kometa navigation module and components of autonomous inertial systems as critical units. The reliance extends beyond electronics to imported rocket-fuel components, carbon fiber, specialized resins, aluminum and titanium alloys, and high-precision machine tools.
Why it matters for sanctions
Russia’s access to Western microelectronics has come under greater scrutiny as its ballistic missile campaign expands.
Since the start of 2026, Russia has fired more than 500 ballistic missiles at Ukraine while also deploying North Korean KN-23 systems.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has assessed that Russia can build up to 1,300 ballistic missiles a year and already holds 600 to 630 in its arsenal. He emphasized that Ukraine's forces are working to blunt Russia's military machine, though he acknowledged that the strikes continue.

articles.title: B-52s Deploy for Bomber Task Force to Australia’s New BUFF Base
articles.body:
U.S. Air Force B-52 Stratofortress bombers landed at a northern Australian air base this week, a major display of the U.S. military’s ability to project force in the Pacific.
Multiple B-52s landed at Royal Australian Air Force Base Tindal in the country’s Northern Territory on Sept. 1, according to official Air Force imagery released Sept. 3 and service officials.
The joint military-civilian airfield near the town of Katherine, which the Pentagon plans to use as a launching pad for operations in the Pacific, has undergone a $1.1 billion upgrade in recent years.
That work enables it to support the deployment of a half-dozen B-52s, giving the U.S. more locations to stage bombers in the region amid China’s growing military might.
The base also houses Australian F-35A Lightning stealth fighter jets and MQ-4C Triton remotely piloted surveillance aircraft.
Australia is south of the U.S. territory of Guam, where Andersen Air Force Base serves as America’s current bomber hub in the Western Pacific. RAAF Base Tindal would give the U.S. Air Force more basing options for long-range missions in the region.
“Operating from RAAF Base Tindal marks our ability to project, sustain, and regenerate decisive airpower across an expanding extended network,” states one photo caption released by Pacific Air Forces. The deployment from the base “deepens our partnership and interoperability” and “highlights our shared commitment to regional stability, ensuring our forces remain agile and responsive in support of a Free and Open Indo-Pacific,” PACAF added in other captions.
It is unclear how long the bombers will be deployed to the region and how many aircraft are operating from Australia. The bombers hail from the 2nd Bomb Wing at Barksdale Air Force Base, La. Air Force Global Strike Command and the Eighth Air Force, which oversees the nation’s bomber fleet, referred questions about the deployment to Pacific Air Forces.
“These missions demonstrate seamless interoperability with our partners and bolster regional security across the region,” a PACAF spokesperson said in a short statement confirming the B-52 deployment to Australia. The spokesperson declined to provide further details, citing operational security concerns.
Multiple wargames on potential conflicts with China have highlighted the strategic and operational value of Australia’s airbases and naval facilities, said retired Col. Mark Gunzinger, a former B-52 pilot and deputy assistant secretary of defense for forces transformation and resources.
“That has been a constant in our wargames: using Australia’s multiple airfields—and not just in northern Australia but in the south too—to generate long-range bomber strikes and tanker sorties to support bomber and fighter operations,” said Gunzinger, the Director of Future Concepts and Capability Assessments at AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies.
“China has a limited number of very long-range ballistic missiles that can reach U.S. air forces stationed at Diego Garcia, in Australia, and other air bases that are not located along the First Island Chain.” Bombers’ longer ranges would allow them to be stationed at airfields even further from China if necessary, Gunzinger added.
Washington and Canberra are increasingly aligned under the AUKUS security pact, which also includes the United Kingdom. The agreement will give U.S. nuclear-powered subs to Australia and allow the U.S. to stage subs out of Australia starting next year. Conceived under the Biden administration, AUKUS has also been embraced by the second Trump administration.
Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Richard Marles met with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Sept. 2 to commemorate the 75th anniversary of the ANZUS Treaty, a mutual defense pact, during which the two defense chiefs “discussed how both nations will continue to advance the alliance and strengthen deterrence in the Pacific.”
“The Secretary noted the alignment between U.S. and Australian National Defense Strategies and also acknowledged that Canberra recognizes the gravity of maintaining a favorable balance of power in the region to ensure that both countries remain safe and prosperous,” the Pentagon said in a readout provided from the meeting. “Both leaders agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises.”
The U.S. has operated fighters and bombers from other Royal Australian Air Force bases, such as RAAF Base Amberley, and the two countries conduct the biennial Talisman Saber, one of the largest and most complex military training exercises held. By 2030, the U.S. Navy expects some 2,300 Americans to be based in Western Australia.
“What we’re seeing is a real increase in U.S. posture in Australia,” said Zack Cooper, an expert on U.S. strategy in Asia and a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. “Sometimes it can take a really long time to build out the infrastructure, but in this case, we’re seeing the U.S. and Australia move pretty quickly on both the air and the naval side. I think it’s emblematic of the step-up in effort we’re seeing from both Canberra and Washington.”
“The U.S. needs to diversify the locations from which it can operate air and naval assets. Australia’s northern bases do that on the air side and the naval facilities in Perth are critical on the nuclear submarine side,” he added.
Equipping a base to handle large bombers with heavy payloads is no small task: runways must be long, sturdy, and adequate, with ramp space, fuel infrastructure, and safe weapons storage facilities.
“That can all drive some considerable investment in airfields, which Australia has made and continues to invest in to bolster regional deterrence,” Gunzinger said.

articles.title: UK preparing to pierce Moscow air defenses with missiles, drones — opposition politician
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 4. /TASS/. Vladimir Zelensky’s statements about the insecurity of Russian airspace suggest that the UK is preparing to breach Moscow’s air defense network through the mass use of ballistic missiles and long-range drones, Viktor Medvedchuk, head of the Other Ukraine movement and former leader of the banned Opposition Platform - For Life party, said.
"The UK is preparing to breach Moscow’s air defense network through the mass use of ballistic missiles and long-range drones. After Zelensky threatened to 'close the sky' over Russia and made it clear that drones would strike civilian aircraft in Russian airspace, the question arises: where does this boldness come from? <...> Where did he get the drones and other weapons to threaten the whole world?" he wrote in an article posted on the movement’s website.
Medvedchuk added that "over several years, the UK has developed a production and testing base for the mass manufacture of reconnaissance and long-range drones, created a mechanism for transferring Ukrainian combat experience to its own industry and, at the same time, established supply chains for engines, warheads, fuel, electronics and other components of missile weapons."
According to Medvedchuk, "former and current high-ranking British and Ukrainian politicians, military personnel and intelligence chiefs are directly involved in managing this system."
"The capabilities and expertise that have been accumulated now allow London, through Ukrainian industrial and military infrastructure, to move from the mass use of long-range drones to the serial production of cruise and ballistic missiles. Against this backdrop, massive attempts to overcome Moscow’s air defense network in the summer of 2026 can be viewed both as strikes and as practical intelligence gathering on the system’s capabilities, the nature of its response and its saturation limits, ahead of a possible expansion in the use of more sophisticated long-range assets that the UK is deliberately producing on a mass scale," Medvedchuk concluded.

articles.title: Agents of chaos: Zelensky’s security services trade accusations after Kiev gunfights
articles.body:
Agents of chaos: Zelensky’s security services trade accusations after Kiev gunfights
The gang-warfare-style clash between Ukrainian security agencies that left three troops shot in Kiev and shocked the country is being spun into competing narratives by the rival parties involved.
Depending on which one of Vladimir Zelensky’s security agencies is speaking, the central figure in the conflict is either a hired gun working for Moscow, or a brave Ukrainian combat officer who was illegally detained for over a week by rogue Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) agents.
What triggered the scandal?
The gunfight on Wednesday morning followed the disappearance on August 23 of Stepan Kaplunov, a reported white supremacist and senior officer in the so-called Russian Volunteer Corps (RDK), a militia commanded by notorious neo-Nazi Denis “White Rex” Kapustin, under the patronage of the Ukrainian Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR).
This week, armed SBU and HUR combat units exchanged gunfire in eastern Kiev, in what was later revealed to have been a standoff over an alleged SBU search of the missing RDK officer’s apartment.
What excuses has the SBU offered for taking the HUR’s man?
On Thursday, as the scandal over the shooting escalated, the SBU accused Kaplunov of participating in a Russian government plot to assassinate a “leader of Russian opposition movement” on Ukraine’s Independence Day, which was marked on August 24.
The agency released a video in which Kaplunov, wearing sunglasses, “confessed” to cooperating with Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), along with several screenshots it claimed had been taken from a messaging app on his phone.
Despite claiming to have foiled the alleged plot, the SBU said it chose not to seek Kaplunov’s formal arrest – a striking admission given that he was effectively being accused of treason.
What did Kaplunov claim he discussed with the “Russians”?
If authentic, the screenshots show the RDK officer – wanted for terrorism in Russia – discussing contract killings in Ukraine.
A test job worth $50,000 targeting “not a general or a politician” could have secured him a retainer that would pay him as much as $300,000 per week, his interlocutor wrote.
The alleged Russian connection was described as a “businessman from border areas” who was the son of someone important, “deals with FSB, etc.” and knew the client.
Where is Kaplunov now?
Kaplunov is presumably at a HUR safehouse, having been released after the debacle erupted across social media. In keeping with standard PR procedure, he subsequently gave an interview to a Ukrainian media outlet.
A decorated officer who has fought with Ukrainian units since 2014 and joined the RDK in 2023, where he serves as the RDK’s deputy commander for combat operations, Kaplunov now claims that the SBU had forced the confession from him, to manufacture legal grounds for searching his apartment.
He claims to have spent ten days in two secret SBU detention facilities, bound, blindfolded, and held incommunicado. He credited a HUR formation nicknamed “Timur’s special unit” – reportedly an umbrella structure for the RDK and several other militia groups working for military intelligence – with securing his release “by force.”
All three personnel injured in the shooting were Timur’s men, Kaplunov said.
“Timur” is the callsign of a man Kaplunov identified as Dmitry Ivanov. He stressed that Ivanov, rather than White Rex, is his direct commander.
“We are all a big family, and ‘Timur’ himself, our commander, will never leave anyone behind, not a soldier nor a commander, he will stand up for everyone,” Kaplunov said.
He blamed “historic competition” between the SBU and HUR for the confrontation and alleged that his “abduction” had been intended as a way to get to Ivanov.
What has the HUR said?
HUR has warned it is being targeted by a smear campaign and urged journalists who receive “dubious information” to report the leaks to law enforcement.
In an interview while wearing a face mask, “Timur,” accused the SBU of unlawfully detaining Kaplunov. He claimed that HUR personnel and the SBU’s Alfa commando unit had peacefully resolved the confrontation before another group of SBU agents arrived at the scene and opened fire.
Were there any repercussions for the agencies?
An embarrassed Zelensky, facing military, economic, demographic, and reputational collapse, fired Oleg Khramov from his position as head of the SBU section responsible for protecting state secrets, although it was not immediately clear whether he had any involvement in the scandal.
Both agencies have suffered a serious reputational blow for the second time this year.
Earlier, Ukrainian investigators accused an active HUR operative and a police officer reportedly serving clandestinely for the SBU of masterminding the Monaco bombing that seriously injured exiled Ukrainian businessman Vadim Ermolaev and members of his family in June.
The principal perpetrator was allegedly murdered by the masterminds after she returned to Ukraine.
Are SBU and HUR rivals?
Both agencies were overhauled with CIA assistance following the Western-backed armed coup in Kiev in 2014, according to media reports.
The SBU is currently run by Aleksandr Poklad, the agency’s acting head and former deputy head, whose promotion has yet to be confirmed by parliament.
Kirill Budanov, now the head of Zelensky’s office, previously commanded HUR before a corruption scandal forced the Ukrainian leader’s previous chief of staff, Andrey Yermak, to resign last year.
Budanov and Poklad reportedly have had strong personal animosity since 2022, when the SBU summarily executed banker Denis Kireev, an undercover HUR agent. Poklad allegedly orchestrated the killing.
Is Zelensky in control of SBU and HUR?
Zelensky’s ability to maintain control over Ukraine’s competing centers of power remains in question. His presidential term expired in 2024, and he has remained in office under martial law without holding another election.
The Ukrainian government has been battered by corruption allegations, with Western-backed anti-graft investigators regularly bringing cases against people close to Zelensky.
In the most recent example, last month a deputy head of Zelensky’s office was accused of laundering several bags of cash to pay bail for a former energy minister who himself faces graft allegations in a separate case.
The Ukrainian military is also under increasing strain as Zelensky has failed to secure additional supplies of Patriot interceptor missiles, the weapons Kiev badly needs to intercept Russian ballistic missiles.
Despite the shortage, he ordered mass strikes in July on Russian cargo ships and retail warehouses, prompting overwhelming retaliatory strikes.
This week, Zelensky also threatened foreign airlines operating in Russia, claiming that Russian airspace belongs to Ukrainian kamikaze drones now.
With the situation rapidly unraveling, it remains unclear what people trained to spy, sabotage, abduct, and kill on behalf of the state might choose to do next.

articles.title: Finland ran Europe’s largest civil defense drill since World War II inside a shelter carved under a sports arena
articles.body:
Finland shut more than 2,000 people into a rock-hewn shelter that is normally a sports hall in Kuopio on 2 September, with some remaining overnight to practice operating the facility, the Associated Press reported. The two-day exercise, Shelter 2026, was the largest civil defense drill in Europe since World War II, by AP's account. Its scenario had cyberattacks cutting power and water while the threat of Russian missile strikes grew.
What two hours underground exposed
Three colleges got the alarm at 11:30 on 2 September, and students had about half an hour to reach the shelter, called Luola, or the Cave, Yle reported that evening. Staff barred the doors behind them. Partitions divided the sports hall into rooms of about 200 people. There were not enough beds, so people rested in shifts, and 60 dry toilets served everyone. The internet worked poorly, and the air grew heavy after an hour. The site holds up to 7,000 people under emergency law.
Antti Haataja, preparedness chief at the North Savo Rescue Department, said the move underground went calmly and faster than he expected. A real emergency would put those inside to work, he added, including emptying the toilets. More than a hundred people stayed through the night into 3 September, Yle said, while AP described hundreds sleeping on trestle beds.
Finland ends nuclear weapons ban as parliament approves major NATO-aligned defense shift
Finland is reading Ukraine's experience
Retired Finnish Army Colonel Asko Muhonen, who organized the drill, said Finland has to learn from Ukraine, where people sometimes have only minutes to reach a metro station. What matters is cover they can actually get to, not a shelter that survives a nuclear blast. Ukraine's parliament is advancing a Finnish-style bill that would put one within 10 minutes of everyone.
Dmytro Untila, 20, a Ukrainian student in Kuopio, was at home in Odesa when Russian missiles hit the city on 24 February 2022, and waited the strike out in his building's entrance hall, having nowhere better to go. Training like this would have helped in Ukraine, he said, "because nobody knew this could happen."
The pressure Finland and its neighbors are drilling against
Finland shares more than 1,300 km of border with Russia and joined NATO with Sweden after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Shelters answer only part of the pressure. Russia is running a campaign of sabotage across Europe, Western officials say, a Russian aircraft is suspected of having entered Finnish airspace on 20 August, and US intelligence has warned that Poland and the Baltic states may face wider Russian hybrid attacks for backing Kyiv.

articles.title: Japan and Germany are forgetting the lessons of 1945
articles.body:
Japan and Germany are forgetting the lessons of 1945
The anniversary of victory over militarist Japan is more than a commemoration of a distant war. It is an opportunity to ask uncomfortable questions: What exactly was defeated in 1945 and what lessons were meant to survive the victory?
What was supposed to end in 1945?
Japan’s surrender ended a catastrophic war in Asia and the Pacific. Germany’s defeat ended an equally catastrophic war in Europe. In both cases, military power had ceased to be merely an instrument of state policy and had become a force shaping policy itself. Countries were destroyed and tens of millions were dead as a consequence.
After the war, Japan was forced to embraced a high degree of military self-restraint, symbolized by Article 9 of its constitution and by the deliberately defensive character of its armed forces. Germany followed a different path but reached a similar conclusion: Military power requires strict limits and could not be treated as the normal measure of national strength.
Neither country ended up completely defenseless. Both retained armed forces and entered alliance structures. But for decades, there was an underlying recognition that more weapons did not necessarily mean more security.
Today, that recognition is fading. Japan is undertaking its most extensive military buildup since World War II. Germany is carrying out the most consequential rearmament of its postwar history. Both are increasing military spending, expanding defense-industrial capacity, acquiring more powerful strike capabilities, and deepening strategic cooperation. More ominously, both are reassessing their relationship with nuclear weapons.
The justification is simple. The Japanese are told to fear China. The Germans are told to fear Russia.
But what if these threats are being systematically inflated – and politically manufactured? What if the preparations supposedly intended to prevent war are making a larger war increasingly likely?
Japan is being told to fear China
Japan’s transformation is historically significant, because its postwar restraint was a conscious reaction to the disaster of the first half of the 20th century. Today, however, restraint is increasingly presented as an obsolete luxury in an age of geopolitical competition.
Japan is expanding its defense budget, strengthening its naval and air capabilities, acquiring long-range missiles, and developing what it calls “counterstrike capabilities.” It is strengthening its military infrastructure and integrating more closely into wider regional military planning. All of this is still framed as defensive measures, but that doesn’t change the fact that Japan is becoming a powerful military actor.
The relentlessly repeated justification is that China is growing stronger, therefore Japan must rearm. China is expanding its naval forces, therefore Japan must expand its own. China possesses increasingly sophisticated missiles, therefore Japan requires long-range strike capabilities.
But this narrative usually omits the strategic environment from which China’s own military policies emerge.
China is not surrounded by Chinese military bases. Instead, it faces a dense US-centered network of bases, alliances, intelligence systems, and military partnerships operating along its maritime periphery. US forces are stationed in Japan and elsewhere across the region. Japan is expanding its own military role and acquiring new offensive-range capabilities. Beijing’s response to this environment is then cited as proof that the original buildup was necessary, creating a vicious cycle of artificial reasoning.
China, like any major power, does pursue its own interests and take part in the global competition for influence. But the idea that China is simply a disguised aggressor waiting for an opportunity to attack Japan ignores both the elementary logic of power politics and Chinese strategic culture.
Why would China deliberately initiate a major war against Japan, knowing that this could bring it into direct conflict with the US and its allies? The more plausible scenario is the opposite, that China will increasingly prepare for a conflict because it sees one being prepared against it.
Germany is being told to fear Russia
Germany is undergoing a parallel transformation. The army is expanding, military procurement is accelerating, arms production is being encouraged, and Germany is openly aspiring to a much larger role in EU military security.
The entire project rests upon a single dominant assumption: Russia is preparing to threaten Europe, and Europe must therefore prepare for war with Russia. Every day, the Europeans are being told that Russia intends to attack Germany or conquer Europe. These claims are absurd.
Russia’s strategic concerns have long centered on the military configuration along its borders and the expansion of hostile infrastructure toward them. These concerns are being consistently ignored, and all it does is show an unwillingness to understand how Moscow calculates risk.
The dangerous habit of contemporary Western policy is to assign cause and effect selectively. NATO’s expansion and military buildup are described as defensive. Russia’s response is described as proof of inherent aggression. More NATO deployments become necessary because of that response. Another example of circular logic.
Portraying Russia as an inherently expansionist force with no intelligible security interests creates the intellectual conditions in which permanent confrontation becomes inevitable. And permanent confrontation is increasingly becoming the organizing principle of German policy.
China and Russia have become indispensable threats for those advocating a historic expansion of Japanese and German military power. Without the Chinese threat, Japan’s transformation would be much harder to justify. Without the Russian threat, Germany’s rearmament would lose its central political rationale.
An external threat is useful to unlock budgets, strengthen arms industries, create political urgency, and marginalize those who ask whether another course is possible. But history repeatedly demonstrates that exaggerated threats can produce genuine catastrophes.
From rearmament to nuclear strategy
The nuclear dimension makes the parallel German-Japanese rearmament even more disturbing.
Germany has long taken part in NATO’s nuclear-sharing arrangements, but discussion is now moving beyond passive acceptance of an existing framework. Berlin is increasingly involved in debates about a broader European nuclear architecture and closer strategic coordination with France. The question is no longer merely whether Germany lives under an allied nuclear umbrella, but how deeply it should take part in planning and arrangements surrounding nuclear deterrence.
Japan’s case is even more historically charged. The only country to have suffered nuclear attacks, Japan built an important part of its postwar identity around the Three Non-Nuclear Principles: not possessing, producing, or permitting the introduction of nuclear weapons. Now, questions regarding nuclear sharing, extended deterrence, and the practical limits of Japan’s non-nuclear commitments are being discussed more openly than before.
This should concern the entire world. Once countries with Germany’s and Japan’s histories begin moving closer to nuclear strategy, a critical psychological barrier is weakened. Nuclear weapons become increasingly normalized as instruments of security policy rather than recognized for what they are: weapons whose actual use would represent a failure of civilization on an unimaginable scale.
Berlin and Tokyo are drawing closer
In March, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius proposed a Reciprocal Access Agreement with Japan during talks with his counterpart, Shinjiro Koizumi.
This agreement would reduce legal and bureaucratic obstacles to the movement of German and Japanese military personnel onto each other’s territory, facilitating joint training, exercises, and potentially operations.
The proposal would give the Berlin-Tokyo military relationship a more permanent operational structure. Germany has already increased its military activity in the Indo-Pacific through deployments and exercises; a reciprocal access framework would make cooperation easier and more routine.
The symbolism is difficult to miss: Countries whose military histories were forcibly ended in 1945 are now building new structures for military access, deployment, and cooperation with each other.
And growing pressure generates resistance. Military blocs generate opposing alignments. The world is once again being divided into increasingly rigid strategic camps – and the countries that spent decades demonstrating the value of military restraint are now helping accelerate this process.
The lesson the world should draw from 1945
Military strength itself is not the problem. States have legitimate security interests and legitimate reasons to maintain capable armed forces. The decisive question is what political leadership does with that power. A strong military under prudent leadership can deter conflict. A rapidly expanding military under leadership convinced that confrontation is inevitable can accelerate it.
China, Russia, Japan, and Germany all have legitimate security concerns. So do their neighbors.
The task of serious statecraft is not to declare one side’s fears legitimate and another’s imaginary. It is to prevent competing security concerns from becoming a machinery of permanent escalation.
Eighty-one years after victory in 1945, Japan and Germany should remember that lesson particularly well. Their postwar restraint was not weakness – it was an understanding born from catastrophe.
Today, Japan is rearming against a supposedly inevitable Chinese threat. Germany is rearming against a supposedly inevitable Russian threat. Both are moving closer to nuclear strategy. Both are expanding military partnerships. Both are being told that there is no alternative.
This is perhaps the most dangerous phrase in international politics. There is always an alternative before war begins.

articles.title: Europe weighs solutions to curtail Russia’s growing hybrid warfare
articles.body:
Russia’s suspected sabotage campaign across Europe appears to be gathering pace again, confronting governments with a problem they have struggled to solve since the start of the war in Ukraine: how to impose a meaningful cost on Moscow for attacks that remain deliberately below the threshold of conventional war.
Over the past month alone, an explosives-laden drone was discovered next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport, Poland has faced suspected acts of sabotage, and a string of unexplained explosions and fires have hit defence facilities supplying Ukraine across Europe.
The attacks, aimed at sowing chaos and undermining support for Ukraine, vary widely in their ambition and sophistication, but share a common feature: they are often difficult to trace conclusively back to Moscow.
That ambiguity is built into the way the operations are organised. Russian intelligence services have shifted away from relying primarily on professional operatives dispatched across Europe. Instead, suspected saboteurs are increasingly recruited remotely, including through Telegram channels, and paid in cryptocurrency to carry out individual tasks – allowing the Russian intelligence officers directing them to remain safely at home.
The pattern was evident in Denmark this week, where authorities warned that Moscow was recruiting Danish citizens to carry out sabotage against defence companies with ties to Ukraine.
But the growing scale of the attacks, and the speed with which European governments are now prepared to point the finger at Moscow, suggest the mood may be changing.
When an incendiary parcel burst into flames at DHL’s Leipzig hub in July 2024, it took about nine months before German investigators reported a concrete link to the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency.
This time, Berlin moved far faster. Within days of the second incident at Leipzig airport, German officials publicly blamed Moscow – a sign both of growing confidence in identifying Russian operations and diminishing patience with what officials see as an increasingly brazen campaign of sabotage.
Yet while Berlin has become quicker to point the finger at Moscow, its punishment for now has followed a more cautious path.
Germany’s response to the failed Leipzig drone attack appeared calibrated to keep tensions in check, underscoring the harder question of what Europe can actually do beyond sanctions and diplomatic expulsions without risking a direct military confrontation.
Berlin announced the closure of a Russian cultural centre and a Russian consulate, prompting Moscow to shut down the already gutted Goethe-Institut – a measured retaliation rather than a real escalation.
Europe’s room for retaliation is also constrained by the powers given to its intelligence agencies. Unlike the CIA, many European services are primarily tasked with collecting intelligence and have far less latitude to conduct covert operations abroad. That leaves governments with relatively few tools between diplomatic and economic punishment on one end of the spectrum and overt military action on the other. To counter the shortcoming, several EU states, including the Netherlands, have recently put forward bills that would greatly expand the surveillance powers of the country’s intelligence agencies
One area where Europe can point to more tangible action is its growing willingness to detain vessels linked to Russia’s shadow fleet. On Wednesday, Norwegian authorities seized a Russian vessel in the Arctic archipelago of Svalbard at Ukraine’s request.
But critics argue that such measures are still not enough to deter Moscow.
“Every time we do nothing, we invite Putin to continue,” said one EU lawmaker, speaking on condition of anonymity.
That argument has been made most forcefully by Poland and the Baltic states, which have consistently pushed their western European allies to take a harder line against Moscow.
“Hybrid war is not just a nuisance on the internet,” the Polish foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, said on Thursday. “Hybrid war means assassination squads, it means arsonists, it means blowing up moving trains, like in Poland, it means breaches of airspace with drones and cruise missiles.”
“We need to convince Putin that such actions are not for free,” he added.
At the same time, Sikorski also appeared to acknowledge, somewhat jokingly, the limits of Europe’s existing toolkit. Recalling Poland’s response to previous suspected Russian operations, he said: “Every time Russia committed arson or tried to blow up a moving train … I closed one Russian consulate, but I ran out of consulates to close.”
Jakub Krupa contributed reporting

articles.title: Ukraine says it struck a Bastion in Crimea, the launcher Russia pairs Zircon and Oniks missiles on
articles.body:
On 4 September, Ukraine's military intelligence agency HUR published drone footage of an August operation against a Russian coastal missile launcher in occupied Crimea, it said on Telegram. Its special unit Group 13 struck the launcher and hit fuel trucks and a command vehicle on the peninsula in the same operation.
What HUR says its operators hit
The target was a Bastion, the carrier of Zircon and Oniks missiles. Russia uses those missiles for terrorist strikes against Ukraine, HUR said.
Group 13 operators destroyed and struck two fuel trucks and a command-and-staff vehicle belonging to Russian forces, the agency said. It placed the work in August 2026 without giving a date or a place on the peninsula.
The footage shows the view from drone cameras closing on the targets. HUR did not say what kind of drones its operators used, and the unit works with both aerial and naval systems, including naval drones rigged to carry FPV drones.
Designated 3K55, the system defends a shoreline and hits both surface and ground targets, warships among them. It takes up to five minutes to deploy, fires supersonic P-800 Oniks and hypersonic Zircon missiles, and reaches from 300 to 600 km depending on the missile and the mode of use. It doubles as an air defense asset, tracking up to 50 objects along the horizon at up to 250 km with passive radar and 450 km with active radar. Russia has fielded it since 2010 and builds it in a mobile version and a silo-based one.
Other Ukrainian services have hit Bastions before
Ukraine's Navy said its forces struck a Bastion's launch positions and deployment site on the peninsula overnight on 16 August, without naming a unit. Ukrainian forces hit a Bastion launcher in the occupied village of Aktachi in March, and in February they struck the concentration area of the Russian brigade that operates the system in Crimea.
In an operation earlier in the summer, one of Group 13's uncrewed boats launched attack drones at two Russian radars in occupied Crimea without the vessel ever reaching shore.
Strikes on the peninsula continued overnight
Drone attacks on occupied Crimea have been running for weeks, and they continued into 4 September, though what was hit this time is not yet known.
Explosions sounded in Sevastopol and Dzhankoi district, Suspilne reported. Monitoring channels logged blasts and drone flights past 04:00, and satellite imagery showed a fire west of the airfield at Hvardiiske, with the cause unconfirmed. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed 490 drones downed over Crimea, other occupied territories, and Russian regions.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: US envoy to visit Kyiv in coming days, Zelenskyy says, as Putin signals ‘chance’ of peace
articles.body:
- 
  Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that US negotiators will soon visit Moscow and Kyiv to resume efforts to end the Russian invasion. The Ukrainian president said in his nightly video address that preliminary dates had been set for the visit. “We expect to see representatives of the US president here in Kyiv,” Zelenskyy said. “There will be a meeting with them in Moscow and in Kyiv. We are expecting a meeting with them in the coming days. It is very important. It is important that America continues to be active.”
- 
  Meanwhile, Vladimir Putin said on Thursday there was a chance of reaching an agreement to end the war in Ukraine. Speaking at an economic forum, Russia’s president said a number of countries including the US and China were ready to support a peace settlement. “Ultimately, however, the problem must be resolved by the countries involved in the conflict – Russia and Ukraine,” he said. “We are grateful to everyone attempting to contribute to a settlement. Is there a chance? In my view, yes, there is.”
- 
  In Washington, Donald Trump said he wanted to see an end to the war and losses sustained by both sides. “I just want to see that end. I think we’ll get it,” the US president told GB News in an interview that aired on Thursday, a day after telling reporters he wanted a summit with Putin when the Kremlin leader is ready for a peace deal. They last met for US-mediated talks in February.
- 
  Trump has said he would ask European nations to pay back the US for military aid and munitions previously sent to Ukraine amid the ongoing war with Russia and appeared to signal a halt in sales to allied nations. In a social media post, Trump on Thursday also slammed reports of heavily depleted US munition stockpiles amid the separate war in Iran, while adding that the US was ramping up production and stockpiling munitions. “We are taking them for ourselves, the U.S.A., rather than selling them to others, but the sales to Allies will soon again, begin,” Trump wrote.
- 
  A Ukrainian strike on Thursday killed four people, including two medical personnel, in an attack on Russia’s border region of Belgorod, officials said. The region’s official headquarters said the dead in Shebekino, just across the border from Ukraine, included a doctor, medic and married couple. Three people were injured. Meanwhile, the head of Russian-controlled parts of eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk Region said three civilians died in drone strikes in three separate districts of the region.
- 
  Russian drones struck and damaged a Coca-Cola plant outside the Ukrainian capital Kyiv on Thursday, Zelenskyy said. Officials said there were no injuries in the strike near the town of Brovary, east of the capital. “Today, the Russians have hit a Coca-Cola plant with their drone. Coca-Cola is such an enemy that they set it on fire with their Shaheds,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly video address, referring to Iranian-designed drones. “It’s a clear Russian signal to America. The Russians cannot be unaware that this is an American facility.”
- 
  A Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv on Thursday injured 10 people, triggered a fire and badly damaged a high-rise residential building, officials said. The city’s military administration initially said one person had died in the latest assault, but later said the report had proved untrue. It said 10 people, including a child, had been hurt. The capital’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said nine people were injured, including six medical personnel.
- 
  Zelenskyy said on Thursday that an investigation would determine what caused a dispute between two of Ukraine’s security agencies to escalate into a shootout in Kyiv this week that left three members of the defence ministry’s HUR military intelligence directorate injured. The dispute centres on the disappearance for nine days of a Russian nationalist activist fighting alongside Ukrainian troops.
- 
  Russia will close German cultural centres on its territory, its foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov, said Thursday in a retaliatory measure reflecting the deepening tensions between Moscow and European countries that are helping Ukraine resist the Kremlin’s invasion. Lavrov’s announcement came after Berlin blamed Moscow for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport on 4 August.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Intel Strikes Russian Bastion Missile System in Crimea
articles.body:
Ukrainian military intelligence (HUR) said Friday that its forces had struck a Russian Bastion coastal missile system in occupied Crimea, a platform used to launch Oniks and Zircon missiles against Ukraine.
The operation was carried out in August by Group 13, a HUR special unit, according to a statement released by the agency.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Group 13 specialists successfully struck a Russian Bastion coastal missile system — a carrier of Zircon and Oniks missiles that the aggressor state uses for terrorist attacks against Ukraine,” HUR said.
The agency also said its operators had destroyed or damaged two Russian fuel trucks and a command-and-staff vehicle on the peninsula.
HUR released footage that it said showed the strikes. The agency did not disclose the operation’s exact location, the weapons used or the extent of the damage to the Bastion system.
The Bastion is a Russian mobile coastal defense system originally designed to engage naval targets. Russia has also used the system to launch missiles at targets inside Ukraine.
Russian forces have adapted Bastion-M systems to launch 3M22 Zircon missiles from land. The missile was initially developed for deployment from Russian nuclear-powered submarines and Project 22350 frigates.
Russian forces have also used Bastion systems in Crimea to launch P-800 Oniks anti-ship missiles against ground targets in Ukraine.
The latest reported strike follows other Group 13 operations against Russian military equipment in Crimea. In early August, the unit struck two S-400 air defense launchers and an antenna used to control Orion drones, according to HUR. The agency said the operation involved Magura multipurpose maritime platforms carrying FPV drones.
Fuel, Energy Crisis in Strategic Russia-Occupied Crimea Worsening
Russia seized and illegally annexed Crimea from Ukraine in 2014. Kyiv has repeatedly targeted Russian military facilities on the peninsula during Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
“The occupiers have nowhere to hide,” HUR said. “The armed struggle continues.”
Last year, a Kyiv Post journalist sat down with “Thirteen,” the commander of special unit Group 13, the team behind the Magura sea drones. He revealed how the unit carried out its first strikes on Russian ships, how naval drone warfare evolved in 2024 and why the Black Sea remains a key battlefield in Russia’s war against Ukraine.
“We started from zero — no equipment, no resources — but we built something that changed the course of the war at sea,” he said.

articles.body:

Germany Retaliates Against Russian Sabotage with Targeting Assistance and Cyber Warfare Powers
Following the attempted explosive drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, the German government publicly attributed the sabotage plot to Russia, abandoning its traditionally cautious approach to hybrid threats, Der Spiegel reported on September 3.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz received near-daily briefings on the investigation throughout August. In late August, he gathered key ministers at Schloss Neuhardenberg to coordinate a response.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
While Merz sought immediate attribution, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul urged a brief delay to protect ongoing investigations and prepare diplomatic countermeasures against anticipated Russian retaliation.
The decision to officially name Russia was ultimately accelerated by a critical tip from a foreign intelligence service in mid-August. According to Der Spiegel, the tip definitively linked several individuals involved in the plot to Russian intelligence agencies.
During internal government discussions, officials concluded that the Leipzig plot was not an isolated incident but marked the beginning of a new phase of Russian aggression in Europe, driven by Moscow’s inability to counter Ukraine’s battlefield successes.
The investigation uncovered a highly organized sabotage operation involving multiple drones and operatives. On August 4, an explosive-laden drone carrying a canister of Semtex military explosive failed to detonate near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane parked at the airport, which serves as a critical logistics hub for NATO and the Bundeswehr.
Ten days later, investigators found a second damaged drone carrying Hexogen explosives in a nearby field. Der Spiegel reported that police later discovered the remains of a third drone and an antenna in a nearby wooded area, indicating a broader operation than initially understood.
Investigators identified at least two suspects linked to the plot. One is believed to have ties to Russian intelligence and a prior July 2024 arson attack on a hardware store in Poland.
The second suspect reportedly traveled from Istanbul to Germany before fleeing to Serbia, which Western intelligence agencies consider a major hub for Russian recruitment and training. The operation is believed to involve a combination of professional Russian intelligence operatives and low-level “throwaway agents,” Der Spiegel wrote.
In response to what Wadephul described as “open hostility” from Moscow, Germany announced a multifaceted retaliation package. Domestically, Berlin is closing the Russian consulate in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin, tightening border controls for Russian citizens, and pushing the EU to crack down on Russia’s shadow fleet.
According to Der Spiegel, the German government is also moving to expand the offensive capabilities of its foreign intelligence service (BND). A proposed intelligence law would allow the BND to conduct “active measures,” such as infiltrating adversarial computer networks to delete stolen data, sabotaging production systems in drone factories, and physically destroying servers used for Russian disinformation campaigns.
Simultaneously, Berlin is drastically increasing its military support for Ukraine. Government sources told Der Spiegel that thousands of attack drones and IRIS-T air defense missiles will be delivered to Kyiv in September. Furthermore, the German government is considering deepening intelligence cooperation with Kyiv by assisting Ukraine in gathering targeting coordinates for military counterattacks.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had also previously condemned the Leipzig airport drone plot as a direct attack by Russian intelligence using military-grade materials on EU territory.
Expressing full solidarity with Germany, she stated that Moscow’s attempt to weaken European resolve had backfired, pledging that the EU would respond to escalating hybrid warfare by intensifying sanctions, closing circumvention loopholes, and expanding countermeasures across the bloc.
