articles.title: Israel and Turkey's uneasy contest to shape Syria's future
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israel and Turkey's uneasy contest to shape Syria's future
Damascus - Syria’s Foreign Minister Asaad Al-Shaibani met with Israel’s Mossad chief Roman Gofman in Jordan on 23 August following days of escalating tensions that resulted in an Israeli strike on a Syrian airbase in northern Idlib.
According to reports, the two met in order to “lower the temperature” following this latest bout of tensions.
Whilst it was not the first round of direct diplomacy between Syrian and Israeli officials, it represented the first instance of direct meetings at such a senior level.
The renewed risk of escalation comes amid growing competition between Israel and Turkey, as each regional power pursues a different - largely incongruous - strategy over Syria’s future.
Yet US efforts to restrain Israeli aggression have achieved some limited success, say analysts.
Growing competition
Israel claimed the strike on Abu al-Duhur airbase on 18 August was due to Turkey being close to breaching “the status quo on security matters” by deploying troops into Syria. Turkey denied that any of its forces had been at the base before or during the attack,
The airstrike was “clearly a message not just to the Syrian administration but also to Turkey,” Caroline Rose, a senior director at The Soufan Centre, told The New Arab.
“They want Turkey to know that they have the ability to strike them anywhere in Syria in order to deter further perceived encroachment.”
According to Muaz Al-Abdullah, Middle East Research Manager at the conflict-tracking organisation, Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), this follows a pattern of behaviour in which Israel strikes any military installation that Turkey seeks to redevelop.
“They also struck T4, Hama and Palmyra airbases following Turkish attempts to redevelop them,” he explained to The New Arab. “It serves a dual purpose of limiting Turkish influence within Syria and preventing the Syrian military from redeveloping.”
This comes amid what Rose describes as “a growing competition” between Turkey and Israel regionally.
Turkish-Israeli relations have soured massively since 7 October. Whilst both countries have full diplomatic relations, Turkey recalled its ambassador in November 2023 in protest over Israeli actions in Gaza.
In February, meanwhile, former Israeli prime minister Naftali Bennett described Turkey as belonging to a “monstrous axis,” alongside Qatar, in part for its hosting of Hamas officials.
A recent article in Israel Hayom, a pro-Likud outlet, assessed the possibility of an Israeli strike on Turkish forces in Syria triggering NATO’s self-defence clause. It concluded that such an attack would not draw in Turkey’s NATO allies.
Turkey recently signed a mutual defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan - what some commentators have taken to calling an ‘Islamic NATO.’
“The mutual defence agreement is a major step,” Issam Al-Reis, a researcher with ETANA, a Syrian research group, told The New Arab.
“For Saudi Arabia, it is a counter to a possible Iranian attack, and for Turkey it is important to deter a possible future scenario in which it's attacked by Israel,” he added.
“There is a sense of increased recklessness from the Israelis and Turkey is likely wondering if after Iran, they are next on the hit list.”
Divided strategies
Part of the tensions are driven by Israel and Turkey’s conflicting strategies in Syria. “Turkey was one of the primary supporters of the Syrian revolution,” says Al-Reis.
“Now their strategy is driven by a desire for a stable Syria that will allow the millions of refugees within Turkey to return home and provide a calm southern border.”
As such, they have sought to develop Syria’s state capacity, and “expand its military footprint in order to stabilise the country and counter groups that they consider to be terrorist organisations like the Syrian Democratic Forces,” explains Al-Reis.
Yet Al-Abdullah cautions about wholly conflating Israel’s attempts to counter Turkey with its own strategy within Syria. “These two dynamics are linked but also separate,” he argues. Israel has its reasons to oppose the Syrian government.
It sees “a Syria capable of launching attacks as a threat and so wants to see Syria weak and fragmented,” believes Rose. “They seek to counter or at the very least delay Syrian rearmament.”
Similarly, Israel has supported non-state actors within Syria, such as Druze Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri’s National Guard in Suweida, in order to keep Damascus weak.
The US, seeking a stable centralised Syria, has been attempting to restrain Israel with mixed results. US Special Envoy for Syria, Tom Barrack, condemned Israel’s recent strike as “an unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability”.
However, Al-Abdullah notes that according to ACLED’s data, the number of Israeli strikes on Syria is consistently decreasing over time, but that “occasionally Israel still decides to act without the US greenlight”.
Stalled talks
Syrian and Israeli officials have taken part in several rounds of talks in Paris, the latest being on 6 January 2026, designed to establish a ‘deconfliction mechanism’ and set out the ground for the possible future security architecture between the two countries.
According to analysts, these talks have been largely inconclusive and have failed to halt Israeli violations both within the newly occupied territories in Quneitra and Daraa and beyond.
On 14 August, following the resumption of Syrian air force training flights, Israel had reportedly planned on striking a number of airbases in order to disable the last vestiges of Syria’s air force.
It is worth noting that 80% of Assad’s air force was destroyed by Israel in the days following the fall of the Assad regime, leaving Syria now with barely a handful of old Soviet fighter jets.
Whilst the planned strikes were reportedly blocked by the White House, the days after saw numerous attempts to resolve the dispute - including a reported phone call between Shaibani and Gofman - which failed to prevent escalation.
Part of the reasoning behind the recent meeting in Jordan is likely to correct this, with both sides discussing the possibility of establishing “a special operations room” in Jordan under US supervision to prevent any confrontation in Syria.
“This meeting is significant both because Syria’s senior leadership actually met with the Israelis but also because it was publicly acknowledged by the Syrians,” says Al-Abdullah.
This represents a step change in Syrian officials' willingness to candidly acknowledge their attempts to foster dialogue with Israel. Despite that, he remains pessimistic about the outcome of talks.
“The two actors are negotiating different things,” he explains. Syria is hoping to return to a status quo ante, which would see Israel leave the newly occupied areas in return for a deconfliction arrangement similar to the 1974 deconfliction arrangement.
Whereas Israel, reflecting a new post-7 October security mindset that is also visible in Lebanon and Gaza, wants to create “an unliveable buffer zone close to their borders through demolitions, eviction and the poisoning of agriculture”.
Ultimately, this would entail Israel leveraging its position to pressure Syria into accepting major concessions like diplomatic normalisation or the recognition of Israel’s 1981 annexation of the Golan Heights - both of which are political non-starters in Damascus.
It is for this reason that he expects this pattern of latent tensions that sporadically erupt to continue.
However, Al-Abdullah stresses that despite the fierce rhetoric on all sides, neither side is seeking a full-blown conflict and so for now “whilst Syria might be a theatre for confrontation, it is not yet the Middle East’s next battleground”.
Cian Ward is a journalist based in Damascus, covering conflict, migration, and humanitarian issues
Follow him on X: @CP__Ward
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Iran strike leaves U.S. Navy with a serious supply problem
articles.body:
- The Navy has about 20 ships and 20,000 personnel in the Middle East, resupplying at sea every five to six days since Iran struck its Bahrain logistics base on February 28.
- The USS Abraham Lincoln spent most of nine months deployed without a port call before docking in Thailand this week en route to San Diego.
The U.S. Navy is running open-ended combat deployments in the Middle East without access to most of its regional supply bases, forcing ships to resupply at sea roughly every five to six days rather than pulling into port, The New York Times reported.
Iran struck the Navy’s logistics hub in Bahrain on February 28, the first day of the current war, according to the Times. Other regional ports large enough to handle an aircraft carrier or a supply ship remain within range of Iranian missiles and drones, making them effectively off-limits.
With nearby bases unavailable, Navy supply ships now sail 2,200 miles to Diego Garcia, a small island in the Indian Ocean, to load food, fuel and other goods before returning to the fleet. The next-closest option is Singapore, 3,700 miles away, a route that requires passing through the Strait of Malacca, one of the world’s busiest commercial shipping corridors.
The Navy currently has about 20 ships and 20,000 sailors and Marines deployed in the Middle East, according to the Times. That includes two aircraft carriers, the USS George H.W. Bush (CVN 77) and the USS George Washington (CVN 73), along with 12 destroyers carrying roughly 3,700 personnel combined, and a three-ship amphibious ready group carrying about 5,000 Marines and sailors. Keeping that force fed and fueled requires more than 420,000 meals and about 8 million gallons of fuel every week, the Times reported. A single carrier’s air wing alone burns roughly 2 million gallons of fuel weekly, even though the ship itself is nuclear-powered.
Resupply at sea requires the receiving ship and the supply ship to sail together on identical course and speed, often for hours, while staying within roughly 150 feet of each other despite wind, waves and current. Sailors fire lines across to the other vessel using rifles, then connect the ships with steel cables that carry fuel lines and pallets of supplies. Helicopters simultaneously ferry additional pallets of food, spare parts and mail between the ships in slung cargo nets.
These deployments have no fixed end date. Ships remain on station until the president and the defense secretary decide otherwise, according to the Times, a practice the newspaper described as unsustainable.
The Navy operates 11 aircraft carriers in total and has sent four of them to the Middle East during the war. Some of the remaining carriers are undergoing extended shipyard repairs and will not be available to deploy again for years, the Times reported.
One of those four carriers, the USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN 72), spent most of its nine months at sea without a single port call, well beyond the roughly monthly port visits the Navy typically allows crews for rest. The USS George Washington relieved the Lincoln on August 20. The Lincoln docked in Thailand on Wednesday morning, where its crew will get several days of shore leave before the ship continues across the Pacific to its home port in San Diego.

articles.title: US urged to consider military strikes to stop China achieving AGI first
articles.body:
US urged to consider military strikes to stop China achieving AGI first
Former White House staffer calls for espionage and cyber options as Washington prepares for a potential Chinese breakthrough
Jacob Stokes, deputy director of the Indo-Pacific Security Program at the Centre for a New American Security (CNAS), said at an online event on Thursday that various US agencies, including the Department of Defense and the National Security Agency, should begin assessing what intelligence they need to justify taking such actions.
“Trying to think through the particulars of that will be especially important, in part because it will help policymakers … start to work backwards based on the unique nature of the technology, in the same way that in a past era, policymakers would learn about nuclear weapons and … work backwards from the science to the policy implications,” he said.
In a new CNAS report published last week, the former Obama administration national security staffer called for the US government to consider the feasibility of diplomatic, espionage, cyber and kinetic measures to prevent China from achieving AGI first.

articles.title: General Dynamics gets $194M deal on nuclear missile program
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy awarded General Dynamics Missions Systems a $194.1 million contract modification for fire control engineering support on the SLCM-N nuclear missile program.
- The Navy has set a 2034 target date for delivering the missile, which Congress kept funded after the Biden administration sought to cancel it in 2022.
The U.S. Navy has awarded General Dynamics Missions Systems a $194.1 million contract modification for engineering support work on the Nuclear-Armed, Sea-Launched Cruise Missile program, according to a Department of War contract announcement.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee modification adds to a previously awarded unpriced letter contract and covers technical and engineering support for the missile’s Fire Control Subsystem. The $194.1 million figure includes optional line items that may or may not ultimately be exercised. Work will be split between General Dynamics’ facility in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, which will handle 75% of the effort, and a facility in Manassas, Virginia, handling the remaining 25%. The contract is scheduled to run through September 30, 2028.
The Navy is obligating $135.3 million in fiscal 2025 reconciliation research, development, test and evaluation funds at the time of award, none of which will expire at the end of the current fiscal year. The Navy awarded the contract sole source under federal acquisition law, after previously publishing notice of the pending award on the government’s SAM.gov contracting portal. Strategic Systems Programs, the Navy office in Washington, D.C., that oversees the service’s ballistic and cruise missile programs, is managing the contract.
The missile at the center of the contract, known as SLCM-N, is a Navy program to develop a low-yield, non-strategic nuclear warhead mounted on a sea-launched cruise missile, intended for deployment on attack submarines and potentially surface ships. The concept was first formally recommended in the Trump administration’s 2018 Nuclear Posture Review as a way to restore a capability the Navy retired in 2010, when it withdrew the nuclear-armed Tomahawk Land Attack Missile from service.
The Biden administration’s 2022 Nuclear Posture Review recommended canceling SLCM-N, citing cost and questions about the adequacy of the existing nuclear arsenal. Congress rejected that recommendation and continued funding the program through subsequent defense authorization bills, establishing it as a formal program of record in the fiscal 2024 National Defense Authorization Act.
Rear Adm. Randy Wolfe, director of the Navy’s Strategic Systems Programs, testified before Congress in May 2025 that the program had spent the prior year working to define the missile’s overall system architecture, an effort spanning the missile itself, its fire control system, launcher system, platform integration, warhead integration, and associated support equipment and training materials. Wolfe said at the time that the Navy expected to deliver the capability in 2034. Sandia National Laboratories announced in January that the program would use the W80-5 warhead variant.

articles.title: Kiev loses some 1,510 troops along engagement line in past day — Russia’s top brass
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 3. /TASS/. The Ukrainian army lost roughly 1,510 troops in battles with Russian forces in all the frontline areas over the past 24 hours, according to the latest data on the special military operation in Ukraine released by Russia’s Defense Ministry.
The latest figures show that the Ukrainian army lost over 315 troops in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup North, over 210 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup West and more than 205 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup South.
During the last 24-hour period, the Ukrainian army also lost over 385 troops in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center, more than 340 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup East and up to 55 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup Dnepr, the latest figures show.
Russian air defenses intercept 998 Ukrainian UAVs, two smart bombs over past day
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 998 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and two smart bombs over the past 24 hours, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down two guided aerial bombs, three rockets of the US-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system and 998 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces take control of Vasilevka, Blagodatnoye, Dolzhanka in Kharkov Region
Over the past 24 hours, Russian troops have taken control of the settlements of Vasilevka, Blagodatnoye, and Dolzhanka in the Kharkov Region, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result of decisive actions, units of the Battlegroup North have taken control of the settlements of Vasilevka, Blagodatnoye, and Dolzhanka in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces strike logistics center for military cargo in Kiev Region
Russian troops used droned to strike Ukraine’s logistics center in Velikaya Aleksandrovka, Kiev Region, used for the storage and distribution of military cargo, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"The Russian Armed Forces continue to carry out coordinated strikes against Ukrainian logistics facilities used in the interests of the armed forces of Ukraine. Overnight, attack drones struck the Biokon logistics center in the Velikaya Aleksandrovka settlement in the Kiev Region, which was used for the storage and distribution of military cargoes," the ministry said in a statement.
Battlegroup North destroys over 240 Ukrainian dugouts, deployment sites near Kharkov
Unmanned systems units of the Russian Battlegroup North’s 11th Army Corps have destroyed over 240 dugout shelters and temporary field deployment sites of the Ukrainian armed forces in the Kharkov region during August, an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operator with the call sign Grif told TASS.
"UAV operators of the Battlegroup North’s 11th Army Corps identified and destroyed over 240 Ukrainian dugouts and temporary field deployment sites in the Kharkov Region in August. The destruction of dugouts and temporary field deployment sites disrupts the deployment of enemy troops, reduces their activity, and hinders the supply of frontline positions," the soldier said.
According to him, Battlegroup North strikes the Ukrainian armed forces’ dugouts and temporary deployment sites using attack UAVs, including FPV drones. "Operators track targets from the air, verify the data received, and monitor the results of the crews’ operations," he added.
Russian forces strike facilities used by Ukrainian army -- Defense Ministry
Russian forces struck transport and energy facilities used by the Ukrainian army over the past day, the Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"Russia’s tactical aircraft, attack drones, missile forces and artillery struck Ukraine’s logistics hubs, fuel and energy facilities and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian army, as well as production and storage sites for unmanned aerial vehicles and their components and temporary deployment points of Ukrainian troops and foreign mercenaries in 155 areas," the statement reads.
Russian Black Sea Fleet destroys six Ukrainian Navy unmanned boats
The Black Sea Fleet has destroyed six unmanned boats operated by the Ukrainian Navy, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
"Black Sea Fleet forces destroyed six unmanned boats operated by the Ukrainian Navy in the Black Sea," the Defense Ministry said.
Russian forces liberate Izhevka settlement in Donetsk People’s Republic
Russian forces liberated the Izhevka settlement in the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR) over the past 24 hours, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Battlegroup South units liberated the settlement of Izhevka in the Donetsk People’s Republic through active operations," the ministry said in a statement.
Ukrainian forces sustain heavy losses in Vasilevka, Kharkov Region
Units of a separate motorized infantry brigade of the Ukrainian armed forces sustained heavy casualties in the fighting for Vasilevka in the Kharkov region, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"To hold the [Vasilevka] settlement, the enemy deployed units from a separate motorized infantry brigade, but as a result of artillery fire, Ukrainian militants suffered heavy losses and were forced to leave the settlement and withdraw from their positions," the ministry said in a statement. On September 3, the ministry reported that assault troops of the Russian Battlegroup North’s 126th Motorized Rifle Regiment, 71st Guards Motorized Rifle Division, took control of the Vasilevka settlement in the Kharkov Region.

articles.title: Middle East live: South Korea mulling military deployment in Strait of Hormuz, media reports say
articles.body:
Israeli troops have driven Hezbollah fighters from tunnels under the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz alleged on Friday. Israel’s armed forces have occupied swathes of southern Lebanon since launching a new campaign against the Shiite group in March. Follow our liveblog for all the latest updates.
New fears of oil supply disruption as US-Iran hostilities resume
Fresh US strikes on Iran and Tehran's retaliatory attacks across the region have brought back fears of oil supply disruption.
Prices are on track for their steepest weekly gain since mid-July, up 7.6 percent, as the US-Israeli war against Iran enters its seventh month.
Twenty-five percent of the world's oil supply comes through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been blocked since the beginning of the war.
FRANCE 24's international affairs editor Philip Turle gives more details.
Israeli police kill Palestinian man in Jerusalem after alleged knife attack
Israeli police said they had killed a Palestinian man after he allegedly attempted to attack officers with a knife in central Jerusalem.
Security forces "neutralised a terrorist who had attempted to attack them with a knife, and his death was pronounced at the scene", police said in a statement.
The incident took place overnight near Damascus Gate, which leads into Jerusalem's Old City, the police said, adding that the dead man was a 33-year-old from Jerusalem.
The Palestinian news agency Wafa also reported the death, saying police had set up a military cordon around Damascus Gate and the Old City.
Ahead of the Jewish New Year on September 11, prayers are being held every night at the Western Wall, a holy site for Jews that borders the Old City.
The holiday period, which lasts three weeks, has seen violent incidents in the past.
In September last year, two Palestinians opened fire at a bus station in east Jerusalem, killing six people and wounding about 20 others.
Red Cross says it transferred four people released by Israel to Lebanon
Humanitarian workers on said they had facilitated the transfer to Lebanon of four more people detained by Israel, a day after another person was freed.
"The International Committee of the Red Cross, at the request of the relevant parties, facilitated the transfer to Lebanon of five individuals released from Israeli detention," the ICRC said in a statement. "One individual was transferred on Thursday, and four others on Friday," it added.
US diesel prices hit a record high of $5.85 on average as Iran war disrupts the flow of fuel
Diesel hit a new record price in the US on Friday, soaring to an average of $5.85 a gallon for the first time ever as the six-month-long war US-Israeli war against Iran continues to disrupt the world’s flow of fuel.
Because diesel is used for many freight and delivery networks, higher diesel prices mean higher transportation costs for a long list of everyday goods. More expensive fuel is increasing bills for businesses across sectors – some of which have already passed off costs to consumers in the form of added fees on online orders and packages in the mail.
Produce, meat and other perishable foods that need to be hauled in and restocked frequently – or even harvested using diesel-powered farm equipment – are also expected to feel the strain, though it can take time for all of those costs to trickle down.
A range of other consumer products are also transported by diesel trucks, trains and boats, including clothing, cosmetics, furniture and more.
Israel's defence minister hails capture of Hezbollah highland as solidifying Lebanon 'security zone'
Israel's defence minister hailed the capture of a strategic highland from Hezbollah as solidifying Israel's "security zone" in Lebanon and vowed that troops would not leave it.
"The capture of the Ali Tahar ridge marks the completion of the phase of securing control in the security zone in southern Lebanon," Defence Minister Israel Katz said in a statement.
Israeli troops continue to occupy swathes of southern Lebanon.
More than 80 people killed in Yemen clashes since Thursday, military sources say
Clashes between Yemen's Houthi rebels and government forces have killed 81 combatants since Thursday, according to a tally of figures from two military officials and medical sources in Houthi-held territory.
A military official on the Red Sea coast reported 24 of his men killed, while another in the inland Taiz area said 15 had been killed there.
At least 42 Houthi militants were also killed, according to medical sources in areas under their control.
Deadly clashes erupted in Yemen on Thursday, after Houthi forces began a ground assault accompanied by rocket and drone attacks near coastal areas in the Red Sea and around the Taiz region.
Military government sources told AFP the rebels were attempting to cut off the key port city of Mokha, under fire for weeks, from other government areas, and advance towards areas bordering the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait.
South Korea says it could contribute to US security efforts in Hormuz
South Korea said Friday that Seoul could contribute to US security efforts in the Strait of Hormuz as long as its own military readiness is not compromised.
"Contributions to the Strait of Hormuz could be managed within limits that do not compromise military readiness," a presidential official said, adding that a review was still underway.
Trump names Adam Telle as acting Army secretary amid Hegseth tensions
US President Donald Trump on Thursday named Adam Telle, a civilian leader in the US Army Corps of Engineers, as the acting Army secretary following the departure of Dan Driscoll amid widespread reports of tensions with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Telle is currently the assistant secretary of the Army for civil works. But he spent more than 20 years working for Republican senators as well as in the White House during Trump's first term, serving as the president's chief liaison to the Senate, according to an Army bio.
"He is a Great Patriot, who is respected by all," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. Hegseth echoed that in his own post on X.
"Huge congrats to Adam. Strong and whip smart," Hegseth wrote. "He is indeed a great Patriot – and will be an immediate asset to the @USArmy."
Oil prices set for steepest weekly gain since July on US-Iran tensions
Oil prices rose on Friday and are on track for the steepest weekly gain since mid-July as rising tensions and renewed US-Iran hostilities heightened concerns over Middle East supply risks.
Brent crude futures rose 15 cents, or 0.2 percent, to $95.67 a barrel at 01:00 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were up 26 cents, or 0.3 percent, at $91.56.
On a weekly basis, Brent rose 7.1% and WTI was 9.8 percent higher, set for the highest gains since the week ended July 20.
South Korea says claims that Seoul has provided no support in Hormuz are 'not true'
South Korea is reviewing practical options, including military measures, for supporting freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, and claims that Seoul had provided no assistance on the issue were "not true", a presidential Blue House official said on Friday.
The official said South Korea-US security talks were "not currently progressing" and semiconductors were among the issues under discussion between the allies.
South Korea weighs military deployment to Strait of Hormuz
South Korea is preparing to deploy military assets to support freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and aims to dispatch them before the end of the year, media reported late on Thursday, citing government and military sources.
The reports in several South Korean media outlets said the government was preparing procedures to seek parliamentary approval for the deployment, including submitting a consent motion to parliament this month after cabinet review.
The government was considering options including sending a maritime patrol aircraft, a logistics support vessel or a mine detection and clearance unit, and had been discussing the scale and nature of a potential contribution with countries including the United States, Britain and France, the reports said.
Welcome to the France 24 liveblog covering events in the Middle East. You can catch up on yesterday's developments here.
• Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu voiced confidence that Iran's Islamic republic could soon fall, saying it was "weaker than ever".
• US Vice President JD Vance has said he would not categorise the Iran war as a war, despite continuing clashes with Tehran six months after the start of the conflict.

articles.title: Chinese firm claims mass production of new interceptor drone
articles.body:
- Shengying Technology says it has introduced the H-07, an AI-guided interceptor drone the company claims can reach 320 km/h and has entered mass production.
- Interceptor drones have grown rapidly since 2024 as militaries seek cheaper alternatives to missiles for countering mass drone attacks like Russia's Shahed strikes.
Chinese company Shengying Technology says it has introduced a new interceptor drone called the H-07, a high-speed platform designed to shoot down other drones in the final seconds before impact.
Interceptor drones have become one of the fastest-growing categories in air defense over the past two years, driven largely by the need to counter cheap, mass-produced attack drones like Russia’s Iranian-designed Shahed loitering munitions. Traditional air defense missiles, which can cost hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars each, are often too expensive to use against drones that cost a few thousand dollars to build. Interceptor drones aim to close that cost gap by using a cheap aircraft to physically ram or disable another drone in flight.
Ukraine has led much of this development under wartime pressure. Wild Hornets, one of Ukraine’s largest drone manufacturers, produces roughly 10,000 drones a month, including its Sting interceptor, which the company says has begun shooting down faster, jet-powered variants of the Shahed that were previously considered too fast for propeller-driven interceptors to catch. Ukraine has also fielded the JEDI Shahed Hunter, described as the first pilotless interceptor drone, which receives target data directly from radar stations and can detect and engage threats on its own. Other Ukrainian systems in service include the Baton family of interceptors and the jet-powered Alexa Spatium, launched from a mobile catapult.
The approach has spread beyond Ukraine. Japan’s defense procurement agency selected Terra Drone Corporation’s Terra B1 interceptor for mass production this year after it beat three competing designs in evaluation testing, part of a program aimed specifically at countering long-range, one-way attack drones. In the United States, systems like the foldable SPART interceptor, developed by Ukrainian engineer Yehor Balytskyi’s company Thermopylae Aerospace, have been demonstrated to the U.S. Air Force as a lower-cost alternative to missile-based defenses.
Shengying Technology’s H-07 claims to fit into this same category. According to the company, the drone has entered mass production, though The Defence Blog has not been able to independently confirm this, or the drone’s specifications, deployment, or testing status. No government, military, or third-party source has verified any of the company’s claims.
The H-07 uses a 7-inch airframe. Most first-person-view style interceptor drones use a smaller 5-inch size, and Shengying Technology says the larger frame lets the H-07 reach a top speed of 320 km/h (199 mph), with a cruising speed between 100 and 200 km/h (62 to 124 mph). That would put it in a similar speed range to Ukraine’s SPART interceptor, which the manufacturer has said reaches up to 350 km/h (217 mph).
The company lists a flight range of 15 km (9.3 miles) and a battery life of up to 10 minutes. It puts the drone’s operating altitude between 50 and 2,000 meters (164 to 6,562 feet).
Shengying Technology says the H-07 is built to detect, track, and intercept other drones, including fixed-wing, delta-wing, and multirotor types. The system relies on an onboard AI module based on a YOLO tracking algorithm, a common computer-vision method for real-time object detection. The company says it can lock onto targets from 300 meters (984 feet) away when firing from the ground, and from 200 meters (656 feet) when intercepting another drone in flight.
The drone can launch from the ground or from a launcher, according to the company, and carries a payload of up to 300 grams (0.66 pounds). Its battery is fixed inside the airframe rather than removable, with a direct plug-in charging dock meant to speed up turnaround between flights. Shengying Technology says the H-07 uses three separate cooling methods during high-speed flight: fan cooling for the electronic speed controller, dedicated ventilation openings, and a cooling system for the video transmitter.
The company says the drone’s injection-molded housing and manufacturing tooling are complete and that the platform is ready for large-scale production. It has not disclosed pricing, a customer base, or any confirmed sale, test, or deployment of the H-07 with a military or government buyer.

articles.title: Russia shifts tactics with round-the-clock air strikes on Kyiv, disrupting daily life
articles.body:
Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday night he hoped to host US President Donald Trump's envoys in Kyiv in the coming days to resume efforts to end the war.
For much of the war, Russian drone and missile attacks on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv followed a particular rhythm; they almost always came at night.
The warnings would begin on monitoring channels on Telegram in the late evening. They announced drones moving south, missiles being launched, air defences working.
Ukrainian civilians judged whether it was prudent to stay indoors or make for shelter in the metro based on the severity of the threat.
Now, Russia has changed tactics with the use of fast-flying, jet-powered drones and the expectation that daylight brings a return to normal life has been shattered.
Since last week, attacks have come day and night, compounding the terror of overnight strikes with the exhaustion of constant daytime disruption.
In Kyiv, the recurring wail of air-raid sirens has become part of daily life. It has interrupted commutes, shopping trips and children’s schools, intruded on life’s biggest moments, from weddings to funerals, and, as these attacks always have, taken lives.
The relentless alerts are exhausting residents, leaving some wondering how long they can stay.
Part of daily life
An alert sounds. People look at their phones or up at the sky. Moments later, in the distance, the familiar sounds of air defences intercepting drones resound.
Plumes of smoke can often be seen rising in the distance. Photos quickly spread across Telegram channels, showing where the destruction has occurred.
An hour or two later, another siren echoes.
In malls, banks and other businesses, air-raid protocols require customers and staff to leave when an alert sounds. A bank transaction can be interrupted mid-conversation; a shopping trip can become a cycle of entering a store, evacuating, returning and evacuating again.
Getting the shopping done has become a nightmare for Volodymyr Bovsunovskyi, who recounts a recent family trip to a mall to buy clothes for his nearly 4-year-old daughter.
They had been inside for about 20 minutes when the alert sounded. They rushed out and saw smoke rising nearby. They never got to purchase the clothes.
“A lot has changed in the last seven days,” he said. Like many residents, he hopes the attacks will relent. But, they have not yet, as Ukraine struggles to find an effective way to counter them.
Train journeys that would normally take a few hours have stretched much longer. In some cases, passengers have found themselves walking for hours through grassy fields after trains stopped on the tracks, carrying their belongings while one air-raid alert followed another.
The same uncertainty extends to getting around the city.
When GPS signals are disrupted to jam drones, using a taxi app becomes a difficult process. A car that appears to be nearby can suddenly appear to be on the other side of the world.
A pickup that seemed imminent suddenly shows an arrival time of thousands of minutes.
Considering leaving
Ivan Datsiv, an IT worker, was in his apartment in Kyiv’s Podil district when a Russian drone tore through the floor on Tuesday, charring the ceilings and walls and completely destroying the flat next door.
Datsiv tries to joke about it, saying he had been meaning to repaint the walls anyway.
The alerts have become so frequent that he no longer sees the point of repeatedly going to a shelter. At this rate, he said, the only alternative would be to live in the basement.
“The alarms sound constantly,” he said. “You don’t even have time to go down and come back up. It’s just a waste of time running back and forth."
He is thinking of leaving Kyiv. “I’m thinking of living in another city, somewhere quiet and without this danger,” he said.
From the blown-out apartment next door, the view looks down onto a playground and basketball court where children are still playing.
Then a siren sounds again. Minutes later, the white zigzagging trail of an intercepted drone can be seen against the sky.
Bovsunovskyi is also considering leaving the city for a while, hoping to give his family, including his pregnant wife, a chance to rest.
The kindergarten his daughter attends must move the children to a shelter whenever an air-raid alert sounds. The alerts have become so frequent that he now simply picks her up halfway through the day.
“There is no stability,” he said.
Ending the war
Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday night he hoped to host US President Donald Trump's envoys in Kyiv in the coming days to resume efforts to end the war.
Diplomatic push to end Russia's four-and-a-half-year invasion has stalled in recent months as the United States has shifted its focus towards the war with Iran.
"We expect to see the envoys of the President of America here in Kyiv. We have confirmation from them," Zelensky said in his nightly address.
"They will have meetings in Moscow and in Kyiv. We are counting on a meeting in the coming days," he added.
Trump's special envoys, Steve Witkoff and the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner, have been involved in shuttle diplomacy between Russia and Ukraine, travelling to Moscow multiple times.
They have never been to Kyiv.
Zelenskyy said that "tentative dates have been set" for the envoys' first visit to the Ukrainian capital, which has endured intensified Russian drone and missile attacks over the past week.
Russia's invasion of Ukraine has turned into Europe's worst conflict since World War II, killing thousands of civilians and hundreds of thousands of troops.

articles.title: West not safe from Ukrainian terror – Moscow
articles.body:
West not safe from Ukrainian terror – Moscow
Kiev’s Western backers cannot guarantee that Ukrainian terrorist attacks will not endanger their own citizens, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has warned.
Moscow has long accused the Ukrainian government of employing terrorist tactics and deliberately targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure. President Vladimir Putin has described Vladimir Zelensky’s recent threat against foreign airlines operating in Russia as “state terrorism.”
“They (Western nations) have created a monster, and we always said that this monster will go rogue, as did all the monsters they created before,” Zakharova told Izvestia on Friday.
“What guarantee do they have that Zelensky won’t strike their own citizens when carrying out those terrorist attacks?” she added. “Nobody could ever guarantee that.”
In June, a female Ukrainian national carried out a bomb attack in Monaco that seriously injured exiled Ukrainian businessman Vadim Ermolaev and members of his family. After returning to Ukraine, she was allegedly murdered by two suspected masterminds of the plot – an active operative of Ukraine’s HUR military intelligence agency and a police officer suspected of secretly working for the domestic security service SBU.
The same agencies were involved in firefights in Kiev this week in what appeared to be a dispute over custody of an HUR operative whom the SBU has accused of involvement in a for-profit plot to organize a political assassination.
German investigators have accused Ukrainian citizens of carrying out the September 2022 bombing of the Nord Stream gas pipelines, which caused one of the most serious incidents of damage to energy infrastructure in recent history.
Media reports have also described clandestine Ukrainian operations in Africa and the Middle East purportedly intended to undermine Russian interests, including the training and arming of local militant groups.
Kiev has also been blamed for dozens of drone attacks targeting commercial vessels involved in Russian maritime trade, a practice Moscow has denounced as outright piracy.
Putin criticized Ukraine’s Western backers in remarks on Thursday, arguing that by failing to condemn Kiev’s criminal actions, they effectively become accomplices.

articles.title: Trump seeks repayment from Europe for past Ukraine aid
articles.body:
- President Trump said the U.S. has "virtually unlimited" munitions and is producing weapons "at levels never seen before" amid Iran war stockpile reports.
- Trump said he will seek repayment from European countries for Ukraine aid, though the U.S. already runs a NATO-backed program where allies pay for U.S. weapons sent to Ukraine.
President Donald Trump said Wednesday the United States has “virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition” and is manufacturing munitions “at levels never seen before,” pushing back against months of reporting that the war with Iran has strained U.S. weapons stockpiles.
Trump made the claims in a Truth Social post published at 7:56 p.m. on September 3, in which he also said the United States would soon resume munitions sales to allies after prioritizing its own stockpiles during the conflict.
“For the treasonous SCUM that refuses to accurately report on our Military Operation in Iran, we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use for this, or for any other War (which is highly unlikely!), that could improbably take place,” Trump wrote. “In addition, we are producing Munitions at levels never seen before. We are stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen. We are taking them for ourselves, the U.S.A., rather than selling them to others, but the sales to Allies will soon again, begin.”
The post is the latest in a series of denials Trump has issued since March, when reports first surfaced that the intensity of U.S. operations against Iran was drawing down stocks of key munitions. The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post reported in early March that Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine had raised concerns about depleted stockpiles ahead of the war’s start. Trump called those reports a “disgrace” at the time and said the U.S. had a “virtually unlimited supply” of certain munitions.
Similar reports resurfaced in July, when The New York Times, NBC News, CBS News and CNN reported that nearly two weeks of daily strikes on Iran had drawn down supplies of defensive interceptors, including Patriot and THAAD missiles, protecting U.S. bases in Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain. U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz disputed the reporting on NBC’s “Meet the Press” that month, saying anyone leaking such information “deserve[s] to be in jail.”
In August, Reuters reported that the U.S. Army had used “virtually all” of its inventories of Army Tactical Missile Systems and Precision Strike Missiles during the five-month conflict, citing people familiar with internal military data. Trump responded at the time by calling the U.S. munitions stockpile “massive” and vowing to hunt down “treasonous” leakers.
In Wednesday’s post, Trump also said the Biden administration had given Ukraine and NATO “far more Munitions” at no cost than the U.S. has used in Iran.
“Hundreds of Billions of Dollars was given to Ukraine and NATO, free of charge, that Europe would have paid for, If they were only asked, but we will be asking for that money, though somewhat belatedly!” Trump wrote.
U.S. military aid to Ukraine under the Biden administration totaled roughly $131 billion, according to figures compiled by the Atlantic Council, most of it disbursed in 2022. European countries have collectively provided more than $227 billion in total aid to Ukraine as of 2025, the same figures show, exceeding the U.S. contribution.
Since July 2025, the United States and NATO have operated the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, a mechanism under which European allies and Canada, not the United States, pay for U.S.-manufactured weapons shipped to Ukraine. The program was established through an agreement between Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. As of October 2025, 26 countries had contributed more than $4 billion through the initiative, according to the Atlantic Council.

articles.title: Trump envoys expected to visit Moscow and Kiev ‘soon’ – RT source
articles.body:
Trump envoys expected to visit Moscow and Kiev ‘soon’ – RT source
A long-expected visit to Russia and Ukraine by US President Donald Trump’s diplomatic envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner could happen “soon,” a source has told RT
Witkoff and Kushner are handling several high-profile negotiations for the American leader. Their linked visits to Moscow and Kiev have been expected for months.
Trump has aimed to mediate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine since returning to office last year. However, what appeared to be a path to a breakthrough following his meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Alaska over a year ago came to a dead end, as Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky refused to compromise on several key issues.
On Thursday, Putin said he valued American efforts and called Kushner and Witkoff, who were involved in trilateral talks involving the US, Russia, and Ukraine, sincere interlocutors.
“Mr. Kushner and Witkoff are always welcome guests here, and we work with them with pleasure.”
In recent weeks, Zelensky has made several public statements about the duo’s possible visit to Kiev, with his latest prediction coming on Thursday night.
Both Kushner and Witkoff have visited Moscow during Trump’s current term, but are yet to travel to Kiev. Zelensky claimed in public remarks that the disparity was unfair to Ukraine.
The Ukrainian government previously failed to secure additional supplies of Patriot interceptor missiles from the US, as the stockpiles of the prized weapons were reportedly depleted by Washington’s war on Iran. Zelensky said Kiev needed 300 projectiles to stop Russian missile attacks throughout the winter.
In June, Zelensky ordered a campaign of mass drone attacks targeting Russian transport ships, refineries and retailer warehouses, which political observers said was designed to convince Trump that Ukrainian forces could secure a military victory and should be provided with additional supplies.
Russian retaliation strikes have left Ukraine virtually with no access to maritime trade through the Black Sea and seriously disrupted logistics.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones attack Russia’s Black Sea coast, sparking a fire at an oil depot
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones attack Russia’s Black Sea coast, sparking a fire at an oil depot
A Ukrainian drone attack on the city of Sochi and the nearby town of Sirius sparked a fire overnight on September 4 at an oil depot, according to the Krasnodar Krai Operational Headquarters.
The oil depot’s owner has not been officially identified, though the independent Telegram channel Astra claimed the facility belongs to Rosneft-Kubanneftprodukt in the Adler district.
Preliminary reports indicated no one was injured, though windows were damaged in several residential buildings and other structures. Black smoke could be seen over Sochi.
The Ukrainian monitoring Telegram channels Exilenova+ and Supernova+ claimed that Ukrainian drones also struck air defense installations: S-300 or S-400 surface-to-air missile systems.
Astra, citing eyewitness photos and videos, reported that one of the strikes hit near the town of Sirius, close to the Psou River, where an air defense battalion equipped with S-300 or S-400 systems is stationed, sparking a fire at the site. Local authorities and the Defense Ministry did not report a strike on the air defense installation.
The video contains profanity.
Drones also struck the Sterlitamak petrochemical plant in Bashkortostan, according to Exilenova+, while Supernova+ reported a strike on Avangard, a federal defense enterprise. Local authorities did not confirm either attack, though an air raid alert was declared in the region overnight.
This spring, Ukraine’s armed forces repeatedly targeted another city in Krasnodar Krai, Tuapse, striking the local oil refinery and a marine terminal that together form a single complex with the refinery. The resulting fires triggered an environmental disaster: “oil rain” fell several times, and oil product spills were found in both the river and the sea.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: South Korea pushes back on reports it is readying Hormuz deployment amid US pressure
articles.body:
South Korea is reviewing a possible deployment of military assets to the strait of Hormuz amid pressure from Donald Trump over Seoul’s reluctance to provide support in the region, according to domestic media reports.
Citing unnamed government and military sources, the reports published on Thursday and Friday said preparations were under way and that the government intended to seek parliamentary approval for a new deployment. The reports, which appeared in major South Korean outlets, said the exact scale and timing had not been agreed.
But the presidential office pushed back, telling the Guardian that such reports were “different from the facts” and that “nothing related to the matter has been decided”, though it said the review was “continuing”.
An official said: “Our government has been closely discussing with the international community ways to make practical contributions for the speedy restoration of free navigation in the strait of Hormuz and peace and stability in the Middle East.”
According to reports, the assets under consideration include a P-8 Poseidon aircraft, which would mark South Korea’s first overseas deployment of a maritime patrol aircraft, and a naval logistics support ship to provide rear support.
One outlet, Seoul Broadcasting System, additionally reported that an explosive ordnance disposal team from the navy’s underwater demolition unit was part of the package.
Any new deployment in principle would require review by the national security council, a cabinet resolution and approval from the national assembly.
South Korea is highly dependent on the strait of Hormuz, importing more than 90% of its primary energy, including roughly 70% of crude oil through the waterway.
In 2020, the government of the then president, Moon Jae-in, expanded the mandate of an existing anti-piracy unit off the coast of Somalia to cover the strait of Hormuz, rather than seeking parliamentary approval for a new deployment.
South Korea’s defence minister, Ahn Gyu-back, in March told parliament that any deployment to the strait would require the national assembly’s consent given how different the mission would be from the unit’s existing anti-piracy mandate.
The reports come amid growing strains in the US-South Korea alliance. Trump has repeatedly complained in public that Seoul turned down his request for help over Iran, claiming in August that South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had told him “No, thanks” despite the US stationing tens of thousands of troops on the peninsula.
Days later, he ordered the Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercises to be scaled back, shortening the drills by six days.
Relations between the two allies have also been strained by delays implementing a $350bn investment package Seoul agreed with Washington last year, reports that the US had restricted intelligence sharing with South Korea, and by a dispute over a data breach at the South Korean e-commerce company Coupang.
Separately, Seoul has expressed interest in taking part in any renewed US-North Korea diplomacy, as Trump signals openness to another meeting with Kim Jong-un.

articles.title: Putin dismisses talk of another mobilization as ‘nonsense.’ But Russia has spent four years closing the loopholes that helped people avoid the last one.
articles.body:
Putin dismisses talk of another mobilization as ‘nonsense.’ But Russia has spent four years closing the loopholes that helped people avoid the last one.
Russian authorities continue to insist there are no plans for a new, large-scale wave of mobilization this fall. On September 1, Vladimir Putin called the rumors “complete nonsense.” There is also no urgent military need to expand the army by several hundred thousand mobilized troops. Still, the media’s constant churning of the topic is clearly frightening Russians. There is indirect evidence that many are looking into the option of leaving the country on short notice. So we decided to explain what people in Russia need to know, whether they trust the authorities’ assurances or believe another mobilization is inevitable. These are the laws Russia has passed since 2022 that would, in one way or another, be useful to the state if it once again decides to forcibly replenish the ranks of the Russian armed forces. What loopholes did they close? What should you remember about deferments? And who wasn’t at risk of mobilization before, but is now?
How the authorities closed the main loopholes for evading the mobilization draft
In 2022, Russians looking to dodge mobilization had two main options: leave the country, or stay and simply skip the summons to the local draft office. The worst that could happen was a 3,000-ruble fine for failing to appear, under the administrative statute “Failure by Citizens to Fulfill Military Registration Obligations.” There was no criminal liability for it. The Criminal Code’s provision on “draft evaders” applied only to conscripts performing mandatory military service. Since then, the authorities have worked systematically to close that “gap.”
- In October 2023, authorities raised the maximum fine for failing to appear at a local draft office in response to any summons tenfold, to 30,000 rubles.
- Still, evading a mobilization summons carries no criminal liability. But the authorities have built a system of punitive measures designed to compel people to appear at the local draft office.
In April 2023, the law on military duty gained a new article: “Temporary Measures Aimed at Ensuring Appearance in Response to a Summons From the Local Draft Office.” The article does not explicitly mention people the authorities plan to mobilize, or mobilization summonses themselves. But it is clear that these measures are meant to apply during mobilization as well.
This is evident, for example, from the technical specification for developing the military registration registry, published by the independent Russian investigative outlet iStories. One of the registry’s subsystems was designed to generate documents like this:
the report on mobilization summonses should provide quantitative data on the process of summoning citizens for the reason “to undergo a mobilization draft board review,” broken down by local draft offices, purposes of summons, and temporary restriction measures, reflecting percentage ratios.
Another piece of “evidence” is a note on the back of a mobilization summons intended for a separate category of Russians:
Failure by a citizen on the military register to appear without valid reason, in response to a delivered summons, more than 20 calendar days after the date specified in the summons, results in the application of temporary measures aimed at ensuring that citizen’s appearance.
So what exactly are these temporary measures threatening people who might be mobilized in the future?
Ban on foreign travel
A mobilization summons now automatically bars anyone liable for military service from leaving the country — even someone who never received the summons and has no idea it exists. That’s because an electronic summons counts as delivered “from the moment it is posted in the citizen’s personal account” in the summons registry, regardless of whether the person ever logged in to see it.
The ban stays in effect at least until the appearance date specified in the summons. If the person ignores the summons and fails to show up on time, no one will lift it. Article 15¹ of the law on procedures for leaving Russia states this explicitly:
This restriction remains in effect until the citizen fulfills the obligation to appear at the local draft office in response to the summons.
In effect, local draft offices now have the arbitrary power to bar anyone liable for military service from leaving the country for up to a month.
Loss of rights for ‘evaders’ who stay in Russia
If a Russian issued a mobilization summons fails to appear at the local draft office on the appointed day, authorities impose a set of restrictions on him 20 days later:
- a ban on registering as an individual entrepreneur
- a ban on registering as a self-employed taxpayer
- suspension of cadastral registration and/or the registration of real estate rights
- restriction of the right to drive vehicles
- a ban on registering vehicles
- refusal to enter into a loan or credit agreement.
Regional authorities may also impose additional restrictions “on citizens receiving payments, benefits, support measures, and other preferences” at their own discretion.
The only way to restore those rights is to appear at the local draft office or prove a valid reason temporarily preventing you from doing so.
How the authorities added just one new mobilization deferment — and even that one was technical
In November 2022, lawmakers amended the law “On Mobilization Preparation and Mobilization in the Russian Federation” to formally expand the list of grounds for a mobilization deferment. Since then, volunteers — people “serving in volunteer units” who had already gone to war of their own free will — can also qualify for one.
In late 2022 and early 2023, opposition lawmakers in the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, introduced numerous bills seeking to expand the list of deferments to cover:
- citizens with three children under 16 (the law requires at least four)
- citizens with four children under 18, or raising a child under 18 without the child’s mother (the law sets the age lower — under 16)
- individual entrepreneurs, as well as heads of peasant and farming enterprises
- citizens with a single retired parent
- citizens with any child with a disability
- citizens with a disabled child under 18 or a Group I disabled person since childhood
- citizens who have not served in the military (under the law, any reservist can be mobilized; this currently includes people who did not complete mandatory service before turning 30)
- citizens holding a doctoral or candidate of sciences degree
- citizens found only partially fit for military service for health reasons (category B) — though only in the case of “partial” mobilization
- close relatives (including grandparents) of service members killed during mobilization
- reservist privates and sergeants over the age of 35 — also only in the case of “partial” mobilization.
All of these attempts failed — or were never even taken up by the State Duma.
Two more bills are now before the lower house, introduced in April 2026 and not yet even at the first-reading stage. They would create a mobilization deferment for:
- members of small Indigenous peoples
- biological brothers and sons of service members and volunteers who were killed.
How the authorities left the question of alternative civilian service during mobilization unresolved
Russia’s Constitution enshrines citizens’ right to alternative civilian service. But the corresponding federal law addresses that right during mobilization only in a referential provision:
Article 9. Organization and performance of alternative civilian service during mobilization, during martial law, and in wartime
Organization and performance of alternative civilian service during mobilization, during martial law, and in wartime are determined by federal constitutional laws, other federal laws, and other legal acts of the Russian Federation adopted in accordance with them.
In November 2022, the law on military duty gained a new Article 17¹, “Performance of Alternative Civilian Service During Mobilization.” It applied only to people who had already replaced mandatory service with alternative service.
1. Citizens performing alternative civilian service in organizations of the Russian Armed Forces, other troops, military formations, and bodies as civilian personnel continue performing alternative civilian service in those organizations when mobilization is announced.
2. Citizens performing alternative civilian service in organizations under federal executive bodies, regional executive bodies, or local self-government bodies may be sent to perform alternative civilian service in civilian personnel positions with the Russian Armed Forces, other troops, military formations, bodies, and special formations, under the procedure set out in the alternative civilian service regulation.
Whether someone could refuse forced mobilization and replace it with alternative civilian service remained an open question. In November 2023, while reviewing a specific case, Russia’s Supreme Court ruled that a person who had previously performed alternative civilian service instead of mandatory service also has the right to alternative civilian service under mobilization.
No laws or regulations governing alternative civilian service during mobilization have ever been adopted.
In October 2022, State Duma lawmakers Sardana Avksentyeva and Maxim Gulin introduced a bill titled “On Citizens’ Right to Replace Mandatory Military Service With Alternative Civilian Service During Mobilization.” The State Duma sat on the bill for a long time before rejecting it in July 2024. In its official response, the Russian government stated only that “the bill requires substantial revision” because it fails to account for the new Article 17¹.
How the authorities expanded the categories of people who can be mobilized or forced to sign a military contract
Prisoners
In November 2022, lawmakers passed a law lifting the general ban on mobilizing people with an outstanding or unexpunged conviction for a serious crime — an intentional crime punishable by more than five years in prison, or a “negligent act” punishable by more than 10. In place of that blanket ban, the mobilization law now lists specific crimes: mostly “terrorism,” “extremism,” and sabotage offenses, as well as sexual crimes against a minor.
On June 24, 2023, the day Yevgeny Prigozhin’s mutiny ended, Vladimir Putin signed a law establishing a formal contract system for prisoners. It replaced an unofficial arrangement for presidential pardons of convicts, whom the Russian mercenary group Wagner had actively recruited. Under the system, the state conditionally releases prisoners and sends them to war. Such a person can receive final “forgiveness” only after suffering a serious wound, reaching the maximum age for service, or when mobilization ends (and, starting in 2024, also for receiving a state award).
That same day, lawmakers also amended the Penal Code to spell out the procedure for releasing prisoners who were called up under mobilization or who had signed a contract during mobilization.
Prisoners who sign contracts face roughly the same restrictions as mobilized prisoners, though the list of “off-limits” crimes is periodically revised. Since August 2026, for instance, smugglers and members of armed gangs and criminal organizations, among others, have been allowed to sign contracts.
People charged with a crime
Since March 2024, a person facing criminal prosecution can sign a contract in exchange for having their case suspended. Like prisoners, they must wait for mobilization to end, or for a wound, an award, or reaching the maximum age of service.
Since the summer of 2023, that age limit during mobilization has been raised to 65 for all service members (except senior officers, whose limit was raised to 70).
Foreigners and stateless persons
Formally, foreigners and stateless persons are not part of the mobilization manpower pool, since they cannot be mobilized through the usual process. In practice, though, they are: they can be forced to sign a contract instead.
In November 2025, for example, Putin issued a decree “On the Temporary Procedure for Granting Russian Citizenship and Issuing Residency Permits in Russia.” Under the new rule, foreign men between 18 and 65 can no longer apply for a Russian residency permit or citizenship unless they have served in the Russian armed forces or been found medically unfit for service.
The decree makes an exception for all Belarusian citizens and certain “privileged” categories of applicants, such as former Soviet citizens or people with direct relatives born within Russia’s current territory.
Imprisoned foreigners and stateless persons
Since July 7, 2025, foreigners and stateless persons who have been convicted of a crime — or merely charged with one — have been explicitly permitted to sign military service contracts during mobilization on the same terms as Russian citizens.
How the authorities toughened criminal penalties for those who have already been mobilized
Immediately after announcing “partial” mobilization in 2022, the authorities rewrote numerous articles in Chapter 33 of the Criminal Code, “Crimes Against Military Service.” Those articles can be used to prosecute only service members, including mobilized ones.
Starting September 24, 2022, several articles gained new clauses imposing harsher punishment for the same crime when committed ”during mobilization or martial law, in wartime, or in the context of an armed conflict or hostilities”:
- Article 333. Resisting a superior officer or coercing a superior to violate their military service duties (up to 15 years in prison instead of eight)
- Article 334. Violent acts against a superior officer (up to 15 years instead of eight)
- Article 337. Unauthorized absence from a unit or place of service (up to 12 years instead of five)
- Article 338. Desertion (up to 20 years instead of 10)
- Article 339. Evading military service duties by feigning illness or other means (up to 12 years instead of seven)
- Article 340. Violating combat duty regulations (now carries a minimum five-year prison sentence)
- Article 341. Violating border service regulations (up to 10 years instead of five)
- Article 342. Violating guard duty regulations (up to 10 years instead of five)
- Article 344. Violating internal service and garrison patrol regulations (up to seven years instead of five).
In addition, since September 24, 2022, committing any crime “during mobilization” formally counts as an aggravating circumstance, meaning courts can impose a harsher sentence within the limits the law allows. But that aggravating circumstance cannot push a sentence above the maximum term or penalty set for the relevant article of the Criminal Code.

articles.title: Ukrainian Drones Strike Russia’s $60 Million Kasta-2E2 Radar in Zaporizhzhia
articles.body:

Ukrainian Drones Strike Russia’s $60 Million Kasta-2E2 Radar in Zaporizhzhia
Ukrainian drones struck a Russian Kasta-2E2 radar station in the Zaporizhzhia region, with the hit confirmed through objective monitoring, Ukraine’s General Staff reported.
According to the General Staff, the strike took place on September 1 near the settlement of Vyshneve in the Zaporizhzhia region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian drones struck both the radar’s antenna and the equipment station of the vehicle operating the Russian system. The General Staff did not provide further details on the extent of the damage.
The Kasta-2E2, also designated 39N6, is a Russian mobile three-coordinate radar system designed to detect and track aerial targets flying at low and extremely low altitudes. The system determines the coordinates of detected targets and transmits the data to air defense command posts.
The radar is capable of detecting aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles, including targets operating at very low altitudes. Its detection range extends from approximately 5 to 150 kilometers (3 to 93 miles), while its altitude coverage reaches up to 6 kilometers (3.7 miles).
A small drone flying at an altitude of around 60 meters can reportedly be detected by the Kasta-2E2 from a distance of approximately 30 to 44 kilometers (19 to 27 miles), depending on the height of the radar’s antenna mast, which can be raised to as high as 50 meters.
Depending on its configuration, the estimated cost of a Kasta-2E2 radar system starts at approximately $60 million.
Ukraine’s General Staff reported that Ukrainian forces targeted multiple Russian military sites in the occupied Donetsk region and Russia’s Bryansk region on September 1 and overnight into September 2. The military also confirmed that earlier operations had destroyed a Russian MiG-29 fighter jet and a Ka-27 helicopter.

articles.title: Burkina Faso Conducts Target Practice With Most Weapons of Chinese Origin
articles.body:
Burkina Faso Armed Forces conducted target practice using Chinese artillery and missile systems.
Footage of the Chinese weapons in action was broadcast by Burkina Faso’s national television.
During the exercises, the country also publicly demonstrated for the first time an air defense missile system not previously observed in its arsenal, which is likely the Sky Dragon 30.
The footage shows live-fire exercises involving CS/SH1 122 mm wheeled self-propelled howitzers, PLL-05 120 mm self-propelled mortars, and SR-5 modular multiple rocket launchers.
The CS/SH1 is a 122 mm artillery system mounted on a 6×6 wheeled chassis, with a claimed range of approximately 22–27 km, depending on the type of ammunition used. The PLL-05 self-propelled mortar is based on an armored vehicle from the WZ551 family and is equipped with a 120 mm gun-mortar. The military also deployed the SR-5 MLRS, capable of firing various types of guided and unguided rockets.
In the second half of the video, the deployment of the radar, operators working at the command post, and the launch of a SAM from a mobile launcher are shown.
According to Janes’ assessment, the dimensions of the launch pod containers are consistent with China’s Norinco Sky Dragon 30 system.
As for the specifications published by the manufacturer, the Sky Dragon 30 missile can engage aerial targets at ranges of up to 30 km and altitudes of up to 18 km. It is equipped with an infrared homing seeker, while the system is claimed to be capable of engaging up to 12 targets simultaneously.
The footage also shows a radar identified in open sources as the IBIS-150. The radar is reportedly capable of detecting aerial targets at ranges of up to 130 km and tracking up to 144 targets simultaneously.
The public demonstration of the Sky Dragon 30 marked the first known confirmation of the system’s presence in Burkina Faso. The country had not announced its procurement officially.
Burkina Faso’s military junta has received significant batches of Chinese-made armored vehicles since 2024.

articles.title: Badenoch says UK must prepare for possible war by 2030
articles.body:
Kemi Badenoch has said Britain must increase defence spending to 3 per cent of GDP by 2030, warning that the country could face a major conflict within the next four years and arguing that higher military spending can no longer be delayed.
In a speech on Britain’s defence on Thursday, the Conservative leader linked the spending requirement to Russia, cyber attacks, threats to critical infrastructure and wider instability, while setting out the case for the £10 billion annual increase in defence spending announced by her party.
Badenoch said: “Before the summer, Keir Starmer was given intelligence that Russia could launch an attack on NATO as soon as 2030. Not enough politicians in Parliament have fully appreciated what that means. By that of course I mean Labour politicians. What this means that within the next 4 years, the UK could be at war with the world’s biggest nuclear armed state. Because under Article 5, an attack on any NATO country is an attack on all of them.”
She also referred to Russian naval activity around Britain and threats to undersea infrastructure, saying: “Vladimir Putin has called Britain Russia’s number one enemy. Russian warships have been sailing through the English Channel and the undersea cables which power our internet and power our entire information and communication network have come under threat. People may not see it in their day to day lives, but hostile states are constantly pushing the boundaries with unconventional warfare.”
Badenoch argued that national security needed to encompass more than conventional military forces, pointing to cyber security, energy infrastructure and national resilience.
She said: “National security is not just about tanks, boots on the ground and planes in the air. It is about our cyber defences, it is about our energy security, it is about our country’s resilience. National security does not just happen we also have to pay for it, and that means spending more money on defence.”
The Conservative leader compared the UK’s position with increased defence investment elsewhere in NATO, citing Poland’s expansion of its armed forces and higher German defence spending. She also referred to Greece already spending around 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence.
Badenoch said: “Being an island might make us feel safer, but it does not prevent conflict from coming to us. And let’s be honest, conflict is coming. We must act now. Because the defence of the nation is the first duty of government.”
She called for defence spending to rise every year until reaching 3 per cent of GDP by 2030, saying: “We need to increase our defence spending every year so we can get to 3% of GDP by 2030, anything after that is too late.”
The Conservatives have proposed increasing annual defence expenditure by around £10 billion by 2029/30 compared with current government plans. The party says the increase would be funded through welfare reductions and reallocating money from other areas of government expenditure, including civil research and development, the British Business Bank and the National Wealth Fund.
Badenoch said: “Finding the money to pay for defence means making tough choices, it means making difficult trade-offs.”
She added: “We have now completed our work to get to 3%.
“And today my team have set out our plan to remove the housing benefit and remove the VAT exemption for Motability, alongside savings from the disastrous Chagos Deal,
“And repurposing money from the British Business Bank into defence, we will be able to hit that 3% target.
“And let’s be clear, 3% is the minimum our country needs to stay safe.”
The speech also connected defence policy with the wider state of the economy, with Badenoch arguing that Britain’s ability to sustain greater military expenditure depends on controlling borrowing and public spending.
She said: “Defence is not separate from the economy. Fiscal responsibility is part of national security.”
Badenoch also repeated the Conservative proposal for a £17 billion Sovereign Defence Fund, which the party says would support military readiness and investment in the British defence industrial base.
The Labour Party was approached for comment on Badenoch’s remarks and the Conservatives’ defence spending proposals, but had not responded at the time of publication.
Closing the defence section of her speech, Badenoch said: “Russia will attack a country it thinks is weak. It will not attack a country it knows is strong.
“We need to be strong. If you want peace, you prepare for war.”

articles.title: Ukraine to face difficulties amid severe air defense missile shortage this winter — media
articles.body:
NEW YORK, September 4. /TASS/. Ukraine’s armed forces will face serious challenges in continuing combat operations this winter because of a critical shortage of air defense missiles, Bloomberg columnist Kollen Post wrote.
The key problem is the shortfall in fresh missile deliveries for US-made Patriot air defense systems, which is linked to US military operations in the Middle East. Under the current circumstances, Washington is giving priority to Iran, negatively affecting NATO’s support program for Ukraine.
Ukrainian authorities have no alternative to US-made Patriot systems at this stage. By their estimates, Ukraine will need about 300 missiles for the system this winter. However, the US arsenal has 800 next-generation PAC-3 missiles, as well as "several hundred" older PAC-2 missiles.
Against this backdrop, European Union countries are urging Spain and Greece to send part of their Patriot stocks to Ukraine. The Ukrainian side is also in talks with South Korea and Japan on the matter but has not yet secured the necessary results.
