articles.title: U.S. Special Envoys to Visit Russia and Ukraine This Weekend – TASS

U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are scheduled to visit Russia and Ukraine this weekend to revive negotiations aimed at ending the war, the state-run news agency TASS reported Friday, citing a source familiar with the matter.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov declined to confirm or deny the report, telling journalists that officials would announce details “when these contacts take place.”
The last round of U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine took place in February, shortly before the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran.

articles.title: Ousted Ukrainian defense chief launches Palantir-backed company
articles.body:
Ousted Ukrainian defense chief launches Palantir-backed company
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov has announced the launch of a new military technology company, with Palantir CEO Alex Karp set to become its lead investor.
Fedorov has remained highly active in business and politics since Vladimir Zelensky dismissed him in mid-July amid reported tensions with then-commander-in-chief Aleksandr Syrsky. The former minister has also grown increasingly critical of Zelensky, claiming he was removed over his anti-corruption efforts and calling for elections, which have been repeatedly postponed under martial law.
Last week, Fedorov unexpectedly emerged as an adviser on “defense innovations” to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto. He said his role would involve helping Rome “develop modern warfare technologies” and “improve the defense sector.”
This week, Fedorov announced building “our own defense tech company” with the CEO of Palantir, a US data-mining and military tech company, which has been providing AI solutions for the Ukrainian military, set to become its key investor. Fedorov shared a video of him meeting with Karp, with the tech mogul showering the ex-minister with praise.
“We’ve worked together for a half decade. I have been absolutely inspired by what you and the Ukrainians have pulled off and very and super delighted that we could play a part. And you and your colleagues are launching a company that I think will be defining for the world, bringing your knowledge and acumen about the art of war as a product to allied countries,” Karp told Fedorov.
The ties between Fedorov and Karp span well beyond the ex-minister’s six-month tenure as defense minister. Before assuming the post in mid-February, he oversaw Ukraine’s digital transformation in various capacities. Immediately after his dismissal, Fedorov claimed to have been offered a job by Karp.
While Western and Ukrainian media have widely portrayed Fedorov as a military visionary focused on drone warfare, the uptick in long-range strikes against Russia during his tenure was primarily built upon the expansion of drone production in Western Europe secured under his predecessors. Fedorov’s repeated pledges to reform Ukraine’s chaotic mobilization drive did not materialize, with the practice of grabbing random men in the streets to force them into the military arguably growing even more violent under Fedorov.
The anti-graft crusade supposedly led by Fedorov has remained questionable at best. Multiple media reports suggest he focused more on wresting contracts away from companies associated with Zelensky’s inner circle and steering them to companies linked to him personally than on truly battling corruption. Federov’s background has further fueled suspicion. Before entering Zelensky’s government, he considered himself a businessman while repeatedly facing allegations of running online and phone scams, laundering money through online advertising, and engaging in other fraudulent activities.

articles.title: German warship secretly fires ballistic missile in Atlantic
articles.body:
A German warship has fired an Israeli-made LORA ballistic missile during a live test in the North Atlantic, with the German Navy saying the launch demonstrated a strike capability with a potential range beyond anything it had previously operated.
German media reports, citing a German Navy spokesman, said two German frigates had deployed to waters between Ireland and Iceland for the test on Tuesday night. Images from the exercise show a containerised launcher positioned on the deck of a German vessel.
The messaging here could hardly be clearer. By disclosing a test that had deliberately been kept secret, NATO was sending a direct signal to Moscow: European forces are developing longer-range strike options, and not every capability will be visible before it is ready.
NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum said the test had been kept secret until after it was completed and involved a German frigate firing the missile in the North Atlantic.
The command stated: “Kept secret. Now revealed. The German Navy just tested the Israeli LORA ballistic missile from a German frigate in the North Atlantic — quietly, deliberately and with a range of 500+ km.”
Kept secret. Now revealed. 🚀🇩🇪
The German Navy just tested the Israeli 🇮🇱 LORA ballistic missile from a German frigate in the North Atlantic — quietly, deliberately and with a range of 500+ km.
NATO 3.0 looks like this:
Europe is taking more responsibility, building serious… pic.twitter.com/K8x2JE61Gs
— NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum – JFCBS (@NATOJFCBS) September 2, 2026
It added: “NATO 3.0 looks like this: Europe is taking more responsibility, building serious capabilities and keeping a few cards close to the chest. Deterrence just got a little more interesting.”
Vice Admiral Jan Christian Kaack, Inspector of the German Navy, said: “With the successful launch of a ballistic missile last night in the North Atlantic, we made naval history. I am extremely satisfied with this achievement.”
Kaack added that the system “can be successfully deployed from our units, and the potential range exceeds anything we have known before.”
In his original statement, the German Navy chief said the trial opened a new chapter for maritime deterrence and readiness, stating that the system could be operated successfully from German units and that its possible reach exceeded previous German naval capabilities.
The test was conducted with Israel Aerospace Industries’ LORA, or Long-Range Artillery Weapon System. According to IAI, the missile has a range of around 400 kilometres and an accuracy of within 10 metres, while NATO’s public account of the German test referred to a range of more than 500 kilometres.
Israel Aerospace Industries said the missile was launched from an operational German vessel equipped with a command trailer and launcher. According to the company, the missile followed its planned trajectory, navigated to the target and successfully struck it, with both the weapon system and missile meeting the objectives of the trial.
Boaz Levy, Chairman of IAI, said: “This is an unprecedented achievement for IAI and the Israeli Ministry of Defense. The successful trial of the LORA missile, launched from a naval vessel and striking its target with exceptional precision, took place overnight in Germany – the country where the world’s first ballistic missile was developed.”
He added: “This trial demonstrates Israel’s technological strength and the unique cooperation between Israel and Germany. It marks another significant achievement alongside the deployment of the Arrow 3 system on German soil, further strengthening Germany’s defense and deterrence capabilities and deepening the strategic partnership between our two countries.”
IAI chief executive Guy Bar Lev said: “Israel Aerospace Industries is proud to take part in strengthening the strategic cooperation between the State of Israel and the Government of Germany. This significant milestone is underscored by the operational live-fire exercise (OPEX) of the LORA system, one of the world’s most advanced and combat-proven ballistic missile systems.”
The German Navy is using its OPEX initiative to trial technologies and operational concepts as part of its Marine 2035 and Beyond programme. The process is intended to allow new systems to be tested rapidly under conditions intended to resemble operational use as closely as possible.
The North Atlantic launch comes as Germany expands its investment in long-range strike and air and missile defence. The country has also begun fielding the Israeli-developed Arrow 3 ballistic missile defence system as part of its wider effort to strengthen national and NATO defensive capabilities.

articles.title: Cabinet proposes NT$145.7 billion in additional Taiwan defense spending
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Cabinet on Thursday approved NT$145.7 billion (US$4.64 billion) in additional defense spending for 2026, including funding for missile systems and uncrewed vehicles excluded from a special defense procurement law.
The Cabinet approved a record NT$607.6 billion in supplemental spending for the 2026 central government budget, per Rti. The defense allocation includes NT$4.1 billion for personnel, NT$8.2 billion for operations, and NT$133.4 billion for military investment.
The personnel funding includes NT$2.5 billion to expand military recruitment and NT$1.6 billion to increase allowances for combat units and eligible personnel. The operating budget includes NT$7.3 billion for ammunition and NT$900 million for the Taiwan Tactical Network integration project.
The military investment portion includes NT$13 billion for seven projects, NT$55.9 billion for three types of drones, and NT$64.5 billion for two classified projects, Rti reported. The package also includes funding for the Integrated Battle Command System, Chien Kung missiles, and uncrewed vehicles covered by the recently passed unmanned vehicle law.
Cabinet Spokesperson Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) directed that the systems be included because national defense could not wait for the legislative process, according to Rti. The Legislative Yuan previously approved a scaled-back version of the special defense procurement law that excluded the unmanned systems and other domestically developed weapons.
Lee said the government would review the legislation and its implementation after receiving it Wednesday. She said the supplemental budget was intended to make up for delays in military buildup.
Department of Strategic Planning Director Lieutenant General Huang Wen-chi (黃文啓) said the special defense budget was originally NT$1.25 trillion and covered 23 items, per CNA. Because the full amount was not approved, the 13 items for domestic production, commercial purchases, and Taiwan-US joint development were included in the supplemental budget.
Huang said the supplemental budget was proposed primarily based on the military buildup schedule, as uncrewed vehicle units began forming last year and all units were in place as of January. The military plans to procure 40,000 coastal attack drones, 600 coastal reconnaissance drones, and 100 small one-way unmanned surface vessels in 2027, per Storm Media.

articles.title: Germany records over 165 suspected acts of sabotage since beginning of year
articles.body:
Germany records over 165 suspected acts of sabotage since beginning of year
German law enforcement authorities have registered more than 165 suspected acts of sabotage and nearly 750 incidents involving suspicious drones over military sites and critical infrastructure since the beginning of 2026.
Source: Germany newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung, citing a confidential report by Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA)
Details: The document was drawn up based on the findings from the first months of work by the Joint Centre for Countering Hybrid Threats (GAZ-Hybrid), which opened in Berlin in mid-June. The threats recorded also included cases of espionage that did not involve drones.
Germany's Federal Prosecutor General and state prosecutors have opened 24 criminal investigations into espionage this year. Half of these concern cyberattacks. Another 40 investigations into suspected cyber espionage are ongoing.
Overall, police have registered 112 offences linked to espionage. More than 60 cases involved unauthorised photography or filming of military sites or equipment, while in 26 incidents law enforcement authorities suspect intelligence activity aimed at carrying out acts of sabotage. The highest numbers were recorded in Brandenburg (23 offences), North Rhine-Westphalia (21), Schleswig-Holstein (21) and Lower Saxony (15).
In addition, security authorities recorded 747 cases involving suspicious drones. These included 1,068 drone flights over critical infrastructure, military bases and defence industry plants.
Drone operators are very rarely arrested. However, in July, authorities in Bavaria detained a Moldovan citizen who had used a drone to spy on a facility belonging to defence company KNDS. Investigators believe he was acting on instructions from Russian intelligence services.
The document also describes an incident that took place on 9 August near a gas processing plant in Grossenkneten, Lower Saxony. A security guard at the facility was trying to locate the operators of drones that had been spotted when he encountered two unidentified people wearing balaclavas near the fence. The suspects slammed his head against the bonnet of a car and fled. They have not been found.
Background:
- In April 2024, authorities in Bavaria detained two agents who held dual Russian and German citizenship. They had been monitoring US military bases and planning attacks on routes used to transport military aid to Ukraine.
- In July 2024, a parcel caught fire at a DHL cargo terminal at Leipzig Airport. German intelligence services later stressed that a cargo plane disaster had been avoided only because the flight was delayed by chance and said Russia was behind the sabotage.
- In July 2026, a fire broke out on a railway line in western Germany between Düsseldorf and Cologne, damaging signalling cables and disrupting train services. Law enforcement authorities are investigating the incident as a possible act of sabotage.
- On 4 August, a drone carrying explosives was found at Leipzig/Halle Airport near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft. Three drones were found in total near the airport. Evidence discovered at the scene indicates that Russia attempted to blow up aircraft.

The world is forgetting how to fear nuclear war
For decades, mutual deterrence among major powers provided the world with a degree of predictability, with the nuclear factor lying at the heart of this system since the middle of the last century. The great powers restrained one another and, in doing so, restrained themselves.
They understood that overly ambitious geopolitical adventures could carry unacceptable risks, thus “strategic stability” was the reassuring term given to what was, in reality, the capacity for mutual destruction. International institutions grew around this balance like mushrooms around a tree trunk, but beneath all the agreements and diplomatic language lay something much simpler: the fear of the consequences of a direct conflict between major powers. Now, however, that system is falling apart.
Many posit that the problem is precisely the loss of fear as political elites have ceased to believe that nuclear war is genuinely possible and hence the declining restraint we see in the conflict in Ukraine, in the Middle East and, potentially, in Asia.
The apparent solution is therefore to remind everyone just how terrifying nuclear war would be. Restore the fear, the argument goes, and states will once again exercise restraint and become ready to negotiate new rules. There’s logic to this, but there’s also an enormous danger.
What happens if nuclear weapons are actually used? Either they produce precisely the catastrophe humanity has feared for eight decades, with irreparable consequences, or something quite different happens, such as there’s terrible destruction, but the world does’t end and the weapon doesn’t even guarantee victory.
In that case, nuclear weapons could cease to be primarily a political and psychological barrier and become simply another means of warfare, albeit an extraordinarily powerful one. Would this restore fear? Or would states instead accelerate the development of nuclear weapons designed for more effective battlefield use? Well, in the present atmosphere of growing recklessness, either is conceivable.
Nuclear weapons are the most powerful weapons humanity has invented and they were created to fight wars, but we discovered that they could perform another function by preventing the largest and most destructive wars from occurring at all. Today, however, perceptions seem to be returning to their starting point that a weapon is a weapon, even when it is nuclear.
Yet expecting weapons to solve the problems between states places impossible demands on them, particularly when warfare itself is becoming increasingly asymmetrical and all-pervasive.
States are finding it harder to hold on to what they can’t afford to lose. The erosion of borders, once celebrated as one of the great achievements of liberal globalization, is acquiring a much more alarming character.
The digital world is borderless by definition as drones cross dividing lines with increasing ease and mew technologies steadily undermine the ability of states to control and defend their territory and, in extreme circumstances, even to define where meaningful borders lie.
States won’t simply accept this loss of control, so every action produces a reaction, which means the struggle will become fiercer. More importantly, the battlefield will increasingly encompass almost every sphere of human activity.
Under such conditions, what does “strategic stability” even mean, and how can it be maintained?
War itself increasingly resembles not a means of resolving conflicts but a permanent form of interaction, even coexistence and there may be no decisive victory or defeat, but only repeated attempts to exhaust an opponent economically, militarily, politically, and psychologically.
However, prolonged attrition produces two contradictory effects. States become more experienced and capable of enduring confrontation, but at the same time, fatigue accumulates, along with the temptation to end an apparently endless struggle by reaching for the most decisive and destructive argument available.
The world is losing the systemic safeguards that once limited such impulses and it increasingly resembles a hunting ground during open season.
So what, then, can we hold on to? For now, perhaps only common sense and an accurate assessment of the relationship between our ambitions and our actual capabilities. It’s a fragile lifeline, but it may be enough to prevent us from feeding the flames and instead keep us clear of them.
At least until the value of restraint, including self-restraint, is once again understood by everyone.
This article was first published by Russia in Global Affairs, translated and edited by the RT team

articles.title: Chinese radios power Russia’s longer-range drone strikes
articles.body:
- Russia has extended live drone operator control to 150-175 kilometers using Chinese-made mesh radios, roughly double its 2025 range, according to KI Insights.
- The mesh network technology has let Russia redirect Geran-2 and Gerber drones toward mid-range strikes that have disabled over 250 Ukrainian gas stations.
Russian forces have significantly extended how far they can fly and control attack drones inside Ukraine over the past year by switching many of them to mesh-network radios, according to a report from Kyiv-based analytics firm KI Insights.
The technology, called MIMO mesh radio, lets a drone act as a mobile relay point in a decentralized radio network rather than depending on a single, direct radio link back to its operator. Since 2025, Russia has fitted the system to several of its drone types, including the Geran and Gerbera strike drones, the Orlan and Supercam reconnaissance drones, and the Lancet, Scalpel and Molniya models, according to the report, authored by Etienne Hertz, a radio-frequency specialist based in Ukraine.
Ukrainian military sources told KI Insights that a chain of mesh-linked drones can now maintain live operator control up to 150 to 175 kilometers (93 to 109 miles) from the farthest Russian ground station, roughly double what Russian mesh networks could manage in 2025. Russian pilots have demonstrated real-time control over Geran and Gerbera drones flying near the city of Dnipro, about 100 kilometers (62 miles) from the front line, the report said.
On July 17, a Geran drone operated by Russia’s 50th Separate Operational Brigade of Unmanned Systems Forces, known as Varyag, struck a gas condensate plant near Seleshchyna in Ukraine’s Poltava region while flying 125 kilometers (78 miles) from Russian-held territory and maintaining direct operator control the entire time, according to the report. KI Insights said Varyag has increasingly struck targets in Ukraine’s Sumy and Chernihiv regions rather than its earlier focus further south, a shift the firm said could signal Russian preparation to intensify operations along a northern front.
The mesh radios enabling this reach are not Russian-made. KI Insights traced the hardware to two Chinese manufacturers, Shenzhen Sinosun Technology and Shenzhen Xingkai Technology, with a Saint Petersburg-based company called Ajax Technologies distributing some of the radios inside Russia. The report said Russia remains fully dependent on Chinese components for the underlying mesh radio hardware, even if Russian engineers have contributed to how the systems are integrated into drones.
Mesh radios cost considerably more than the alternative many drone operators use, SpaceX’s Starlink satellite terminals, which run slightly above $400. Russia’s Chinese-made mesh modems cost between $2,000 and $12,000, and their range drops off sharply beyond 100 to 200 kilometers, unlike Starlink’s near-global coverage. Mesh links also carry higher latency, or delay, than Starlink, making them less useful against fast-moving targets, according to the report. Bureau 1440, a Russian satellite company, is expected to extend Russian drone operator range further later this year through a new satellite constellation called Rassvet, KI Insights said.
The report highlighted one specific case: Russian forces in the Zaporizhzhia area have converted the low-cost Molniya 2R drone, which normally costs $800 to $1,200, into an airborne mesh relay node by adding cameras, onboard computer-vision processors and a mesh radio, raising its cost to an estimated $4,000 to $5,000. Because the modified Molniya can both process its own sensor data and forward signals from other drones dozens of kilometers away, it lets Russian forces maintain aerial relay coverage cheaply and repeatedly, without relying on more expensive, harder-to-replace drones like the Orlan.
KI Insights said the range and video quality this technology provides has helped Russia shift many of its piston-engine Geran-2 and Gerber drones away from long-range strikes deep into Ukraine, where Ukrainian air defenses intercept 90 to 95% of incoming drones, and toward mid-range attacks on stationary infrastructure such as passenger trains and gas stations. The firm said this campaign has disabled or damaged more than 250 gas stations across northeastern, eastern, central and southern Ukraine.
KI Insights assessed that Russia’s mesh-drone capability is moving toward technological parity with NATO drone fleets and could pose risks to NATO logistics in a future conflict involving Russia or Belarus, though the firm noted Russian video links still carry higher latency than NATO systems typically tolerate. The report did not specify a timeline for when Russian capabilities might reach that level, or how Ukraine’s own electronic warfare units plan to counter the expanding mesh networks.

articles.title: Beyond missiles: Why Israel’s civilian infrastructure needs stronger defenses - editorial
articles.body:
When five major Mediterranean desalination plants went offline earlier this week, household taps didn't run dry. It exposed why water, electricity, food, and shelters must be treated as matters of national security. That is precisely why the incident should be treated as a warning rather than dismissed as a crisis successfully contained.
The plants were forced offline after unusually high seawater turbidity, apparently caused by microalgae carried north from the Nile Delta. Some subsequently resumed operating, but three remained offline on Wednesday.
The authorities protected residential supply, while municipalities were instructed to reduce nonessential consumption, and agricultural water was temporarily cut in parts of the country. Negev farmers warned that crops at the height of the growing season could suffer irreversible damage within a day.
On one level, the outcome demonstrates the water system’s strength: Israel maintained household supplies even after losing most of its desalination capacity. That is a considerable accomplishment in a dry country that once lived at the mercy of rainfall.
Exposing the concentration beneath the success
But the incident also exposed the concentration beneath that success. A small number of large facilities produce much of Israel's drinking water, and all require usable seawater, electricity, and functioning pumping infrastructure. A single natural event was enough to interrupt several at once.
A recent preprint by researchers from Ben-Gurion University of the Negev and the Max Planck Institutes modeled scenarios in which drought, electricity disruptions, war, cyberattacks, and marine pollution overlap. The research has not yet undergone peer review, but the question it raises is immediately relevant: Is Israel preparing for several systems to fail at once, or is each ministry still preparing for its own isolated scenario?
Israel understandably speaks about national security through the language of armies, borders, intelligence, and missile defense; those threats are real and immediate. But civilians cannot live beneath Iron Dome alone.
Security also means that the lights remain on, hospitals keep functioning, food reaches supermarkets, and families have somewhere protected to go when the air-raid siren sounds. These are not softer alternatives to national defense; rather, they are what allow a country to absorb an attack and continue operating.
Recent State Comptroller’s Reports have revealed a recurring weakness in precisely these areas. In January, the comptroller found that one-third of Israelis lacked adequate access to standard protected spaces, and that 12% of public shelters were unfit for use. A February audit found that emergency planning for the electricity sector had not kept pace with changes in the industry, and that responsibility for critical diesel stocks remained unresolved years after the government ordered it transferred.
No single government body overseeing the full picture of emergency food security
Last October a report found no single government body was overseeing the full picture of emergency food security, and there was no long-term national strategy. A separate February audit found that prior to the October 7 massacre, Israel did not have an approved operational plan for mass civilian evacuation, leaving local authorities to improvise as some 210,000 residents were displaced.
Since then, some of the relevant government bodies have taken steps. The Energy and Infrastructure Ministry, for example, has cited a NIS 1 billion program launched during the war to strengthen infrastructure and emergency stocks. This week’s uninterrupted household water supply also reflects serious advance planning.
The argument, therefore, is not that nothing works; it is that Israel repeatedly relies on capable workers and emergency improvisation to close gaps that should have been resolved beforehand. Across sectors, responsibility remains divided, plans age without being updated, and corrective action accelerates only once the danger becomes visible.
That is partly a problem of political incentives. Air-defense procurements and military operations produce announcements that maintenance, redundancy, and coordination between ministries rarely do. When they succeed, nothing dramatic happens: The tap runs, the refrigerator stays cold, and the local authority knows what to do.
With a little under two months until the October 27 election, parties asking Israelis to trust them with national security should be expected to address this side of it as well. They should explain who will hold binding responsibility for civilian preparedness, which deficiencies have been corrected, what deadlines remain, and how weaker municipalities will be brought up to standard.
The desalination disruption should not be forgotten when the last plant returns to operation. Israel’s strength is measured not only by whether it can strike its enemies or intercept their weapons, but by whether ordinary life can continue under pressure.

articles.title: Estonian defense minister quits after wasting €70 million on faulty shells for Ukraine
articles.body:
Estonian defense minister quits after wasting €70 million on faulty shells for Ukraine
Estonian Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur has announced his resignation after it emerged that Tallinn paid €70 million ($81 million) in advance for artillery shells for Ukraine to a company with no track record of producing the ammunition.
The scandal erupted on Wednesday after the Eesti Ekspress newspaper reported on the botched procurement and the ensuing legal dispute. In August 2024, Tallinn signed a contract with Italian-registered Datasel, owned by Indian company Neco Defence Munitions, to supply artillery ammunition for Ukraine. The government paid €15 million upfront despite neither company having any previous record of manufacturing artillery shells.
A second deal followed in October, with Estonia paying another €10 million in advance. The first batch was due to reach Ukraine in November, but Datasel reported problems and repeatedly delayed delivery.
Despite the setbacks, Estonia signed two more contracts with the company, eventually bringing total advance payments to around €70 million. The money came from the EU’s European Peace Facility, which has been extensively used to fund weapons and other military assistance for Kiev. Tallinn is now disputing the contracts in a case before the European Court of Arbitration in Strasbourg.
The government acknowledged the blunder, with Pevkur taking the “political responsibility” and announcing his resignation. The outgoing minister, who will stay in the role until a replacement is picked, appeared, however, to shift the blame for the affair on the country’s procurement authority, the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK).
“The defense minister does not conduct contract negotiations. The defense minister does not count socks and ammunition. The defense minister makes the fundamental decision to support Ukraine,” Pevkur said.
RKIK head Elmar Vaher acknowledged that his agency was to blame for the scandal, but shifted the responsibility to his predecessor, Magnus-Valdemar Saar.
“I have been familiar with the matter since January. I cannot see inside people’s heads to know how they were thinking and what the main arguments behind their decisions were,” Vaher told ERR. “The decision was made by RKIK’s former director general.”
It is unclear to what extent the contracts remain unfulfilled, since Estonian officials provided conflicting accounts. Pevkur said “tens of millions of euros’ worth of the ammunition” were delivered and are currently sitting “in a warehouse in a European country.”
The shells, however, were “not of sufficient quality” to send to Ukraine, according to the outgoing minister. The Defense Ministry’s secretary-general, Kaimo Kuusk, described the consignment as “wholly incomplete.” The Eesti Ekspress report called the munitions useless and faulty.

articles.title: Kiev demands global flight ban over Russia
articles.body:
Kiev demands global flight ban over Russia
Kiev has demanded that the UN aviation watchdog effectively shut Russian airspace to civilian traffic after Vladimir Zelensky threatened that Ukraine’s expanding long-range drone campaign would make flying over the country increasingly dangerous.
Ukrainian newspaper Zerkalo Nedeli reported on Wednesday that Infrastructure Minister Nikolay Kalashnik had sent a letter to Juan Carlos Salazar, secretary general of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), calling for action against flights through Russian airspace.
The letter urged the watchdog to “encourage aviation authorities, air navigation service providers and airlines” operating in Russia to take measures to “protect” civilian aircraft, including a complete ban on flights through Russian airspace by carriers from ICAO member states. 
“The presence of civilian aircraft in Russian airspace may entail particularly high risks,” Kalashnik reportedly wrote in the letter obtained by the outlet.
ICAO later issued a general statement on aviation safety but mentioned neither Russia nor Ukraine and did not directly address Kiev’s demand. Instead, it appealed to all member states to “assess the safety of airspace controlled by them and take all appropriate measures.”
Kiev’s demand followed an explicit threat from Zelensky to foreign airlines, insurers and governments on Tuesday that continued Ukrainian drone attacks would put civilian aviation in Russia at risk. 
“The safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” he said, urging carriers to reconsider flights to Moscow, St. Petersburg and other major Russian destinations.
Russian President Vladimir Putin described Zelensky’s warning as a move toward “state terrorism” and vowed that Moscow would respond if Kiev’s threats resulted in tragedy. “Let no one doubt that,” he said.
Ukraine has intensified long-range drone strikes on Russia in recent months, repeatedly grounding flights and causing prolonged disruptions at airports as air defenses respond to incoming UAVs. The attacks have also targeted Russian ports, energy facilities and civilian infrastructure, including e-commerce warehouses.
Drones have also struck residential areas, including high-rise apartment buildings and houses.
An attack last month on the Black Sea resort of Gelendzhik in southern Russia killed at least eight people, including four children, and wounded dozens more. Another strike on industrial and civilian sites in Nizhnekamsk, in Russia’s Republic of Tatarstan, killed 13 people, while a July 18 attack on a Wildberries warehouse in the town of Kotovsk in Tambov Region left seven workers dead.
Moscow has described the intensified Ukrainian strikes as indiscriminate terrorist attacks intended to distract from Kiev’s battlefield setbacks and has responded with renewed long-range strikes on Ukraine. The Russian military maintains that it does not target purely civilian facilities, saying its attacks are directed at military, defense-industrial and dual-use sites.

articles.title: Schiess Sworn in as New Space Force Chief: ‘We Must Grow with Intention’
articles.body:
JOINT BASE ANDREWS, Md.—Gen. Douglas A. Schiess assumed leadership of the Space Force on Sept. 3, succeeding Gen. B. Chance Saltzman as Chief of Space Operations during a change of responsibility ceremony here.
Schiess is just the third CSO in the Space Force’s history since the service was created in 2019. In his first address to Guardians, he emphasized the important role space has come to play in modern military operations—and the growing threats it attracts from adversaries intent on targeting space assets in orbit and on the ground.
“Every day, our potential adversaries advance their efforts to disrupt, degrade, and destroy our space capabilities, and they try to add to their own capacity to exploit space to their advantage,” Schiess said. “We cannot, we will not let that happen.”
A career space operator, Schiess has performed a number of missions in his career including missile warning, GPS, command and control, and launch. In 2023, he became the first commander of U.S. Space Forces-Space, USSF’s component to the U.S. Space Command combatant command. Most recently, he served as deputy CSO for operations, developing and implementing the policies that guide Space Force operations around the world.
That experience, he said, will inform the way he leads Guardians trained “to operate in the cold, dark vacuum of space” from operations centers on the ground that are also under threat—as evidenced in ongoing operations in the Middle East, where Iran has targeted ground-based space and missile defense infrastructure.
“Our Guardians operate from the ground, some in harm’s way—some in harm’s way today—and they require battlefield skills and the warrior mentality as much as our Soldiers, Sailors, Airmen, Marines, and Coast Guardsmen in our sister services,” he said.
Schiess’ emphasis on the growing threats and the warfighting contributions of Guardians continue themes that his predecessor, Saltzman, repeated often throughout his tenure.
Over the past four years, Saltzman helped grow the Space Force from 8,000 uniformed Guardians to 10,000—and he has positioned the force for even more expansion in the coming years. The service is on a path to double in size to 20,000 Guardians over the next five years, and its $71 billion budget request for fiscal 2027 is more than twice what USSF requested last year, as demand increases for space capabilities.
Speaking during the ceremony, Saltzman said he’s proud of the progress the Space Force has made, evidenced in recent months by its delivery of “critical effects” during multiple operations.
“We delivered critical effects on time and on target under fire, and we sustained that effort,” Saltzman said. “When called to action, the U.S. Space Force was ready, combat capable, and mission effective, and that about says it all.”
Saltzman praised Schiess’ leadership, operational experience, and genuine concern for Guardians, their families, and the joint and allied partners they serve alongside.
“He knows how to build teams, how to drive performance, and how to coax bureaucracies into mission success,” Saltzman said. “He has the expertise to make wise decisions. . . . He cares deeply for the people that do the work.”
In his first message to the force, issued shortly after his swearing in, Schiess harkened back to the Space Force’s early days and looked ahead to the future, calling on Guardians to “capitalize on our foundation and evolve to meet the demands of a new era.”
“As we drive our deliberate growth and execution, we will arm our Guardians to acquire, field, operate, and exploit the full spectrum of capabilities required to secure decisive space superiority,” he said. “Integrating into the Joint Force demands a rapid scaling of both our manpower and space capabilities. We must grow with intention, leveraging our industry partnerships to advance our weapon systems and the way we fight.”
Along with Schiess’ ascension to the service chief job this week, the Department of the Air Force also welcomed its assistant secretary for space acquisition and integration, Erich Hernandez-Baquero, who was sworn in at the Pentagon on Aug. 31. Hernandez-Baquero, who will oversee a growing space acquisition portfolio, fills a position that has been vacant since January 2025, though several officials have served in an acting capacity.

articles.title: USS Lincoln crew hits the streets of Thailand's Pattaya after nine-month deployment
articles.body:
USS Lincoln crew hits the streets of Thailand's Pattaya after nine-month deployment
US sailors and Marines streamed into the Thai resort city of Pattaya Thursday after a record-breaking nine months at sea. Local police said there had so far been no major incidents connected to the 5,000-strong contingent of US service members, though two sailors were sent back to the ship after a drunken bar brawl.
Buses carrying crew members of the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier streamed into Thailand’s seaside resort city of Pattaya on Thursday, as part of a port call after a lengthy deployment to the Middle East.
Read moreUSS Lincoln carrier docks near Thailand's Pattaya resort after nine months at sea
The Lincoln was supporting the US-Israeli war against Iran, and its deployment included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 260 days. Its lengthy deployment drew concerns last month about deteriorating mental health among the crew, including reported attempted suicides, as well as shortages of key food supplies aboard.
The Navy downplayed any problems, and US President Donald Trump maintained that the deployment was “not nearly long enough”.
The ship has been deployed for a total of 286 days, according to the US Embassy in Bangkok. Its total uninterrupted time at sea before Wednesday’s arrival in Chonburi province was 264 days.
The ship is expected to depart Thailand this weekend and continue its journey back to the US.
Pattaya draws in huge crowds of foreign tourists, both for its beach resorts and its nightlife. The seaside city has come under heavy scrutiny for its widespread sex tourism industry.
Thai authorities launched a crackdown on sex workers ahead of the ship's visit, although they denied it was linked to the sailors' arrival.
Shore leave
After clambering down from buses, laden with luggage, several service members told the Associated Press they were excited to be in Thailand.
Vendors and travel agents gathered outside the Hard Rock Hotel, the designated pickup and drop-off point for troops travelling from the Lincoln, which is docked nearby at Laem Chabang port.
They swarmed service members as they arrived, offering a range of souvenirs and services. Many sailors waved them away while waiting for their rides.
Two other ships from the Lincoln’s strike group are docked elsewhere in Thailand, with the destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. at Chonburi’s Sriracha port and the cruiser USS Robert Smalls in Map Ta Phut in neighbouring Rayong province.
A-ngoon Sombat travelled 200 kilometres between Pattaya and the central province of Ayutthaya to sell colourful braided bracelets to the visiting crew, as she does every time she hears a US ship is coming for a port call in Chonburi province.
She set up opposite the hotel entrance and had managed to make some sales, but said she is still unsure if business will be good this week.
“There are many vendors around. It’s really up to how lucky each of us are,” she said.
Dozens of service members could be spotted strolling around Pattaya's Terminal 21 mall with shopping bags in their hands as the afternoon sun was blazing outside.
A 20-year-old serving as a navigator aboard the Petersen, who declined to give his name because he was told not to speak to media while ashore, said the morale among his crew members was really high now that they had arrived in Thailand.
The sailor said it was his first deployment for the US Navy. He said it was a bit of an ordeal but he was happy to finally be on his way home.
He declined to comment when asked about the reports about the conditions on the Lincoln.
Other service members seem to have been less restrained.
Two sailors were sent back to the ship after a drunken altercation, Thai police said Friday.
Police were alerted to a "small scuffle" involving the sailors in the early hours of Thursday near Pattaya's nightlife hotspot Walking Street, city police chief Colonel Anek Srathongyoo told AFP.
"The sailors were drunk and they were fighting, making loud noise," he said.
