He described the incident as "trivial" and said local residents had only called police to prevent it from escalating.
The unidentified sailors were not charged as "they did not violate any Thai law", Anek said.
The US Navy sent the pair back to the ship, he added.
The police chief said there had been no other notable incidents since the Lincoln docked, and one Pattaya masseuse said it had been calmer than previous military port calls.
'Engineering marvel'
A spot just outside the Laem Chabang port had turned into a small attraction by Wednesday evening, as people gathered to catch a glimpse of the Lincoln.
People arrived by car and motorcycle to peer through a mesh fence at the ship, which is as long as about three American football fields. They took photos and videos, excitedly chatted with strangers about their chance to see the vessel.
American Keith Eldridge, who has lived in Thailand for five years, travelled from the neighbouring province of Chachoengsao just to see the ship. He was too late to catch the Lincoln docking but found the viewing spot through a recommendation from other enthusiasts he met along the way.
He said it was impressive for him to get to lay his eyes on this “engineering marvel”.
“When you get to look at something so big, wrapped up with so much technology, the radars, the sonars, the weapon systems, the propulsion systems, it is truly amazing that we can build it, float it, and we fight from it,” he said.
The Lincoln’s commanding officer, Captain Dan Keeler, said the ship will be heading home soon, but may make further supply stops. He declined to comment on the exact date the strike group is expected back in the US.
(FRANCE 24 with AP and AFP)

articles.title: ‘West wants to dictate’: Lavrov on ‘Fuhrer Ursula’ and NATO’s drive to divide Eurasia (KEY REMARKS)
articles.body:
‘West wants to dictate’: Lavrov on ‘Fuhrer Ursula’ and NATO’s drive to divide Eurasia (KEY REMARKS)
The EU and NATO are pursuing an increasingly aggressive campaign to attempt to divide Eurasia, contain Russia and China, and preserve Western global dominance, while hurting themselves in the process, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
Speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok on Thursday, Lavrov also said Moscow would not “beg” European nations to lift sanctions and accused the West of seeking to freeze rather than resolve the Ukraine conflict.
Addressing a lecture organized by the Russian Znanie Society, Lavrov presented the confrontation with the West as part of a broader struggle over the emerging multipolar world order. He argued that Western powers are trying to counter the rise of new economic and political centers while Russia is seeking closer cooperation across Eurasia based on “equality, mutual benefit, and honest dialogue.”
Here are the key takeaways from Lavrov’s address.
West ‘needs an enemy’
The EU and NATO are pursuing anti-Russia policies “even more fiercely, if not frantically” in an attempt to split the Eurasian continent, Lavrov said. He pointed to “walls and trenches” being built along EU borders with Russia, mocking claims that such measures are needed to prevent an alleged Russian invasion.
“This is sick imagination, but I think it is not so much sick imagination as deliberate policy,” he said.
According to Lavrov, both NATO and the EU need Russia to remain an enemy in order to justify their policies at home. “If this artificially created image of an enemy in the form of Russia disappears, the overwhelming majority of governments in the EU and NATO countries will simply be swept away by voters,” he stated.
He went on to accuse Europe of being unable to cooperate “honestly,” arguing that for more than 500 years it had been “the main source” of global upheaval, including two world wars. Europe, he said, is attempting to preserve what it sees as its right to global hegemony.
“Europe has never lived by its own means and its own mind,” Lavrov said. “It has always lived at the expense of others.”
‘Neo-Nazi spirit’ in Europe
The foreign minister said that a “neo-Nazi spirit” remains “very, very resilient” in parts of Europe and singled out Germany, where he said the “metastases of Nazism” were re-emerging.
Lavrov pointed to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s pledge to make Germany Europe’s leading military power “again,” saying the choice of word had left him “stunned.”
“If this person does not understand what the word ‘again’ means in this context, then this is extremely dangerous for Europe,” Lavrov said, accusing the region of once again becoming a source of ideas of “national and racial superiority.”
‘Dictate’ rather than ‘negotiate’
Lavrov linked Western policy in Europe to persistent “neo-colonial habits” elsewhere in the world. Western diplomacy, he argued, is increasingly based not on reaching agreements but on coercion.
“The West does not want to negotiate, it wants to dictate,” he said, adding that diplomacy has effectively been “replaced by sanctions.”
He accused Western states of seeking to undermine the consensus-based architecture built around the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which he praised for emphasizing consensus, mutual respect, and mutual benefit. According to the minister, Washington and its allies are instead creating smaller groupings designed to erode ASEAN’s central role.
He cited AUKUS – the US, UK, and Australia – as well as various “trilateral” and “quadrilateral” arrangements, and pointed to NATO’s expanding infrastructure in Asia. Lavrov said these structures ultimately serve a strategy of containing China and, “along with it,” Russia.
Multipolar alternative
Russia’s answer, Lavrov said, is to strengthen open regional platforms rather than build closed military groupings. He cited the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, the Eurasian Economic Union, ASEAN, BRICS, and other structures whose cooperation Moscow wants to deepen.
He highlighted the “ASEAN plus partners” model, saying its participants have equal rights and decisions are based on inclusive principles rather than diktat.
Lavrov linked these efforts to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s proposal for a “Greater Eurasian Partnership” open to all states on the continent and based on shared economic and development interests. He described the broader shift toward a multipolar world as an objective historical process that the West cannot stop.
EU ‘shot itself in the foot’
Lavrov also argued that the EU has inflicted severe economic damage on itself by abandoning Russian energy and accepting the destruction of the Nord Stream pipelines, describing the EU’s response to the sabotage as “self-humiliation.”
The bloc has effectively “shot itself in the foot and in the head,” he said, noting that Russian gas had been at least three times cheaper than current European prices. Soaring energy costs are now pushing industry to the US, where energy is three to four times cheaper, he added.
The EU is thus voluntarily squandering its economic advantages while transforming itself from an economic association into an “openly aggressive anti-Russian military bloc” supporting NATO.
Russia will not ‘beg’ Europe
Moscow, however, will not “beg” European nations to lift sanctions or restore economic ties, Lavrov said.
He argued that European leaders had assumed Russia valued its economic relationship with the EU so highly that it would eventually come “running and begging” for sanctions to be removed.
“That will not happen,” Lavrov said. “It is absolutely not in the genetic code of our people. We have, if you like, our own pride.” Russia has enough countries willing to cooperate “honestly,” he added, and does not need to seek reconciliation with Europe on its terms.
‘Fuhrer Ursula’
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen – “we call her Fuhrer Ursula,” Lavrov said – is stripping national governments of their powers and concentrating them in Brussels.
He stated that von der Leyen was trying to pull into the European Commission powers that EU members had never transferred to Brussels and which “remain with national governments.”
Lavrov also recalled von der Leyen saying Europeans would have to “suffer” from substantially higher energy prices so that Ukraine could defend “our European values.”
“Nobody asked her what those European values were,” he said, pointing to restrictions on the Russian language and the Ukrainian Orthodox Church. “If the legislative ban on the Russian language in education, culture, everyday life, and the media reflects European values, then welcome back to Nazism for Europe,” Lavrov said.
West wants to ‘freeze’ Ukraine conflict
Turning directly to Ukraine, Lavrov said Western governments had abandoned – or at least played down – their previous rhetoric about inflicting a “strategic defeat” on Russia and were instead seeking an immediate halt to fighting along the current front line.
Under that scenario, he said, Western countries would deploy “stabilization forces” to the territory remaining under Kiev’s control and provide security guarantees while refusing to recognize Russian control of Crimea, Donbass, and Novorossiya.
“They do not want to settle this conflict, but to freeze it, preserving this threat on our borders,” Lavrov added. Accepting such an outcome would also amount to abandoning Russia’s stated goal of “denazification,” he argued, saying Moscow would not agree to preserve an anti-Russian government in Kiev.
“We would betray our ancestors who defeated Nazism in 1945,” he said. “I do not think our people are ready for that.”

articles.title: “There is no such thing as a ‘sense of humor’ in the Criminal Code”: Russian stand-up comedians on surviving war and censorship
articles.body:
Russian stand-up comedy has changed dramatically over the past four and a half years of full-scale war. In early 2026, a Russian court sentenced comedian Artemy Ostanin to five years and nine months in prison for a joke about a legless Jesus. Within the stand-up community, the case was seen as a warning: anything said onstage can lead to very real trouble. Venues now ask performers in advance to keep their shows “apolitical,” while comedians themselves remove potentially risky material from acts or hide it behind hints and innuendo. Some comedians left Russia during the mobilization but later returned after finding that they could not afford to remain in exile. The Insider spoke to stand-up comedians who live and perform in Russia. They described what can be joked about today, how fear and self-censorship have changed the scene, and why even audiences are no longer always interested in political humor.
- 1.“Relax. I’ll go to prison, and you’ll be fine.” Stand-up comedian Viktor P.
- 2.“The audience has no idea how many jokes never make it to them.” Stand-up comedian Mikhail Z.
- 3.“Professional comedians are already consulting lawyers.” Stand-up comedian Alexei B.
- 4.“It’s making everyone a little paranoid.” Stand-up comedian Pavel V.
“Relax. I’ll go to prison, and you’ll be fine.” Stand-up comedian Viktor P.
Recently, I hosted a show at a popular bar in central Moscow. The organizers immediately asked us not to do anything political. There used to be times when someone would shout “Russia!” or start singing the national anthem or “Mother Earth” — none of that is allowed now, either.
And this is a bar in central Moscow, where young, modern people go — as modern as people can be these days. There is undoubtedly a demand for something political. You can give a little wink here and there. The kind of wink Ivan Urgant used to give — that’s about as far as you can go now.
For example, at one point my partner says, “I can’t talk about this.” And I say, “The only things we can talk about here are this or apples. Nothing else.” The audience understands that we’re talking about the party, and there’s an immediate, strong reaction. So you flash something for half a second — and that’s it.
There is an internal censorship among bar owners, comedians themselves, and stand-up club owners. The case of Artemy [Ostanin] shows how quickly things can escalate. Even if you didn’t mean anything by it, even if you hardly said anything at all, it’s still better to keep that in mind.
My audience is pretty modern and understands everything. But you still think: someone might record it, send it to someone, and then some activist could pick it up and make a big deal out of it.
I don’t think I’m important enough for anyone to want to put me in prison. But the news scares me — stories about completely unknown people being jailed for something, sometimes just for a repost. And you don’t always even understand what exactly the person did. It’s the same with performing onstage: you think not only about what you said, but also about how it might spread. Like with Nurlan Saburov: someone records something, and then it starts taking on a life of its own, separate from you. So you just become more careful.
The story of Artemy Ostanin, of course, shocked and deeply affected many of my friends and the stand-up community as a whole. When the whole avalanche was just beginning, many people told him to leave. But he treated what was happening as some kind of joke. Then he and his girlfriend tried to leave through Belarus, and they were eventually detained.
In the past, when something happened to comedians, the community reacted differently. Take Idrak Mirzalizade or Sasha Dolgopolov, for example. I clearly remember that when Idrak was having problems, we could end a show by saying, “Idrak is innocent,” or “Idrak should be free.” And we weren’t the only ones doing it. But when it happened to Artemy, nobody spoke out because they were scared. After that, venues became especially insistent: nothing about the “special military operation,” nothing about the war.
But, again, there is still a demand for it. And whenever I feel I can, I try to give a little wink. Sometimes, on the contrary, I take the position that everything is fine. For example, I see that people in the audience have understood, and I say, “America is complete garbage.” Everyone knows it’s post-irony. But technically, those are the words I said. As far as I know, the Criminal Code has no concept of a “sense of humor.”
Sometimes, though, the audience gets tense when political subjects come up. They’ve come to relax, to hear awkward stories about sex or the subway. I even say from time to time, “Relax. I’ll go to prison. You’ll be fine.” I’m not a political comedian. What matters to me is that people have fun.
Once, after a show, a couple of guys came up to me. They said, “That was great, we really loved it. Can we take a photo with you now and send it to a friend? He’s serving at the front right now.” What am I supposed to say to them? Of course, sure. I don’t want to get into a confrontation with them. I don’t want to try to change anyone’s mind or get into a political argument at a stand-up show. I don’t see myself as someone who can do that, and I don’t think it’s my job anyway. At the same time, I’ve been to protests. I was detained. I later emigrated, but I came back. You need money to live in exile, and I’m not a wealthy person.
There are, of course, comedians who describe their stand-up as political. Some joke about sanctions and liberals, perform in Donetsk, and so on. There’s one comedian, for example, who likes to call Vladimir Vladimirovich [Putin] “Uncle Vova” onstage and say, “I’ve got some political material.”
I keep an eye on comedians who have left, but at this point it’s really a matter of taste. I like what Idrak Mirzalizade does, and I like the club they run in Poland. I hardly watch Denis Chuzhoy, for example. Sometimes I feel that some comedians abroad lean too heavily into this “holier-than-thou” attitude. I accept that the problem may be with me. Maybe I just don’t want to admit that I’m also part of what’s happening because I’m still here. They chose to leave, and I didn’t. Well, I did, but then I came back. And when people tell me all this from abroad, sometimes I just don’t find it funny.
Sometimes I feel that some comedians abroad lean too heavily into this “holier-than-thou” attitude
I don’t watch comedians who joke about people who left or about emigration. I don’t even want to make myself angry over this propaganda. I have enough anxiety of my own. I don’t have the energy to sit around hating someone. I have to think about how I’m going to pay the rent.
These days I keep thinking about Ivan Urgant. His first appearance after Evening Urgant was canceled was a broadcast with Ayaz Shabutdinov. Ivan was talking to him about his business and creative work, and they were doing a presentation. The presentation had some blue-and-yellow charts. Ivan said, “Interesting choice of colors by whoever made this presentation.” Or there would be a shot of Dmitry Nazarov — and we know where he stands. Just very subtle things like that. But who finds that funny? I don’t know. It’s not really something for a mass audience anymore.
Do I feel hopeless? No. Probably because I simply don’t want to. I try to stay positive. I didn’t choose the time I was born into. And I still want to be happy. But I guess I’ve stopped expecting hot water to be a given. I’m just trying not to lose heart.
Of course, everything that’s happening gets me down. Sometimes I feel completely drained because I don’t know what else I can do or say. Maybe the only thing I can do is help the audience let off a little steam when I go onstage.
Yes, I don’t have the money to emigrate. But I actually like living in Russia. I’d like to be able to live here and travel at the same time. But I don’t feel like, “That’s it, I can’t make a joke about this subject onstage anymore — what a nightmare, my life is over.” I have no idea what will happen next. Maybe a year from now I’ll look back and think, “Wow, remember when we talked with that journalist? Those were the good old days. Things are nothing like that now!” Or maybe it’ll be the other way around.
“The audience has no idea how many jokes never make it to them.” Stand-up comedian Mikhail Z.
I perform at various venues around the city, and everything there is very chaste. Before a show, the organizer reads through my material and cuts anything that isn’t allowed. I had a pretty innocent joke about women who provide paid call-out services — caregivers. They told me, “Rephrase it so there’s no hint of prostitution.” But how am I supposed to rephrase it? In the end, I said, “A woman with an elevated level of social responsibility.”
Before a show, the organizer reads through my material and cuts anything that isn’t allowed
You can’t joke about VPNs. Crude jokes are off-limits, too — although it’s not clear what counts as crude. I had a joke: “My eyesight is so bad, I vomit farther than I can see.” They even banned the word “vomit.” So someone sits there reading through the material, marking things in red: cut this, absolutely not.
The organizer is about 25, but I understand why he does it: he’s simply afraid. Everything could be checked, someone could come along and jot something down in a notebook, and then there could be trouble. After all the cases of people being detained or punished for things they’ve said at concerts or on air, everyone is now playing it safe.
In fact, it’s even worse than ordinary censorship. Nobody directly orders the organizers to cut a joke about a caregiver or the word “vomit.” Instead, people try to anticipate what they could theoretically be punished for and ban even more — just to be on the safe side.
I don’t perform in clubs, although things are a little easier there. My audience is pretty academic, though: they sit politely, nobody drinks. So I’m grateful for everything. Of course, it’s frustrating when half your material gets cut. But as long as I can still perform, that’s something. Especially since the audience laughs — even if they have no idea how many jokes never made it to them.
“Professional comedians are already consulting lawyers.” Stand-up comedian Alexei B.
I suppose I should start by saying that in March of this year, stand-up comedian Artemy Ostanin was sentenced to prison. And that, of course, sent shockwaves through the stand-up community because it was the first high-profile case of its kind.
Before that, in September of last year, Dima Gavrilov was sentenced to 13 days in jail. At the time [of his alleged offense], he was living either in Armenia or Georgia, and during a performance he said something about the phrase “Russian pigs go home” — he said he liked that they were written there because they made him feel at home. He had a whole monologue about Russophobia, and that ultimately led to him being prosecuted.
But he asked us not to get involved in the case in any way or draw attention to it. He said he would deal with it himself with his lawyer and didn’t want to attract even more public attention. And, in fact, things turned out more or less fine and he was released.
Before Artemy was detained, I even messaged him to ask how things were going and whether he needed any help. He replied that everything was fine and that he would get out of it without a scratch. He didn’t.
A lot of comedians simply don’t know that laws like these exist. After what happened to Ostanin, though, they started getting nervous. Some have sent me their scripts and jokes and asked, “Do you think this could get me prosecuted under this law?” It’s pretty sad, because there’s no real legal awareness among the public.
Sometimes I listen to a monologue and think, Guys, you really can’t do that. And the person simply doesn’t understand that if he jokingly draws a Hitler mustache, sketches a swastika, or makes an ambiguous gesture, that could already be enough to trigger a prosecution. You explain it to him, and he looks at you as if to say, “Are you joking or are you serious?”
It seems to me that changes to the law like these simply don’t generate much public attention. They’re in the news, of course. People have been detained under these laws for years. But many simply don’t pay attention. There’s also this feeling that, “It definitely won’t happen to me. I’m not doing anything like that.” And then one day they could come knocking with a search warrant.
There are several factors at play. First, people are unaware of the law. Second, there’s a sense that things aren’t really that bad, that liberal media outlets are exaggerating it all and stoking panic. It’s like living under a dome: this hasn’t affected me so far, so it won’t affect me in the future, either.
We have a big chat for comedians with almost 3,000 people. Basically anyone who wants to perform can join, not just professional comedians. And after what happened to Artemy, there was a huge discussion there. But time passes, and everything quiets down again. I’ve been going to open mics lately, and I’m hearing jokes about Jesus, Hitler, terrorism, and 9/11 all over again. Almost nobody touches the “special military operation.” But the other subjects are coming back.
I’ve been going to open mics lately, and I’m hearing jokes about Jesus, Hitler, terrorism and 9/11 all over again
A novice comedian comes onstage and says, “I’m going to tell this joke now!” Sometimes it’s pure luck that nobody who matters happens to hear him. People regularly say some pretty controversial things from the stage. Sometimes the whole room even falls a little quiet and gets wary — okay, what’s he going to say next?
I joke a lot about the place where I was born and raised, the post-Soviet space, unrecognized territories, and all that. And I’ve noticed that people always get a little tense when those subjects come up. They’re waiting to see what I’ll say and what position I’ll take — whether I’m for or against. In other words, people want to establish my position first and only then follow me further into the subject.
And if I sense the audience isn’t ready, I usually steer things elsewhere. Because there’s also a sense that it isn’t safe. For example, people have started showing up at our shows whom we privately take to be employees of the “E Center.” They’re hilariously bad at disguising themselves. It’s like a cartoon where a bumbling supervillain’s sidekick is practically announcing, “Boss, I’ve hidden the bomb perfectly.” Someone shows up in plain clothes, but the jeans and the fanny pack… They just don’t fit the atmosphere. That obviously affects how you behave onstage.
I’ve had situations where I was finishing a joke and realized halfway through that it might not be safe.
When you’re writing material, you’re not sitting there with the Criminal Code in front of you. Then you go onstage, deliver the joke, and suddenly think: Okay, could that fall under some law? I’ve even said directly to the audience, “Come on, laugh a little louder, so that if anything happens, I won’t be the only one being taken to a pretrial detention center.”
If I’m performing with other comedians, I try to arrive at the very beginning of the show and listen to the host interact with the audience so I can get a sense of who’s in the room that night. For example, the host asks a man where he works, and he says he’d rather not say. We immediately suspect he works in the security services. And you subconsciously start going through your material in your head.
I know which of my jokes come close to the line. Some I cut; others I simply don’t dare tell. Sometimes I deliberately restructure my set. If I feel I’ve ventured into sensitive social territory and the audience reacts worse than usual, I quickly switch to safer subjects. I feel this constant juggling of topics because I’m a fairly anxious person and I keep a close eye on the news.
Professional comedians I know are already consulting lawyers: they send them their material and revise their jokes with the legal risks in mind. But a beginner who has simply come along to try stand-up may have no idea that he’s running afoul of some law. Especially since some of the wording is extremely vague — “insulting the feelings of believers,” and so on. At this point, you don’t even know what might be considered offensive, or to whom.
There’s a comedian who is writing material about marriage. Even he consults lawyers. There’s now this whole discourse around traditional values, family, and “traditional foundations.” He’s simply joking about not understanding the institution of marriage. We talk about love, about the higher feelings between two people, and then those two people go on Gosuslugi and click a button. It’s a completely everyday joke. But even here, he thinks: "Is this really safe?" Because you just don’t know anymore what might become a problem, or when.
Women tend to talk more about the battle of the sexes, sexism, and relationships. And sometimes that gives them a relatively safe way to talk about the war in general. For example, a woman comes onstage and says, “There seem to be fewer men around. I’m on dating apps, and it’s getting harder to meet anyone.”
Technically, she hasn’t said anything political at all. But everyone understands why there might be fewer men. It’s a form of Aesopian language. The comedian may not have intended any political message, but the audience reads one into it.
Feminist themes are complicated, too. At the same time, there’s now a major women’s stand-up scene, or fem-stand-up. There are women-only open mics. At one point, it even felt as though women’s stand-up had become stronger than men’s. It was as if the girls had really embraced that girl power.
Even if someone in the audience shouts something at a woman, she’s still in a stronger position. She’s onstage. She has the spotlights on her. She’s holding the device that amplifies her voice — a microphone. If some heckler shouts something, she can easily outplay him.
As for comedians who have left, I don’t think there’s any widespread resentment toward them within the Russian stand-up scene. Almost everyone has a friend who lives abroad. Everyone understands how hard it is to live in a foreign country — without your native language, your friends, your home, the culture you’re used to, and even the basic things of everyday life.
You can go to a place where there is freedom of speech and self-expression, but when that means abandoning everything you’ve built here — your work, your connections, your audience, your home — many people choose to stay.
When one side of the scales holds freedom of speech and the other means abandoning everything you’ve built, many people choose to stay
I currently live and work in Moscow. And for me, choosing between leaving behind everything I’ve built here and having the freedom to say everything that’s been weighing on me isn’t so simple. Just two years ago, I swore I would never set foot in another country. Now I realize that if things become too uncomfortable for me, I’ll leave. Of course, it’s frightening to think that I’d have to start my career almost from scratch. I’ve built relationships with organizers here, earned their trust, and developed my own audience.
I started thinking about emigration this year primarily because of something very personal: I started thinking about having a family and children. And at some point, I asked myself: "do I want my children to grow up in this country?" The answer was no longer clear-cut.
I’d say I still choose Russia about 90% of the time. But that 10% of doubt is there. It has to do, among other things, with my political views and with how I feel about what’s happening around me. The war has also started to feel physically closer. There are more reports of drone attacks and of things happening in Moscow and other regions. Every day you read the news: something is happening in Kursk, Belgorod, the Urals, the North.
You come across economic forecasts and new laws, and you inevitably start wondering how much longer this can go on. You ask yourself: "am I ready to get used to this new normal?" And, more importantly, "am I ready for my children to grow up accustomed to it?"
When my friends and I talk about politics, we generally understand each other. We’re mostly centrists; we don’t like radicalism, and we’re against the war. At the same time, we understand that there’s a vast political system in which different people make money and make decisions.
I watch Varlamov, Katz, various news sources, Sobchak, and others, and somehow piece together a reality I can live in. Then I visit my parents in another country and see that they watch all kinds of different channels: Russian, Ukrainian, and local.
I start watching all of it with them. You turn on Russian television, and some of the things I see there are physically hard for me to watch. Then you switch to Ukrainian news, sometimes in Ukrainian, and see what they’re saying there. Then you watch international news.
After trips like that, I usually return to Russia feeling more liberal, because I’ve had a chance to look at it from the outside, even if only a little. My parents lived through an armed conflict themselves in the 1990s. My father took part in it. They understand very well that war is horrible. But they also understand something else: these kinds of decisions aren’t made by ordinary people. Not by the public. They’re made by people at the top who have the power to make them. And everyone else is then left to find a way to live with the consequences.
“It’s making everyone a little paranoid.” Stand-up comedian Pavel V.
There’s a children’s show on STS Kids, one of the few TV programs featuring stand-up. The kids perform themselves, and everything is geared toward a young audience. Some of the participants are already 14 or 15, and those limits are starting to feel restrictive. They want to joke about teenage subjects, about things that are actually bothering them. But they perform alongside nine-year-olds for whom those topics are still taboo. And because it all airs on a children’s channel, there are pretty strict limits on what they can talk about.
At the same time, teenagers are quite happy to make political jokes among themselves. While they’re still young, they can get away with a lot because nobody takes them seriously. But once they turn 18 and start saying the same things into a microphone, the consequences can be very different.
Some of them understand this, while others aren’t thinking about it at all yet. They’re kids; they don’t think that far ahead: "Will I still be doing this in the future? Where will I be five years from now?" I started performing at around their age, when I was about 14. And if you compare what it was like then with what’s happening now, a huge amount has changed.
Even in early 2022, you could still say certain things onstage. People just made sure nothing was recorded and that no video got out. Now that thought barely even occurs to anyone. Self-censorship has changed dramatically. And it’s not just the comedians — the audience has changed too. If you suddenly start saying something like that out loud, it makes everyone a little paranoid. It’s as if one thought immediately hangs in the air: “This isn’t being recorded, is it?”
I remember that feeling well, when someone would still try to slip in a little joke or hint. People in the audience would literally sit up straight. Not necessarily because they disagreed, but because they were struck by the fact that someone had just said it out loud from the stage at a public event. It was as if everyone immediately thought: “If anything happens, I wasn’t laughing.” It’s not outright terror, more a constant sense of tension. There’s already too much of that around us as it is.
A lot of comedians have also reconsidered why they go onstage in the first place. Sometimes a beginner wants to make a statement, to say something important. But an experienced comedian understands that your primary job is to entertain people, make them laugh, and give them a good time. And some subjects are now such that people are more likely to tense up than to laugh.
Some topics have become off-limits not because anyone has officially handed you a list, but because people are intimidated. The atmosphere has changed. And I don’t sense much of a demand for political humor anymore. It seems to me that a large share of those who had a strong appetite for it have left. What remains are mostly people to whom it wasn’t that important to begin with. And, frankly, people are simply scared now. Sometimes you want to add a comparison to an everyday joke, then realize that it vaguely touches on politics — and that’s it. Better not.
Some topics have simply become off-limits, not because anyone has officially handed you a list, but because people are intimidated
Overall, there’s been more everyday comedy: observations about relationships, family, and things everyone can relate to. It’s safe. But you still don’t feel free. Probably because there are simply too many things you can’t talk about.
Of course I’ve thought about emigrating. In fact, I did leave. When the mobilization was announced, I was one of those Russians who left. And I got a taste of what it was like to have freedom in my material. At some point, the mere possibility of discussing something openly with people really hits you. You think, “Wow, so you can actually just say this out loud.” My situation is also somewhat complicated because, in a way, I’m avoiding military service. So even unnecessary interactions at the border are frightening.
Here, by contrast, there are things you simply don’t discuss publicly. In that sense, I really like what’s happening in Poland, for example. And it makes me sad that even just traveling there is quite difficult for me now. In general, it’s become harder for Russians to travel anywhere. But I find the Polish comedy scene fascinating because several languages are mixed together at once.
I lived in Armenia and spent time in Georgia and Uzbekistan. The industry is smaller in Uzbekistan. In Armenia, a stand-up club can operate in two languages, and both Armenians and Russians attend shows in either language. Everyone makes an effort to understand one another. Poland is even more interesting: there are Poles, Ukrainians, Belarusians, and Russians. A single stand-up club can host shows in three languages. That’s really cool.
In Russia, there are some pretty strange things happening around the English language these days. I performed at an English-language open mic in Moscow. The organizers are foreigners — British and American. And they were trying to figure out how to label an English-language open mic in Russian so that people searching for an event in English would still understand what they were going to. A foreigner living in Moscow who wants to attend an English-language event first has to see the event listing in Russian. It’s pretty strange.
In general, there’s this sense of a kind of legalized lawlessness in the air. There are brief moments when you think, “Oh, maybe things are going to get a little freer?” During the whole Yabloko episode, for example, there were literally a couple of weeks when it felt like, “Wait, what? Are we a liberal society again?”
One comedian had a joke about presidential experience. The idea was that if you’re an ordinary professional and you’ve gained a lot of experience at one job, you can take that experience to another job. It’s considered an advantage. But if you’ve been president of Russia for many years, you can’t take that presidential experience and get a job as president somewhere else. There’s no criticism in the joke. Nothing at all. It’s simply a name used for comparison. But the comedian says “Putin,” and the audience immediately goes, “Mmm.” Like Voldemort: a name that’s better left unspoken.
“Putin” is like Voldemort: a name that’s better left unspoken
The story of Artemy Ostanin has had a profound impact on everyone, of course. It’s horrifying, but also revealing. And what I find important is that people are waiting for Ostanin. That’s probably the best thing about the whole situation. He wasn’t some superstar comedian with a huge audience. By the standards of the broader comedy world, he was practically a nobody. And yet people haven’t forgotten him. So much has happened since then that any other news story could easily have been pushed out of people’s minds by the next one. But this story is still there.
Of course, there are stupid comedians, idiotic comedians, and fucking assholes who think it’s his own fault: “He shouldn’t have touched those subjects in the first place.” No. It’s not his fault. What the fuck? They simply took what he said, interpreted it in a certain way, and that was it. It doesn’t even matter that much whether the joke itself was good. You can listen to it a hundred times and say, “Well, it’s not the funniest joke in the world.” But destroying people over their words is horrifying.
And this case also made something else very clear: if you still want to talk about things like that, you now have to do it much more subtly. In terms of censorship, we’ve come very close to the Soviet satirists. If you want to say something, you have to speak in Aesopian language. You can’t simply state the point outright.
If you have a joke like that, people have to get it from the hint. You can only hint at it. If you want to talk about something, you have to really contort yourself. You can’t just say something about Putin or the authorities directly anymore. It has to be all half-hints.
As for pro-government, or what you might call "Z-humor," it certainly exists. There are venues where this kind of comedy is performed. Some projects even feature military personnel doing stand-up. There are comedians who joke about people who have left, about other countries, and so on. But I don’t think it’s becoming a genuinely popular genre. I simply try not to perform at those kinds of venues, so I don’t encounter much of it in my circle. And I don’t think audiences are particularly interested in it, either.
People are already tired of all this. Politics is more likely to trigger people than make them laugh. They go to stand-up to switch off. I can easily imagine someone living on the outskirts of Moscow. At night, he hears several drones being shot down. In the morning, he goes to work. He works all day. In the evening, he decides to go to a stand-up show in the city center, just to take his mind off things for a while. And then you start talking to him from the stage about drones. He still has to go home afterward — back to the place where those drones are. Why the hell would he want that?
It also seems to me that demand for stand-up itself has declined somewhat. Maybe people simply have less money. A ticket costing 1,000 or 2,000 rubles is already a significant expense for some. It’s entertainment, after all, and the price of everything has gone up. Even television stand-up projects, from what I can see, have started buying less material. Maybe that’s because viewership has fallen. And if demand is down, why buy something people aren’t watching?
Still, I want to believe this isn’t forever. I just want to be fucking blown away one day when I suddenly discover: “Wait, we can do this now?” Because I know exactly what that feeling will be like. I already experienced that high when I was living in Yerevan. You suddenly realize you can actually just talk about this subject — not in a whisper, not in hints, not checking whether someone is filming you on their phone. You can just say it. And I really want to feel that way here one day.

articles.title: Air defense neutralizes 103 drones used by Russian forces to attack Ukraine overnight
articles.body:
Air defense neutralizes 103 drones used by Russian forces to attack Ukraine overnight
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Air Force Command's press service said this in a Telegram post.
"As of 09:30, air defenses had shot down or suppressed 103 enemy UAVs, including Shahed-type UAVs, Gerberas, drones of other types and S8000 Banderols, in the north, south, east and center of the country. Hits by enemy aerial attack weapons were recorded at 15 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at six locations," the statement said.

articles.title: Trump wants Biden’s Ukraine billions back
articles.body:
Trump wants Biden’s Ukraine billions back
US President Donald Trump has said he intends to present Europe with a belated bill for billions of dollars Washington spent arming Ukraine under his predecessor, Joe Biden.
In a post on Truth Social on Thursday, Trump renewed his criticism of the scale of the Biden administration’s support for Kiev, claiming that “Hundreds of Billions of Dollars was given to Ukraine and NATO, free of charge, that Europe would have paid for – If they were only asked.”
“We will be asking for that money, though somewhat belatedly!”
Trump did not specify how much Washington would seek, which European countries would be expected to pay, or how any retroactive payments would be arranged. Earlier this week, he said Biden gave Ukraine more than $300 billion worth of weapons “free.”
This figure is disputed. A report in May by the Special Inspector General for Operation Atlantic Resolve put total US appropriations for Ukraine and the broader response to the conflict at around $195 billion since February 2022, including $67.8 billion committed in defense articles and services to Kiev.
Under Trump, Washington has shifted the cost of new US weapons supplied to Ukraine through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) to other NATO members and partners. Launched last year, the scheme allows them to pay for US-made weapons and ammunition supplied to Kiev. NATO says more than $6 billion worth of US military equipment has been funded through the program.
Moscow has maintained that additional Western weapons will not change the outcome of the conflict, arguing that they will only prolong the fighting.
Trump’s latest remarks came as he pushed back against reports that the conflict with Iran has severely depleted ammunition stocks, saying the US is ramping up production and currently keeping newly produced munitions for its own forces rather than selling them abroad.
The administration has also portrayed the Ukraine conflict as imposing a broader economic cost on the US. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week that Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, coupled with the Iran war, contributed to an “energy shock” pushing up prices in the US.

articles.title: UN's Sudan probe says foreign fighters fuelling conflict
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UN's Sudan probe says foreign fighters fuelling conflict
Foreign fighters and support networks are fuelling the conflict in Sudan and worsening violence against civilians, a UN-backed investigation warned Thursday.
The United Nations' independent fact-finding mission on Sudan said foreign involvement was strengthening the military capabilities of the country's warring parties, enabling increasingly sophisticated military operations, with devastating consequences for ordinary people.
Since April 2023, the conflict between Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has killed tens of thousands and forced millions to flee their homes.
In a report, the probe documented the recruitment, training and deployment of foreign personnel to support the RSF, with transnational entities also facilitating the transfer of weapons, ammunition, military technology and logistical support.
It also said there were reasonable grounds to believe that the regular army used foreign-supplied drones in its operations that harmed civilians and civilian infrastructure.
"This external support has not brought greater protection for civilians," said the fact-finding mission's chairman Mohamad Chande Othman.
"Instead, civilians are paying the price through attacks on homes, hospitals, schools, markets and places of refuge."
The UN Human Rights Council established the probe in October 2023, to begin gathering evidence of violations in Sudan.
The independent investigative team does not speak on behalf of the United Nations.
Colombian contingent
The investigation documented the deployment of up to 2,000 ex-military Colombian contractors who directly operated combat drones, artillery and advanced weapons alongside RSF units.
Witnesses also reported fighters from South Sudan, Chad and Ethiopia, "including women, serving primarily in frontline, rather than technical roles", identified by language, accent "and, in some cases uniforms", the report said.
Private entities, intermediaries and recruiters operating from countries including Colombia and the United Arab Emirates used transit locations in Chad, Libya and Somalia to facilitate the delivery of personnel, training, weapons and logistics to the RSF in Sudan, the report said.
It found that foreign suppliers had boosted the RSF and the army's drone capabilities, allowing them to strike far beyond the front lines.
The mission found reasonable grounds to believe that the army and RSF attacks it documented may amount to war crimes.
Responding to the report, the United Arab Emirates insisted in a statement it was "not involved in the civil war in Sudan, nor has it provided arms or any related material to any party in Sudan since the outbreak of the conflict", and strongly condemned violations of international law by all sides.
The United States last month urged the UN Security Council to expand an arms embargo on the Darfur region to cover all of Sudan -- a call echoed by the fact-finding mission.
"Protecting Sudan's civilians requires action not only against those fighting the war, but also against the individuals, entities and networks that enable it to continue," said Chande Othman.

articles.title: What Each F-35 Variant Really Costs Right Now
articles.body:
The base cost of an F-35A, the Air Force variant of the Joint Strike Fighter, is going up 11.5 percent from $82.5 million to $92 million for the latest lots of the fifth-generation aircraft, Air & Space Forces Magazine has confirmed.
A spokesperson for the F-35 Joint Program Office gave cost estimates for each F-35 variant, averaged across Lots 18 and 19, in current-year dollars. A recent Pentagon acquisition report gave the estimates in 2012 dollars, when the program was rebaselined. The new figures give insight how inflation is affecting the program.
Manufacturer Lockheed Martin lists the price of F-35 variants for Lots 15 through 17 on its website.
The totals are average flyaway costs, which refer to all the basic costs it takes to produce one aircraft. The JPO confirmed those price tags include the cost of the jets’ engines and radars, which are provided to manufacturer Lockheed Martin as government-furnished equipment.
The cost of the F-35A went up the most in recent lots, at 11.5 percent, with the F-35B almost identical in terms of percentage growth. The F-35C went up the least, at just 8.5 percent.
But the F-35A remains the cheapest and least complex variant of the three. The F-35B—the short takeoff and vertical landing variant flown by the Marine Corps—is the most expensive and complicated, given its unique swiveling engine nozzle and hovering capabilities. And the F-35C, flown by both the Marine Corps and the Navy, is closer in price to the F-35B and has bigger wings than the F-35A to help with carrier landings, as well as folding wingtips to help with storage in close quarters.
The revelation of the price tags for the F-35s’ upcoming lots—the highest in the nearly $2 trillion program’s history—follows the Pentagon’s release of a modernized selected acquisition report which said the total estimated acquisition cost for the F-35, including both airframes and engines, had grown more than 10 percent to $536.2 billion.
The selected acquisition report, which was released in August, pointed to inflation and critical upgrades as causes of the F-35’s cost growth. But the report only included flyways costs for the three variants in 2012 dollars, leaving the full effects of inflation unclear. Those costs were:
- $78 million for the F-35A, up 7.3 percent from the previous report in 2023.
- $110.3 million for the F-35B, up 10.5 percent from the previous report.
- $93.4 million for the F-35C, up 6.6 percent from the previous report.
The fact that the actual costs are seeing greater percentage increases could suggest inflation is having a significant effect on the jet’s price tag.
Lockheed officials have been sounding warnings about the growing effects of inflation on the F-35 for some time now.
Greg Ulmer, then-president of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics, told Defense One in July 2024 that keeping the F-35’s price under the rate of inflation would be challenging for Lots 18 and 19.
“Inflation is real,” Ulmer said at the Farnborough Air Show in England. “The cost of raw materials has gone up. The cost of everything has gone up, so there is just inflation pressure in the system.”
The JPO, Lockheed, and other F-35 contractors have also been working on adding more capabilities to the jet, including additional computing and processing power under the Technology Refresh 3 program and additional weapons, sensor, and sensor fusion capabilities as part of the Block 4 effort.
The JPO pointed to information in the selected acquisition report when asked for comment on the Lots 18 and 19 cost growth. Lockheed Martin said in a response to a query that the recent acquisition report shows the program is moving into full-rate production, resuming high-volume development deliveries, and growing globally.
“It also shows that the hard work has shifted from proving the basic aircraft to executing major modernization, improving fleet readiness, and controlling long-term sustainment and integration costs,” a Lockheed spokesperson said.
The JPO had previously declined to release the cost for each variant in current-year dollars and said those numbers were considered controlled unclassified information. The office eventually released the figures after further queries from Air & Space Forces Magazine.
The JPO and Lockheed Martin in September 2025 struck a final “definitized” deal for Lots 18 and 19, which would buy 296 fighters for nearly $24.3 billion. That deal was for just the airframe and did not include engine costs, meaning the average cost of just the airframe across all variants will be $82.4 million.

articles.title: Germany will close Russia’s Bonn consulate after attributing Leipzig Airport drone attack to Moscow
articles.body:
Germany will close Russia’s General Consulate in Bonn, terminate the agreement concerning the Russian House in Berlin, and tighten entry controls for Russian citizens. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul announced this at a joint press conference with Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt on 1 September, after German authorities formally attributed the attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport to Russia.
German investigators have identified two suspects allegedly linked to the operation: a Russian-born man with a Latvian passport and a Belarusian man with a Russian passport. This information was reported by Süddeutsche Zeitung. Investigators believe both have links to Russian state structures, according to the report.
Both men have already left Germany, complicating efforts to bring them to justice, Tagesschau reports. One of Berlin’s responses was the closure of Russia’s Consulate General in Bonn — the last Russian consulate general remaining in Germany.
Germany tightens its Russia policy
Russia’s General Consulate in Bonn will close on 18 September, according to Wadephul. Germany will also seek additional EU sanctions against people linked to Russian hybrid attacks, increase pressure on Russia’s “shadow fleet,” and strengthen entry controls for Russian nationals.
He stated that since the beginning of "the unlawful war of aggression" against Ukraine, Germany's goal has been to bring the war to an end, restore the peace order in Europe, and return to a constructive relationship.
"However, this requires a minimum level of willingness on the Russian side. We must acknowledge that Russia shows no willingness to reach an accommodation,” Wadephul said.
Moscow rejected the accusations. Russian President Vladimir Putin called Germany’s response a “grave mistake,” TASS reports.
The investigation leads to two suspects
According to German investigators, the Belarusian suspect left DNA traces on one of the drones, inside a container containing explosives, and on an antenna found near the airport. The Russian-born suspect, who holds a Latvian passport, is believed to have coordinated and directed the operation, entered Germany through Berlin, and then traveled toward Saxony.
The Russian-born suspect left Germany two days before the attack, while the Belarusian suspect also left the country.
What happened at Leipzig Airport
The diplomatic response stems from a sabotage attempt on 4 August, when a bomb-laden drone struck a Ukrainian An-124 cargo aircraft but failed to detonate. The drone, carrying explosives, remained unnoticed for about four hours before being discovered, while later analysis indicated it had been aimed at the aircraft near its fuel tanks.

articles.title: Russia Is Paying for the War with Its Future Economy
articles.body:
Andriy Dubas, President of the Association of Ukrainian Banks
For several years, massive government spending related to the war was one of the main drivers of the Russian economy. Military contracts ensured demand for businesses, supported employment, household incomes, and consumption. Now, this model is producing significantly weaker results: economic growth is slowing, the cost of capital remains high, and budgetary and production constraints are becoming more visible.
This is clearly evident from GDP trends. After growing by 4.9% in 2024, the Russian economy expanded by only 1% in 2025. In 2026, the Russian Ministry of Economic Development expects growth of just 0.4%, while the Bank of Russia forecasts growth in the range of 0–1%.
Government procurement supports demand; resources are concentrated in military sectors
The Bank of Russia explicitly identifies the consumer sector and the portion of the manufacturing industry focused on government procurement as key drivers of economic growth. This explains why significant government spending has long allowed Russia to sustain economic activity despite sanctions and other restrictions.
This model concentrates resources in sectors that serve government contracts. Meanwhile, parts of the civilian economy face more challenging conditions.
The need to maintain a balance between the military and civilian sectors is already being discussed within Russia itself. Putin’s special representative, Boris Titov, has warned against an excessive concentration of the economy on the needs of the military-industrial complex.
This is an important signal: while military demand remains significant, its ability to drive growth across the entire economy is gradually weakening.
High borrowing costs are accompanied by production constraints.
Another factor is the high cost of financing. Following a prolonged period of tight monetary policy, the Bank of Russia’s key rate stood at 14% in July. For businesses, this means expensive loans and more challenging conditions for new investments.
In August, the manufacturing PMI fell to 48.8 points. Companies reported declines in production and new orders, weaker demand, and rising costs for fuel and imports.
The Bank of Russia is already anticipating a further economic slowdown due to a “temporary loss of capacity” in manufacturing and logistics. This is a fundamentally important point: the issue is no longer just about demand or the cost of borrowing, but about the economy’s ability to produce and supply goods.
The consequences of Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy and logistics infrastructure are emerging as a separate factor. In particular, Russia has already revised its oil production forecast for 2026 downward, and Reuters cites the effects of the war and strikes on oil refineries among the reasons.
Budgetary pressure is becoming increasingly evident
The changes are most evident in public finances. According to preliminary data from the Russian Ministry of Finance, the federal budget deficit for January–July 2026 amounted to 6.455 trillion rubles, or 2.8% of GDP. The current annual plan calls for a deficit of 3.786 trillion rubles. The Ministry of Finance itself attributes a significant portion of the accumulated deficit to front-loading of expenditures.
Oil and gas revenues to the federal budget fell by 16.8% year-over-year over the seven-month period, to 4.595 trillion rubles. During the same period, expenditures rose by 14.5% to 28.567 trillion rubles.
Military and security spending remains substantial. The 2026 budget allocates approximately 16.84 trillion rubles for defense, security, and law enforcement combined.
The pressure is also evident at the regional level. According to Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, in 65 of 85 Russian regions, real budget revenues at the end of 2025 were lower than in 2021. Among the reasons are reductions in federal transfers and corporate income tax revenues.
The Russian economy has so far managed to maintain its export revenues, large domestic market, and ability to reallocate significant budgetary resources. However, an ever-increasing portion of these resources is being directed toward the war effort, which limits opportunities for civilian investment, modernization, and regional development.
The cost of the war is becoming increasingly visible for Russia. In fact, it is already paying for it with its own future.

The Islamic Republic’s ability to surveil the Strait of Hormuz and lay mines in the vital waterway has likely been significantly degraded by American attacks, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed, noting that increased oil flows through the strait on September 1 suggest Iran is having difficulty preventing some commercial vessels from using the southern route.
United States officials told Axios on Wednesday that approximately 40 vessels carrying millions of barrels of oil transited the strait on September 1.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright also confirmed that oil tankers transported over 17 million barrels of oil through the strait on August 31, the highest volume of oil exports through the waterway since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran.
The figure of 17 million barrels is close to pre-war levels, which averaged 21.6 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter of 2025.
These developments, according to ISW, suggest that Iran is having difficulty preventing some commercial vessels from using the southern route.
Additionally, ISW reported growing indications that Iranian forces are facing operational constraints preventing them from efficiently identifying vessels and laying mines in the strait.
IRGC turns to alternative methods as Hormuz surveillance is degraded
According to ISW, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) recently attempted to use shore-based rocket launchers instead of fast-attack craft to deploy mines.
It has also reportedly used fast-attack craft to physically identify vessels because Iran has only a few functioning radars capable of covering the southern route.
ISW assessed that these less-optimal methods suggest that US strikes have degraded some of Iran’s maritime surveillance and mine-laying capabilities.
Though the IRGC has repeatedly claimed that vessels are striking naval mines in the strait, ISW’s assessment of the claims likely forms part of an effort to preserve the perception that the southern route remains dangerous. US Central Command previously reported that US forces had cleared naval mines from the strait.
CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said last week that US forces had cleared an effective pathway for ships to leave the Persian Gulf, adding that the mines had been “highly degraded.”
However, Ebrahim Zolfaghari, an Iranian military officer and spokesman, claimed on Wednesday that new mines had been laid.
“During last night’s operation, more naval mines were laid along the illicit routes south of the Strait of Hormuz. The only thing CENTCOM could do in response was rename the strait using Photoshop,” he wrote on X/Twitter. “Problem solved! You can just use Photoshop to get the oil tankers through, too!”
Iran appears to be investing in rebuilding its radar systems, ISW noted, citing a claim by US President Donald Trump that Iran had nearly rebuilt some of its radar systems before the US struck them again on September 1.
CENTCOM strikes targets on September 1
CENTCOM confirmed that its September 1 strikes targeted Iranian air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine-laying capabilities, and communications sites.
ISW noted that Iran is likely to continue attempting to reconstitute these capabilities because control of the Strait of Hormuz remains one of Tehran’s core objectives.
With Iran’s radars degraded, ISW suggested that the regime would seek alternative ways to attempt control over the strait.
An unnamed American source told Saudi-based Al Arabiya on Wednesday that CENTCOM’s Tuesday night strikes were a preemptive response to the Islamic Republic considering disabling undersea cables.

articles.title: Civil rights groups campaign against deepening US-Israel defense cooperation
articles.body:
Dozens of civil rights and advocacy groups are urging Congress to scrap a defense bill provision that would deepen US-Israeli military technology ties, according to a letter seen by Reuters, at a time of growing US skepticism toward the longtime ally.
The provision would deepen cooperation between the US and Israeli defense sectors by accelerating joint military technology development and other partnerships. The bill passed the House of Representatives in July and awaits Senate action.
The provision of the 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, known as Section 219, seeks to set up frameworks for joint ventures, licensing agreements and US-based co-production partnerships with the Israeli industry.
In Thursday's letter addressed to leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees, 56 groups said deeper integration with Israel's defense sector would be "exceptionally dangerous" and urged lawmakers to remove the provision.
The groups include Amnesty International USA and the civil rights network National Lawyers Guild as well as Arab and Jewish advocacy groups.
"At a time in which American interests are increasingly diverging from those of Israel, and American public opinion is turning increasingly against unconditional support to Israel, creating new points of influence for Israel in the US defense-technology ecosystem is exceptionally dangerous," said the letter, which has not been previously reported.
Israel is one of Washington's closest allies in the Middle East, and the two countries cooperate extensively on defense and intelligence issues. Supporters say deeper ties could help speed military innovation and technology development.
A spokesperson from the Israeli Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this story.
But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a May interview with CBS that he hoped to wean Israel off US military support within a decade. In a June letter to a US congressman, he wrote that the time has come for Israel "to move from aid recipient to partner."
US public support for Israel declines
US public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48% of voters and 66% of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% and 20% when the question was first asked in 2017.
Support for Israel among Democratic voters has plummeted, candidates critical of Israel are winning Democratic primaries, and even moderate lawmakers are increasingly willing to challenge decades of US support for Israel.
The Islamist militant Hamas group, in an October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, killed nearly 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals and took hundreds hostage. More than 73,000 Palestinians have since been killed in Israel's subsequent assault on Gaza, according to Gaza health officials.
The letter criticizes Israel for its potential violations of international humanitarian law in its war in Gaza and rising settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. It says such developments should prevent any discussion of deepening military ties.
US-Israel military aid agreement nears 2028 expiration
A memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8 billion in annual US military aid to Israel is approaching its expiration date in 2028, and conversations are under way on how Washington's assistance to Israel would evolve beyond that date.
Some members of Congress have already tried to strip the provision from the fiscal 2027 NDAA. Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Democratic Representative Ro Khanna of California introduced an amendment to block it, but it did not make it into the House version of the bill.
Once the House and Senate write their versions of the NDAA, members of the two chambers work out a compromise version of the bill, which must pass both chambers - typically near the end of the calendar year - before it can be sent to the White House for President Donald Trump to sign into law or veto.

articles.title: Arctic limbo: What you need to know about the Russian ship seized by Norway
articles.body:
Arctic limbo: What you need to know about the Russian ship seized by Norway
Norway has seized a Russian research vessel in Svalbard at the request of Kiev, prompting Russian President Vladimir Putin to denounce the capture of civilian vessels as “state terrorism.”
The vessel, called the Professor Molchanov, was detained while docked in Barentsburg, a Russian-operated settlement on the Norwegian-administered Arctic archipelago. The ship has been barred from leaving after a local court granted a request by Ukraine’s state-owned energy company Naftogaz.
Moscow has since summoned Norway’s ambassador in protest and vowed to challenge the seizure.
Why was a Russian state vessel in Norway in the first place, why does Kiev want it, and what could happen to the ship now?
What exactly happened
The Professor Molchanov arrived in Barentsburg on Tuesday on a scheduled voyage from Murmansk carrying scientists, passengers and supplies for the Russian settlements on the Norwegian-administered Arctic archipelago of Svalbard.
Norwegian officials first boarded the vessel for what Svalbard Governor Lars Fause described as an ordinary border and customs inspection, of a kind the ship had undergone numerous times before.
On Wednesday, Norwegian police, accompanied by an interpreter, boarded the ship again and read a court order to its captain, barring the vessel from leaving. Nobody aboard was arrested.
The order was issued on August 31 by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court after an application from Ukraine’s Naftogaz.
What happened to the passengers and crew
The exact number of people on board when the ship arrived in Barentsburg has not been officially confirmed. The Professor Molchanov can accommodate up to 80 people, including at least 20 crew members and as many as 60 scientists and other expedition personnel.
Norwegian media have reported that around 50 passengers and crew were affected by the seizure.
Russian officials have said that 21 people remained on board. They have been supplied with everything they need and continue working, with no Norwegian police or officials stationed on the vessel.
Those who had already gone ashore were not detained and have been able to continue their planned work. They include participants in the Arctic Biennale art-and-science project.
The seizure has, however, left some passengers without their planned transport back to Russia. Norwegian authorities have said they are working with Arktikugol to resolve the situation for those affected, but no alternative route has yet been announced.
The Professor Molchanov
The ship, named after renowned Soviet meteorologist Pavel Molchanov, is a Russian state-owned, ice-strengthened research vessel with more than four decades of experience operating in polar waters.
Built in Finland for the Soviet hydrometeorological service and launched in late 1982, the 71-meter-long ship was designed for Arctic oceanographic and weather research. It carries four laboratories on board and can accommodate dozens of researchers alongside its crew.
The ship continues to be actively used in Arctic research, including studies of weather, marine ecosystems, microbiology, biodiversity and environmental conditions in the Barents and Kara seas.
Why is goes to Svalbard
The voyage to Svalbard was part of a regular route between Murmansk and Barentsburg, a Russian mining settlement where the state-owned Arktikugol trust has operated for decades.
Since 2025, the Professor Molchanov has carried scientists, Arktikugol employees, contractors, family members and supplies to Barentsburg and another Russian settlement called Pyramida. Ten round trips were planned for 2026.
It is currently the only vessel providing a direct passenger connection between the Russian mainland and the archipelago after direct air links between Russia and Svalbard ended in 2020.
While Svalbard is under Norwegian sovereignty, it is governed by the 1920 Svalbard Treaty, which grants nationals of signatory countries rights to conduct commercial and scientific activities on the archipelago.
Why Ukraine wants the ship
The seizure of the vessel stems from a long-running dispute over Crimea. Ukraine’s Naftogaz has claimed that it lost energy assets after the peninsula’s reunification with Russia in 2014 and took the case to an arbitration tribunal in The Hague.
In 2023, the tribunal ordered Russia to pay around $4.22 billion, plus interest and legal costs, ruling that Naftogaz’s assets in Crimea could be treated as Ukrainian “investments” in Russian territory and were protected under a bilateral treaty.
Moscow has rejected the ruling, arguing that the tribunal had no jurisdiction over the dispute and that the treaty did not apply to assets that had already been located in Crimea before its reunification with Russia.
Nevertheless, Naftogaz has since tried to collect the award by targeting Russian state property abroad. It has pursued assets in several Western countries, including Finland, Britain and France, and says the arbitration award can also be enforced in Norway.
According to Reuters, lawyers acting for Naftogaz had been monitoring the Professor Molchanov for months before seeking its seizure.
Will Kiev actually get the ship?
Not automatically. The current order only prevents the Professor Molchanov from leaving Barentsburg while the case proceeds. The vessel remains Russian property and has not yet been transferred to Ukraine.
Naftogaz ultimately wants Russian assets seized abroad to be sold, with the proceeds used to cover part of the $4.22 billion award. According to Reuters, its lawyers sought not only the arrest of the Professor Molchanov, but also its eventual compulsory sale.
However, even if the ship were to be sold, it would cover only a tiny fraction of Kiev’s multibillion-dollar claim.
Russia has also said it will challenge whether the ship can be seized or sold at all. While Naftogaz has claimed that the vessel has a commercial function, Moscow has stressed that it is state-owned, operated by Roshydromet, and used for scientific research and supplying Russian settlements in the Arctic.
Moscow’s response
Moscow has protested the seizure and demanded that Norway release the vessel. On Thursday, the Russian Foreign Ministry summoned Norwegian Ambassador Heidi Olufsen and delivered a “strong protest” over the detention of the ship.
The ministry stressed that the vessel was carrying out a scheduled trip between Murmansk and Barentsburg and was transporting scientists, Arktikugol employees, and supplies needed by Russian settlements on Svalbard.
It accused Oslo of using the restrictions against Russia to undermine Moscow’s longstanding presence on the archipelago, saying Russian organizations and citizens there had effectively been placed in a “state of blockade.”
The ministry also accused Norway of violating the 1920 Svalbard Treaty and said Russian authorities would work to have the seizure lifted.
Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova described the detention as another example of Western “piracy,” while Far East and Arctic Development Minister Aleksey Chekunkov called it “legal nihilism and lawlessness” and said Moscow would challenge the decision.
President Vladimir Putin described the capture of civilian vessels, attacks on merchant ships and threats against civilian aircraft as manifestations of “state terrorism.” He added that Western countries which ignore such actions risk becoming “accomplices in international terrorism.”
Part of a broader campaign against Russian vessels
Western countries have increasingly moved beyond sanctions and begun physically detaining or seizing vessels they accuse of helping Russia bypass restrictions on its trade, claiming the ships are part of a so-called “shadow fleet.”
A number of ships linked to Russia have been held in European waters since 2025, including tankers and cargo vessels detained by Germany, Estonia, France, Belgium, Sweden, and Britain.
Moscow has repeatedly decried the seizures while dismissing the “shadow fleet” designation as legally meaningless.
Putin warned in August that attempts to seize Russian ships and sell their cargo amounted to “piracy and robbery” and said Moscow could respond in kind against vessels carrying cargo for countries involved in such actions.
An attempt to limit Russia in the Arctic?
Russian officials and experts have linked the seizure to a wider Western effort to weaken Moscow’s position in the Arctic. Murmansk Governor Andrey Chibis accused Norwegian officials of trying to “push us out of Svalbard,” stressing that Russia has longstanding economic and scientific interests on the archipelago and that such efforts would fail.
Arctic expert Aleksey Fadeev similarly described the detention as another attempt by Western countries to pressure Russia under the pretext of confiscating property for Ukraine, warning that it could further increase tensions between Moscow and NATO states in the region.
Military analyst Aleksandr Stepanov warned the seizure could set a precedent for disrupting Russian maritime access not only around Svalbard but across northern waters more broadly.
Russian experts have also described the arrest as a potential blow to Russia’s ability to conduct Arctic research, noting that the Professor Molchanov is used for climate, weather, and environmental studies with relevance beyond Russia itself.

articles.title: Russian occupation authorities sentence abducted Ukrainian journalist Iryna Levchenko to 15 years in prison
articles.body:
Russian occupation authorities sentence abducted Ukrainian journalist Iryna Levchenko to 15 years in prison
Melitopol journalist Iryna Levchenko has been sentenced to 15 years in a penal colony by an occupation court in Zaporizhzhia Oblast. Levchenko was unlawfully imprisoned in 2023.
Source: Institute of Mass Information
Details: A statement about the verdict appeared on the occupation court's website and Telegram channel, saying that Ukrainian journalist Iryna Levchenko had been found guilty of alleged "espionage".
The occupation court stated that Iryna Levchenko remained in occupied Melitopol after the start of the full-scale invasion and did not renounce her Ukrainian citizenship.
The occupation authorities claim that "having contacted a resident of territory controlled by Ukraine's armed forces via the Telegram messenger, the woman agreed to assist Ukrainian special services by transmitting data about the locations of office buildings and Russian government officials, movement routes of personnel, military equipment and weapons of Russia's armed forces and other military formations on the territory of Zaporizhzhia Oblast".
According to the occupation authorities, Levchenko allegedly "transmitted information about Russian government ministries and agencies, including those responsible for security and law enforcement, along with their addresses and lists of employees" in February 2023.
"The transmission of said information to the Ukrainian side could have led to strikes on the locations of these strategic facilities," the occupation authorities stated.
In 2023, the occupying forces abducted journalist Iryna Levchenko and her husband in occupied Melitopol and held them in a basement. Levchenko was regularly transported from the Donetsk pre-trial detention centre to occupied Melitopol for investigative actions.
According to RIA Pivden, the journalist's case was completely closed off, and even her lawyer did not have full access to it.
In June 2026, it became known that Iryna Levchenko had been transferred from the Simferopol pre-trial detention centre to the Krasnodar pre-trial detention centre in Russia. According to RIA Pivden, the journalist's husband Oleksandr Levchenko was released in August 2024.
For reference: Iryna Levchenko has been in journalism since 1981. She worked at factory newspapers, the Melitopol district newspaper Novyi Den, and was a local correspondent for oblast and national print publications.
Iryna Levchenko is on the list of civilian journalists in Russian captivity maintained by the Institute of Mass Information.
