articles.title: Russian strike on Ukraine’s Odesa damages residential buildings, killing one and injuring several
articles.body:
Russian strike on Ukraine’s Odesa damages residential buildings, killing one and injuring several
Russian forces launched a massive overnight strike on civilian infrastructure in Odesa and the Odesa region on September 4, local authorities said.
In one of Odesa’s districts, residential buildings and vehicles were damaged. Ukraine’s State Emergency Service specified that a nine-story building was hit, destroying apartments on the sixth through eighth floors and damaging neighboring buildings. One person was killed and three others were injured.
Russian drones also struck private homes, destroying two of them, and damaged a nonresidential building along with private and service vehicles. A civilian and a child were injured.
Russian forces have targeted Odesa and the Odesa region since the start of the full-scale war, with the region coming under near-daily attack in recent months. Russia’s Defense Ministry claims the strikes target infrastructure, including ports and warehouses linked to the Ukrainian military, while Odesa authorities report hits on civilian infrastructure and residential buildings.

articles.title: Leonid Slutsky was promised second place in the September elections, sources tell Meduza. Frustrated that the Kremlin stopped helping, he’s now saying LDPR belongs to the security services instead.
articles.body:
Leonid Slutsky was promised second place in the September elections, sources tell Meduza. Frustrated that the Kremlin stopped helping, he’s now saying LDPR belongs to the security services instead.
Leonid Slutsky, who leads Russia’s Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR), has begun casting it as a “party of security officials” rather than as a party of the Kremlin’s civilian staff. That is how Slutsky describes the party in private conversations with allies and with businesspeople close to the Liberal Democrats, and even in public campaign materials.
A post on LDPR’s Facebook page says security officials are running for the party in elections to the State Duma, Russia’s lower house of parliament. Slutsky made the same point on his VKontakte page. The party’s social media posts read (errors as in the original):
Our team is made up of heroes and builders. LDPR’s list of State Duma candidates includes 111 people who know firsthand what it means to defend the Motherland. They are veterans of the “special military operation,” volunteers, and security officials. Among them are brigade commander Alexey Vereshchagin and Sergei Antoshin, leader of “Bars-Bryansk.” Our guys on the front lines are correcting past mistakes today, strengthening the Russian World.
Two LDPR members and a strategist who works with the political bloc of Russia’s Presidential Administration told Meduza about the shift in positioning.
The party changed its image because Slutsky is unhappy with the work of the political bloc headed by Sergei Kiriyenko. The reason for his displeasure is the party’s declining ratings and the fear that comes with them — that LDPR will fail to take the coveted second place, or even third.
“[At the political bloc] they promised second place, but they’re not delivering. It didn’t work out in the presidential election, and they’re not helping in the Duma election,” said one party member, summing up Slutsky’s complaints.
The same member said Slutsky now coordinates the campaign not with Alexander Kharichev, head of the Social Monitoring Directorate, but with Andrey Yarin, head of the Domestic Policy Directorate.
Under the Kremlin’s informal division of labor, Kharichev — who is close to the head of the political bloc — oversees election campaigns; Yarin handles day-to-day “operational” matters with regional authorities. Yarin has always been seen as closer to the security officials than to Kiriyenko’s team.
After the full-scale invasion began and Vladimir Zhirinovsky, LDPR’s founder, died in 2022, the Presidential Administration’s political bloc did try to pull LDPR into second place in regional elections. It managed to secure that result only last year, when LDPR finished second in seven of the 11 regions electing legislatures.
In the 2024 presidential election, LDPR’s new leader finished only fourth, behind not just Russian President Vladimir Putin but also Communist Party (KPRF) nominee Nikolai Kharitonov and Vladislav Davankov of the New People party. That happened even though the political bloc had sent Andrey Polosin, an experienced political strategist close to Kiriyenko, to help Slutsky, and even though the leaders of KPRF and New People took no part in the campaign.
According to the strategist working with the political bloc, “that’s when the mutual grievances between Slutsky and Kiriyenko’s team began.”
“Andrey [Polosin] did good work, but Slutsky and [Maria Voropayeva, the head of the party’s staff] complained about him to Kharichev constantly. They tried complaining to Kiriyenko, too. At some point SVK stopped talking to him and handed Slutsky off to Kharichev — that stung as well,” the strategist said. “Though at a congress or a public event Kiriyenko will, of course, say hello and toss out a line.”
The political bloc’s complaint, which Meduza has reported before, is that Slutsky cannot pull off the role of a public politician and that he himself “doesn’t understand this,” according to the strategist who works with the Presidential Administration and another source close to the Kremlin. Even so, Slutsky is seriously trying to become the party’s frontman: he has led and continues to lead LDPR’s lists in regional legislative elections.
“In the Russian system, it’s not a problem for a loyal party to be run by an uncharismatic man — no,” said a political strategist who works with the Kremlin. “You can be smarter about it: push other, more public figures to the front. Or just work with slogans and branding and try to take second place that way, especially when your interests line up with the Presidential Administration’s. But that doesn’t suit Slutsky’s vanity.”
The party is repeating that mistake in the current campaign, he said: its leader takes part in debate after debate and puts himself front and center in LDPR’s campaign videos, in which he urges voters to “save Russia” by voting for the party.
Another prominent LDPR figure appears in one of those videos: Viktor Bout, an arms dealer convicted in the United States, whom Russia exchanged in 2022 for basketball player Brittney Griner, who had been detained at Sheremetyevo Airport with hashish oil for a vape pen. Bout is on the federal portion of the party’s State Duma list, but in this ad he, for some reason, plays an ordinary businessman.
A source in the party said the campaign built around Slutsky is aimed mainly at a loyalist, patriotic electorate, and he sees no problem with that. He acknowledged, though, that internal polling shows Slutsky’s name recognition is low even among LDPR sympathizers.
After Zhirinovsky’s death, LDPR continued to use his image in some regional elections, and it remained the centerpiece of Slutsky’s 2024 presidential campaign messaging. In the current State Duma campaign, though, the founder’s name is almost absent.
Under Zhirinovsky, LDPR eagerly played up the issue of “fighting migrants.” By the early 2010s, however, the party had scaled back its use of the “Russian question” in its messaging at the Kremlin’s prompting. Under Slutsky, LDPR returned to anti-migrant appeals, riding a wave of xenophobic sentiment that grew among Russians in the 2020s.
Now the party’s leadership is unhappy with the political bloc’s unspoken ban on flirting with nationalist ideas. Still, posts with xenophobic appeals continue to go up on LDPR’s social media accounts.
“It [the nationalist theme] would give us a good boost, but Slutsky apparently didn’t get the go-ahead. Maybe he couldn’t have. And yet he presented himself as someone the Presidential Administration supports and helps in every way!” said a party member critical of the LDPR leader.
Both he and the strategist working with the Presidential Administration believe that recasting the Liberal Democrats as a party of security officials, and Slutsky’s outreach to Yarin, who is close to the security officials, are meant to paper over, within the party, the evident lack of understanding between Slutsky’s team and the political bloc’s leadership.
“Slutsky came into the party leadership as the political bloc’s man. If something is wrong in his relationship with Kiriyenko, [Slutsky, for appearances,] needs a new patron — real or imagined — who will deliver the necessary result. The security officials and Yarin became just that. And Slutsky really does go to Yarin — on day-to-day party business. But it’s Kharichev who oversees the elections,” said the strategist who works with the Presidential Administration’s political bloc.
Meduza’s sources do not rule out that LDPR could finish not second but as low as fourth in the State Duma elections. Second place, by their account, will go to KPRF, and New People may contend for third.
The party A Just Russia, in their view, will make it into the State Duma only if the political bloc receives instructions to that effect from Putin. “In the polling, public and internal alike, they don’t clear the threshold. The story with [A Just Russia leader Sergei] Mironov will only push their ratings down. But there’s no clarity yet on whether they’ll be in parliament. If the president wants to keep the current lineup of Duma factions, A Just Russia will get help,” said the strategist working with the Presidential Administration.
In his view, the Kremlin will not put in the effort to pull LDPR up to second or third place: “If they get to third on their own — which is realistic — no problem. If they don’t, that’s their problem. They’ve been helped every way possible for years as it is.”
LDPR had not responded to Meduza’s request for comment at the time of publication.

articles.title: Russian criticism of Finnish President Alexander Stubb reaching new levels, expert says
articles.body:
Finnish President Alexander Stubb has come under unusually harsh criticism in Russia, with Russian state media and senior officials repeatedly attacking him in recent weeks.
Russian outlets and officials have criticised Stubb in the past, but the tone has now escalated significantly, according to Arkady Moshes, programme director of the Russia, Eastern Europe and Eurasia Research Programme at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.
"Virtually no other Western leader has been insulted as much as Stubb. This exceeds all norms of civilised behaviour," Moshes says.
The criticism intensified after Stubb joined several other European leaders in Kyiv on August 24 to mark Ukraine’s Independence Day. During the visit, he expressed support for Ukrainian attacks on Russian logistics centers.
Russian TV insults Stubb
One of Russia's most popular current affairs programmes claimed on Sunday that the Finnish President's actions have given rise to a new Russian expression, meaning "dumb as Stubb".
Vladimir Chernyshov, host of NTV’s Itogi nedeli programme, also commented on Stubb's appearance, comparing the Finnish president to a character from a 1990s American comedy.
On Rossiya-1, another major state television channel, the presenter claimed that Stubb was seeking territory from Russia.
"Dreams of a Greater Finland reaching the Urals seem to still be alive in Stubb," the Vesti nedeli programme claimed.
Russia has long used state media to portray Finland negatively and rewrite the history of the Winter War. Last year, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov described Finland as one of Adolf Hitler’s most loyal allies.
In a Sunday broadcast, REN TV described Stubb’s comments on Ukrainian attacks on Russian logistics centres as "bloodthirsty".
According to the channel, Stubb’s claim that such attacks make military strategic sense was "no longer even madness or psychopathy, but terrorism".
Russian officials join attacks
Senior Russian officials have also targeted Stubb personally.
Foreign Ministry spokeswoman, Maria Zakharova, said in an interview last week that Stubb had "degenerated as a statesman, politician and human being".
Former President and current Deputy Chairman of Russia’s Security Council Dmitry Medvedev called Stubb a "real idiot" and a "moral monster" in a social media post.
Medvedev also accused Stubb and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham of betraying their voters by suggesting that Russia could be defeated.
Stubb has consistently supported Ukraine’s military efforts while also calling for dialogue with Russia.
In an interview with German newspaper Bild published on Saturday, he said Europe should seek to restart political dialogue with Moscow.
"I believe that someone in Europe needs to restart the dialogue with Russia so that we understand what is happening there. We need to talk to each other on a political level," Stubb said.
Finland has become a "traitor" to Putin
According to Moshes, the attacks are partly rooted in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s personal view of Stubb.
Moshes says Putin divides people into three categories: friends, enemies and traitors.

He also argues that Finland’s decision to join Nato has contributed to Putin viewing the country as a "traitor".

Evidence points to direct US hit on Iran wedding – Reuters
The deadly strike on a wedding in southern Iran earlier this week was likely a direct hit by a US munition, Reuters reports, citing its own analysis.
The strike on Kuhestak, Hormozgan Province on Tuesday left five people dead and nearly 70 wounded. The Iranian authorities said the victims were three women and two children aged 4 and 16.
Four weapons experts who reviewed images and videos verified by Reuters said the damage was inconsistent with debris or a ricochet from another target. Three concluded that the munition was likely American rather than an errant Iranian air-defense missile, while one suggested that it may have missed its intended target.
Two US officials confirmed to the outlet that US forces specifically targeted a telecommunications tower around 135 meters from the wedding site. Weapons experts previously cited by AP and the New York Times identified recovered fragments as belonging to a US air-delivered guided munition, most likely a JSOW.
US Vice President J.D. Vance said on Thursday that Washington is investigating the incident. “We’re investigating it because obviously we care. We want to know,” he told reporters. The US military said it does not target civilians and has not accepted responsibility for the strike.
The Iranian Red Crescent asked the International Criminal Court to investigate the incident. Iran’s UN envoy urged the Security Council to condemn it.
Iran responded to the latest US attacks with waves of missile and drone strikes on US military facilities in Kuwait, Bahrain, the UAE, Jordan, and Iraq’s Kurdistan Region.
The wedding strike follows other incidents involving civilian casualties during the conflict. On the opening day of the war in February, a US attack hit an elementary school in Minab, killing 175 people, most of them children. At least 21 civilians, including seven children, were also killed in Lamerd that day.
Tehran has accused Washington of war crimes throughout the conflict, reporting up to 3,000 civilian casualties since the US and Israel launched the war against Iran in February.

articles.title: Sanctions on Russian oil buyers won’t resolve Ukraine conflict – Indian foreign minister
articles.body:
Sanctions on Russian oil buyers won’t resolve Ukraine conflict – Indian foreign minister
India has defended its continued purchases of Russian oil, with the foreign minister saying restrictions on the energy trade will not bring a resolution to the Ukraine conflict, which has to come through dialogue and diplomacy. 
“This conflict, which is today in its fifth year, will not be solved because somebody is buying or not buying oil or alumina or minerals or metals or fertilizer,” Jaishankar said after talks with his Ukrainian counterpart, Andrii Sybiha, in the capital, Kiev. “This conflict will be solved by dialogue, by diplomacy, by negotiation.”
Asked whether India will reduce its Russian oil purchases if Washington imposes steep sanctions on Russia’s top oil customers under a new bill, Jaishankar pointed to the challenges of providing energy for 1.4 billion people amid a “very, very difficult” global energy situation.
Russia was India’s largest crude oil supplier last month, providing around 2.1 million barrels per day, or 45% of the country’s imports, according to maritime intelligence firm Kpler. Volumes were lower than the record 2.8 million barrels per day imported in July as Indian refiners scaled back some purchases.

Jaishankar said New Delhi respects Ukraine’s perspective on Russian energy, but expects India’s position to be respected as well.
The exchange comes as the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 awaits consideration by the US House of Representatives. The legislation, which cleared the Senate last month, would allow tariffs of up to 100% on the top five buyers of Russian oil and gas. Ukraine has been lobbying US lawmakers for the bill’s passage. 
Jaishankar also reiterated India’s position that a resolution will not emerge from the battlefield, saying the continuation of the conflict will only bring more death and destruction, while offering India’s help to the parties in finding a way forward. New Delhi has maintained engagement with both Moscow and Kiev.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on August 31, where he said “we have to move from endless war to the end of war, which is in humanity’s interest.” The two leaders are expected to meet again at the BRICS summit in New Delhi next week. Jaishankar’s trip was the first dedicated bilateral visit to Ukraine by an Indian external affairs minister.

The Missouri supreme court blocked a Republican-drawn new congressional map from being used in November’s midterm elections, a blow to the party’s odds for maintaining its narrow US House majority.
The ruling could save the House seat of longtime Democratic U.S. Representative Emanuel Cleaver. His Kansas City-based district had been dismantled under the redrawn map.
“Despite the cynical and deeply shameful attempt to silence many of our neighbors, the people fought back and won,” Cleaver said in a social media post on Thursday.
The decision marked a setback for Republicans in a national redistricting battle, AP reported, as Republicans had hoped Missouri’s new congressional boundaries could help them win an additional seat and hold on to their slim House majority in the midterms.
“The referendum petition was legal, sufficient, and timely, and the secretary incorrectly concluded otherwise,” the court said in its ruling. The legislation containing the new districts “did not go into effect and will not go into effect unless and until approved by the voters.”
As a result, the congressional map adopted after the 2020 census “remains in full force and effect for the November 2026 general election.”
Missouri attorney general Catherine Hanaway, a Republican, said she would immediately appeal to the US supreme court, asserting that the decision “has thrust our state into a full‑fledged constitutional crisis.”

Trump condemned the ruling in a post on Truth Social, saying it was “a Dark Day for ’Justice’ in Missouri!”.

articles.title: US military turns off ad trackers on devices amid Middle East targeting reports
articles.body:
US military turns off ad trackers on devices amid Middle East targeting reports
WASHINGTON – US military officials say they have disabled advertising trackers on a range of phones and computers, according to letters released on Sept 4 by US Senator Ron Wyden and statements given to Reuters, a development that follows reports that commercially available location data had been used to target American forces in the Middle East.
The Air Force told Wyden that it disabled the advertising identifiers on computers and mobile phones two months ago.
US Special Operations Command said in a separate letter that it had “recently” disabled them on its Windows devices.
The Army told Reuters that advertising IDs tied to mobile devices had been disabled since earlier in 2026.
Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, has pressed the Pentagon on the issue for months.
The disclosures highlight a growing national security concern: that location data collected by the advertising industry and sold by data brokers – companies that collate and resell personal data – can be used to track and target military personnel deployed to war zones.
The Air Force and Special Operations Command declined further comment.
Similar letters from the Army and Navy to Wyden said they disabled advertising IDs on military devices but gave no indication of when the restrictions were imposed.
The Army said in a statement that advertising IDs had been blocked on Windows computers “since before 2021” but that Android and Apple mobile devices had only had it disabled by default “since at least February 2026”.
Messages seeking comment from the Navy went unreturned.
The effort to reduce the location data generated by smartphones comes as military officials weigh increasingly strict restrictions on phone use overall.
In July, Reuters reported that some deployed personnel in the Middle East could be ordered to surrender their phones amid concerns that mobile videos they were posting to the internet were helping Iran target American bases in the region.
Wyden and US Representative Pat Harrigan, a North Carolina Republican, sent a letter to the Pentagon on Sept 4 asking for an investigation into whether the military had properly countered the dangers of the location data trade.
The letter included the updates from the various service branches on their efforts to disable advertising IDs on military devices.
Wyden said in a statement that it was clear that the military’s efforts “have not been effective at neutralising this threat”. Harrigan said that US enemies “should not be able to pull out a credit card and buy information that helps them track American troops”.
The Pentagon said in an e-mail it would respond to the lawmakers directly.
Mobile advertising IDs, often abbreviated MAID, are unique identifiers tied to specific devices that can be used to track a person’s activity across mobile apps and pinpoint their physical location.
Zach Edwards, co-founder of privacy ad tech company Decryptads, said that efforts to disable MAID on military-operated devices were “definitely a positive thing”.
The restrictions “will essentially ensure their location isn’t being included in bulk data sales being done by numerous vendors”, although he cautioned that personnel might still be tracked through apps in other more complicated ways, for example by triangulating technical device details with network data or location information. German police have launched an investigation into a suspected arson attack near the Munich premises of defense contractors Rohde & Schwarz and Helsing, detaining two Bulgarian nationals in connection with the incident.
Two incendiary devices were thrown from a car at a construction site around midnight on Thursday, Bavarian police said. One ignited and was extinguished by officers, while a bomb disposal team defused the second. No injuries or significant damage were reported.
Police shortly afterward detained a 28-year-old woman and a 38-year-old man, both Bulgarian citizens.
The motive remains unclear, although police noted that “several defense companies are located” at the site. Because a political motive cannot be ruled out, the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office and the Bavarian Central Office for Combating Extremism and Terrorism have taken over the investigation.
Die Welt later reported, citing a police spokesperson, that a letter claiming responsibility had appeared on a platform linked to left-wing extremists.
Several defense contractors are based near the site, including Rohde & Schwarz, which supplies radio and communications equipment to German security agencies and the military, and drone manufacturer Helsing.
Since the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in 2022, EU officials have repeatedly alleged Russian involvement in suspected sabotage and other incidents described as ‘hybrid attacks,’ although Moscow has denied responsibility and conclusive evidence has not been publicly presented.
In another high-profile case, an explosive-laden drone was discovered between Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said on Tuesday that authorities believe Russia was behind the incident.
Berlin subsequently announced the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin, along with other measures.
Moscow has rejected the allegations. Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Berlin of seeking to distract from its domestic economic problems by “planting the evidence” to implicate Russia.
Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova likewise dismissed the accusations as an “absolutely trumped-up and far-fetched” pretext for closing the Russian facilities.

articles.title: Israel says it has cleared Hezbollah fighters from tunnels under key Lebanon ridge
articles.body:
Israel says it has cleared Hezbollah fighters from tunnels under key Lebanon ridge
BEIRUT/JERUSALEM, Sept 4 - Israel's military has cleared Hezbollah fighters holed up in tunnels under the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Friday, though the Iran-backed group did not immediately comment.
Israel had said Hezbollah fighters were embedded in tunnels under the ridge, which overlooks a wide area and had become one of the most hotly contested areas in the Israel-Hezbollah war, despite a ceasefire announced in June.
Reuters reported on Thursday that Iran had warned the United States last month that it would respond forcefully to an Israeli assault on its Hezbollah allies' positions within the ridge.
"The mission was completed and the tunnels were cleared of terrorists," Katz said on social media, after a statement by the military late on Thursday saying it had operational control of the ridge.
The military said some Hezbollah fighters had been "eliminated", while others had fled.
Hezbollah did not immediately respond to a request for comment and Reuters was not able to independently verify the status of the ridge.
The Shi'ite Muslim group is believed to have built an underground command centre and weapons stores within the ridge and had said it would resist any Israeli assault.
ISRAEL RELEASES FIVE LEBANESE DETAINEES
Israel has expanded its military presence across swathes of southern Lebanon since launching a new campaign against Hezbollah in March.
On Friday, Israeli authorities transferred four people who had been detained in Israel to Lebanese authorities via the International Committee of the Red Cross.
One Lebanese man had been released earlier on Thursday. The release of the detainees is part of confidence-building measures agreed in U.S.-brokered talks between Lebanon and Israel.
Israel said on Thursday that none of the five had been found to have ties to militant groups.
A Lebanese committee advocating for Lebanese in Israeli custody says Israel has detained dozens of people inside Lebanon over the last six months. Some have been released after days or weeks, others remain in Israeli custody.
The ICRC said on Friday that it had not access to anyone in Israeli detention since October 2023.
"Many families in Lebanon are still waiting for answers about the fate of loved ones who may be detained, deceased or otherwise unaccounted for," it said.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said on Friday that those freed this week were among a "first batch", suggesting more could be coming.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Lebanon would also transfer the remains of Jewish figures killed in Lebanon in the 1980s to Israel, although there were no details of names or any timeframe. REUTERS

articles.title: Ukrainians in Indian jail involved in drone attack on Myanmar passenger plane – report
articles.body:
Ukrainians in Indian jail involved in drone attack on Myanmar passenger plane – report
Six Ukrainians and an American currently in prison in India were allegedly involved in a drone attack on a civilian aircraft in neighboring Myanmar, India’s anti-terrorism agency told a Delhi court.
The seven, described as mercenaries, were arrested by the National Investigation Agency (NIA) in March from different cities in India while trying to fly out of the country.
The Indian government “has received credible information indicating the involvement of certain Ukrainian and US nationals in a drone attack on a civilian aircraft in Myanmar,” the agency told a Delhi court on August 19 while seeking to interrogate two from the group – Ukrainian Viktor Kaminskyi and American Matthew VanDyke – in prison.
The court granted the agency permission for the interrogation. The details of the court filings were reported by the Indian Express on Friday.
The agency said 14 Ukrainians entered India on tourist visas on different dates and flew to Guwahati in the northeastern state of Assam, where they traveled to the state of Mizoram without the required permits, and entered Myanmar illegally to conduct a “pre-scheduled training on drone warfare, drone operations, assembly, and jamming technology” for ethnic armed groups fighting the military government.
Burmese news outlets reported that a drone struck an ATR-72-600 aircraft of Myanmar National Airlines, which was preparing to depart from Myitkyina Airport to Mandalay, on February 20. The plane, which carried passengers at the time of the attack, suffered damage to its nose, mid-fuselage, and tail sections. It is not clear if the NIA was referring to the same attack.
The drone was a first-person view drone (FPV) of the type that is widely used in the Ukrainian conflict. The mercenaries were arrested on March 13 after they crossed back into India.
The NIA said many of the ethnic armed groups in Myanmar are also known to support certain banned Indian insurgent groups with weapons, military hardware, and training.
The agency earlier claimed it found that several consignments of drones from Europe were delivered by the accused to individuals and groups in Mizoram. The arrested mercenaries also allegedly confessed that they were in contact with and helped in the activities of “unknown terrorists carrying AK47 rifles.”
The agency said it wants to confront Kaminskyi and VanDyke with certain witness statements to “unearth the larger conspiracy” in the case, details of the other suspects, and the masterminds of the operation.
It said data extracted from devices seized from them contained images, videos, voice samples, among other things, which have to be corroborated with direct questioning.
Soon after their arrest, Ukraine rejected “any insinuations regarding the possible involvement of the Ukrainian State in supporting terrorist activities” and demanded that India release its nationals.
VanDyke, the American, is the founder of Sons of Liberty International, which provides military training in conflict zones. He has reportedly been involved in other conflicts, including fighting with Libyan rebels in 2011.
The court in July allowed him special food items and a cook after he complained that the “spicy and oily” prison meals affected his health, but it rejected his request for treatment at a private hospital, and to communicate with his family in the US.

articles.title: Bloomberg: ‘Sanctions from hell’ bill against Russia stalls in U.S. House of Representatives
articles.body:
Bloomberg: ‘Sanctions from hell’ bill against Russia stalls in U.S. House of Representatives
A bill imposing new sanctions on Russia will likely be pushed back until after the U.S. midterm elections in November, the Bloomberg news agency reported.
The bill, which Republican Senator Lindsey Graham championed during the final year of his life, would give the U.S. president authority to impose 100% tariffs on countries that are major importers of Russian oil.
Bloomberg said the legislation, which would expand President Donald Trump’s tariff authority and risks pushing up fuel prices, is unlikely to come up for a vote ahead of the midterms.
The Senate passed the bill, dubbed the “sanctions bill from hell” bill by American media, in early August. According to Bloomberg, senators voted for it in part in memory of the late Lindsey Graham.
The measure faces less support in the House of Representatives, where Democrats worry Trump could use it as another legal basis for new import tariffs, even as tariffs he has already imposed remain under court challenge.
Big business representatives have also objected, arguing the bill would let tariffs be imposed on countries that are U.S. trade partners and allies, and warning that it “unintended consequences for consumers.”
The bill would impose 100% tariffs on five countries that are the leading buyers of Russian oil and gas. It doesn’t name the countries, but India and China are the largest purchasers of Russian energy.
